The primary purpose of developing mobility skills is to increase the difficulty of terrain that Soldiers can move in unroped while carrying packs and combat loads. This expands the range of patrolling activities without the tactical disadvantage of using rope systems for fall protection, which is any anchor clipped to a running rope used in belay systems that limits the distance a roped climber falls, should a fall occur.

heading: MOBILITY SKILLS
text: The hallmarks of individual movement skill proficiency are surefootedness and endurance. They describe a Soldier's ability to walk, scramble, and climb safely without the need for protection. Fitness is an important component in developing mobility skills. General fitness infrequently translates to high mobility skill without specific movement technique training. After sustainment, these are the most important skills to build warfighting capability in mountainous terrain.

heading: TECHNICAL ROPE SKILLS
text: Technical rope skills are necessary for units to access and move in operational terrain above level 2. Although it is seldom necessary for large units to move in such high consequence terrain, small-specialized teams can use it to provide tremendous advantage for their parent units by doing so. Snipers, reconnaissance teams, fire support teams, forward observer teams, or special operations teams can use unlikely avenues of travel located there for concealment and position themselves on points of domination, which are inaccessible to the enemy. From there, they can provide real-time intelligence to commanders, direct air assets, indirect fires, or provide overwatch for troops moving through easier terrain that is vulnerable to enemy attack. Advanced military mountaineers with technical rope skills must guide them safely through such hazardous terrain.

heading: TECHNICAL ROPE SKILLS
text: The unit requirement for personnel who are highly proficient in technical rope skills is relatively low. Technical rope skills, though complex to teach, are the lowest priority skills for units preparing to operate in mountainous terrain. This does not mean that these skills should not be taught but that other skills should be prioritized.

heading: TECHNICAL ROPE SKILLS
text: Unit training programs should focus on training most Soldiers to low or moderate (level 1) mountaineer levels of rope use proficiency, and a minority of particularly interested and capable Soldiers to high proficiency (level 2).

heading: SUSTAINMENT AND ENHANCEMENT TRAINING FOR MILITARY MOUNTAINEERS
text: Formally, qualified military mountaineers provide training to non-qualified members and require sustainment and skills advancement training. The Basic Military Mountaineer Course successfully introduces graduates to the full array of level 1 skills and techniques but is only 2-weeks long and does not fully teach them how to integrate with level 2 mountaineers to maximize a unit's mobility capability during the conduct of specific missions in mountainous terrain. The same is true for the Advanced Military Mountaineer Course. Graduates should have been exposed to all skills and techniques necessary to access all levels of terrain during military operations, but they should not be considered experienced. To be operationally capable, both levels 1 and 2 mountaineers require additional training experience fulfilling their roles and improving proficiency.

heading: Individual Training for Untrained Mountain Soldiers
text: Units with members who have experience in harsh environments and moving in steep terrain possess a significant advantage. Soldiers who are unprepared to live and move in the mountains will find it difficult to conduct combat operations there. Commanders should ensure all Soldiers in their formation are familiarized with the skills and knowledge outlined in paragraphs 2-34 through 2-40 when planning mountain operations.

heading: Individual Training for Untrained Mountain Soldiers
text: These Soldiers should be trained in foundational skills necessary for sustainment and mobility in mountainous terrain. These skills include characteristics and hazards of the mountain environment, cold-weather sustainment, basic minimalist bivouac techniques, rough terrain walking, load management, simple movement techniques, basic knot tying, and rope handling.

heading: Individual Training for Untrained Mountain Soldiers
text: Level 1 mountaineers, under the supervision of higher-level military mountaineers, should train untrained Soldiers IAW the commander's mountaineering program.

heading: Individual Training for Untrained Mountain Soldiers
text: Units should create regular opportunities for untrained mountain Soldiers to integrate sustainment and mobility skills into their tactical training events.

heading: Continued Individual Training for Level 1 Mountaineers
text: Training for level 1 mountaineers should focus on improving sustainment skills, mobility skills, low-level technical skills, and assisting level 2 mountaineers in establishing technical rope systems.

heading: Continued Individual Training for Level 1 Mountaineers
text: Level 2 mountaineers should provide technical sustainment and improvement training for level 1 mountaineers IAW the commander's mountaineering program and under the guidance of a level 3 mountaineer.

heading: Continued Individual Training for Level 1 Mountaineers
text: Units should create regular opportunities for level 1 mountaineers to integrate sustainment and mobility skills into their tactical training events. Examples are incorporating low-angle CASEVAC scenarios in rough terrain or using simple fixed lines to help squad movement on steep slopes into platoon situational training exercises.

heading: Continued Individual Training for Level 2 Mountaineers
text: Typically, level 2 mountaineers should be provided the time and resources to conduct sustainment and improvement training. This training should be planned and conducted under the guidance and supervision of level 3 mountaineers. Optimally, periodic, high-commitment mountain training events should be planned for level 2 and led by level 3 mountaineers. All training for level 2 mountaineers should focus on building experience in those skills that the commander determines necessary to perform operationally. In the absence of specific mission-essential task list tasks to focus on, level 2 training should concentrate on route selection, sharpening mobility skills, and climbing protective techniques in 5th-class terrain, leading small groups in 4th-class terrain, and conducting technical rescue training. These should be conducted in both summer and winter environmental conditions.

heading: Shadowing
text: Whenever possible, level 2 mountaineers should participate in providing formal mountaineering training by shadowing or by being an assistant instructor for the Basic Military Mountaineer Course or Advanced Military Mountaineer Course. Opportunities to do so can be coordinated through the Army Mountain Warfare School in Vermont, the Northern Warfare Training Center in Alaska, and the 5th Ranger Training Battalion in Georgia. Participating in formal mountaineering training programs ensures level 2 mountaineers are exposed to current techniques and training safety measures, provides experience with developing training programs, and helps prepare them for level 3 qualification and responsibilities.

heading: Vertical Danger Area Ascent or Descent
text: Units should occasionally create opportunities for level 2 mountaineers to integrate higher technical skills into tactical training events, such as a vertical danger area (VDA) ascent or descent task. A vertical danger area is steep terrain that significantly restricts a unit's ability to maneuver, thereby putting the unit at significant tactical disadvantage should enemy contact be made while moving through the VDA. As units integrate linear danger area crossings into a field training exercise or live-fire exercise, they can also integrate a VDA ascent or descent task into a squad training lane. Training employs a unit's level 2 mountaineers, refreshes level 1 tasks, and adds a level of realism and rigor to an otherwise normal squad situational training exercise lane.

heading: Continued Individual Training for Level 3 Mountaineers
text: Even the most accomplished mountaineers require periodic sustainment training. Most often, this can be accomplished by participating in level 2 training. However, new mountaineering techniques are regularly developed, so whenever possible, level 3 mountaineers should undergo specialty training that is focused on increasing unit capability IAW the commander's intent. Additional training in mountain rescue operations and avalanche forecasting may be particularly useful to units anticipating operations in more committing mountainous terrain. Opportunities exist for this at Army mountain training centers or through appropriately certified civilian mountaineering training organizations. This page intentionally left blank.

heading: Environmental Injuries
text: Operations in mountainous areas will expose Soldiers to a variety of harsh environmental conditions not found in lowland areas. Soldiers exposed to these conditions are at a heightened risk of becoming a casualty. This risk increases with lack of experience and training. Troops conducting operations in mountainous regions often encounter cold temperatures that can degrade physical performance, impact morale, and create cold-weather casualties. The lack of oxygen in high-altitude environments impairs many aspects of normal Soldier tasks. Soldiers may develop altitude illnesses that can produce debilitating symptoms and require immediate MEDEVAC. If not accounted for in the planning process, these conditions will negatively impact the mission. Soldiers will become fatigued sooner in this environment and must reduce their pace or lighten their load to remain healthy and effective. With experience and proper training, Soldiers will become more durable and lethal in this environment.

heading: SECTION I - ENVIRONMENTAL INJURY PREVENTION
text: Units operating in mountainous regions are exposed to various types of injuries and illnesses unassociated with other areas. Medical considerations are like those for other environments; however, there are some unique aspects of mountain operations to consider to provide effective support.

heading: ILLNESSES AND INJURIES
text: Most injuries in the mountain environment are orthopedic and soft-tissue injuries. These include sprains, strains, abrasions, contusions, and fractures. Skills in basic first aid are essential to all Soldiers operating in the mountains and should be reinforced with regular sustainment training. (See TB MED 505 for more information.) Medical personnel should receive training in identifying and treating these prior to deployment.

heading: TREATMENT AND EVACUATION
text: In harsh mountain weather, the most important course of action is to provide injured Soldiers with medical aid as soon as possible. Immediate first aid is given on site. Due to rough terrain, medical units can seldom reach unit aid stations by vehicle to evacuate casualties. Litter bearers must move casualties to the rear where they can be evacuated by ground or air to clearing stations. The victim must be protected from the weather and shock during transportation. Rendezvous points are coordinated with medical units as far forward as possible. All litter bearers must receive training in evacuation techniques and first aid. Lightly wounded personnel may need assistance to move over rough terrain. (See chapter 15 for CASEVAC TTP in mountainous terrain.)

heading: INJURIES RELATED TO COLD EXPOSURE
text: There are several common injuries associated with cold temperature exposure. Some are more commonly associated with hot weather but present just as serious a threat in cold conditions.

heading: DEHYDRATION
text: Dehydration is the loss of bodily fluids that prevents or slows normal bodily functions. This is usually caused by overexertion and improper water intake. Although the mechanism that causes dehydration is not specifically cold temperatures, the environment and the body's natural response to the cold often lead to Soldiers becoming dehydrated. Dehydration precedes all cold-weather injuries and is a major symptom of acute mountain sickness (AMS). Dehydration contributes to poor performance in all physical activities, even more so than lack of food. Cold-weather requirements for water are no different from in the desert. In fact, they may exceed desert requirements because of the increased difficulty in moving with extra clothing and through the snow. At high altitudes, the air is dry. Combined with a rapid rate of breathing, as much as 2 liters of liquid may be lost each day through respiration. A Soldier needs about 3 to 6 liters of water each day to prevent dehydration when living and performing physical labor in a cold or mountainous environment. Leaders should monitor their Soldiers' water intake, since motivation to drink cold water in a cold environment is low. Coffee and tea are diuretics and cause excessive urination, which contributes to dehydration. They should be avoided. However, providing other noncaffeinated hot liquids is a good way to encourage Soldiers to drink more water. The adequacy of liquid intake can best be judged by the color of urine and volume. Dark, amber-colored urine instead of light yellow or the absence of a need to urinate upon awakening from a night's sleep is an indicator of dehydration. Thirst is not a good indicator of hydration.

heading: Contributing Factors
text:
Factors that contribute to dehydration in cold weather are--
- The thirst mechanism does not function properly in cold weather.
- Water is often inconvenient to obtain and purify.
- The air in cold climates and at high altitudes lacks moisture.
- Cold causes frequent urination.

heading: Symptoms
text: Symptoms of dehydration include darkening urine, decreased amounts of urine being produced, dry mouth, tiredness, mental sluggishness, lack of appetite, headache, fainting, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, higher temperature, upset stomach, and unconsciousness. The symptoms of dehydration resemble those of hypothermia. To distinguish between them, open the victim's clothes and feel the stomach. If the stomach is cold, the victim is probably hypothermic; if it is warm, the victim is probably dehydrated. However, this test is inconclusive since cold-weather dehydration can also lead to total body cooling. The cold environment may act as a diuretic and impair the body's ability to conserve fluids. Cold diuresis is an increase in urine output, which is the body's response to cold-weather immersion. This can contribute to dehydration, which is the precursor to several other cold-weather injuries, both freezing and non-freezing.

heading: Treatment
text: Prevent dehydration by consuming 3 to 6 liters of fluids each day (forced drinking in the absence of thirst is mandatory) and avoid caffeine and alcohol. Keep the victim warm and treat them for shock. In advanced cases, administer fluids by mouth if the victim is conscious. Ingesting snow will contribute to loss of body heat. Allow the victim to rest. If the victim fails to improve within 1 hour or is unconscious, evacuate to a medical facility immediately.

heading: HEAT INJURIES
text: Heat injuries, although associated with hot weather, can occur in cold-weather environments. Planning, periodically inspecting personnel clothing (ventilation) and equipment, balancing water and food intake, and resting can prevent most heat injuries.

heading: Heat Cramps
text: Heat cramps are muscle spasms that result from loss of large amounts of salt and water through exertion. Heat cramps are caused by an accumulation of lactic acid in the muscles and a loss of salt through perspiration.

heading: Contributing Factor
text: Strenuous exertion causes the body to rise in temperature and to produce heavy perspiration.

heading: Symptoms
text: Symptoms of heat cramps include pain and cramping in the arms, legs, back, and stomach. Victims sweat profusely and cannot quench their thirst.

heading: Treatment
text: Have the victim rest in a cool, shady area, breathe deeply, and stretch the cramped muscle as soon as possible to obtain relief. Loosen the victim's clothing and provide cool water to drink. Monitor the victim's condition and seek medical attention if pain and cramps continue.

heading: Heat Exhaustion
text: Heat exhaustion is rapid water and salt depletion that can occur after exposure to high temperatures or intense exertion. It is often accompanied by dehydration. Heat exhaustion may occur when Soldiers exert themselves in any environment and overheat. The blood vessels in the skin become so dilated that they reduce blood flow to the brain and other organs.

heading: Contributing Factors
text: Factors that contribute to heat exhaustion are strenuous activity in hot areas, troops that are not acclimated, inappropriate diet, and insufficient water or rest.

heading: Symptoms
text: Symptoms of heat exhaustion may resemble fainting but may also include weakness, dizziness, confusion, headache, cold clammy skin, and nausea. The victim may also have a rapid but weak pulse.

heading: Treatment
text: Move the victim to a cool, shady area and loosen clothing and boots. Have the victim drink water and, if possible, and if weather conditions are conducive, immerse the victim's body in water to aid in cooling. Elevate the victim's legs to help restore proper circulation. Monitor the victim's condition, and seek medical attention if symptoms persist. Without proper intervention, heat exhaustion can lead to heat stroke.

heading: Heat Stroke
text: Heat stroke occurs when the core body temperature exceeds 104 degrees F, commonly a result of prolonged exposure to or physical exertion at higher temperatures. Heat stroke is a life-threatening situation caused by overexposure to the sun. The body is so depleted of liquids that its internal cooling mechanisms fail to function.

heading: Contributing Factors
text: Factors that contribute to heat stroke are prolonged exposure to direct sunlight, overexertion, dehydration, and depletion of electrolytes.

heading: Symptoms
text: Symptoms of heat stroke include hot, dry skin; dizziness; confusion and incoherency; headache; nausea; seizures; breathing difficulty; a slow pulse; and loss of consciousness.

heading: Treatment
text: Cool the victim immediately and restore breathing and circulation. If the victim is conscious, administer water. If possible, and if weather conditions are conducive, submerge the victim in water to reduce temperature, treat for shock, and prepare for immediate evacuation.

heading: SOLAR INJURIES
text: Solar injuries can happen in warm or cold weather. These types of injuries can be just as incapacitating as most other injuries but usually are not fatal. Peak hours of ultraviolet (UV) radiation are between the hours of 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. Because of the long wavelengths of UV light, cloudy days can be more dangerous than sunny days. On sunny days, the Soldier takes more care due to the bright conditions. On cloudy days, the Soldier tends not to wear sunglasses or sunscreen.

heading: Sunburn
text: Excessive UV radiation from sunlight is a serious threat to military personnel operating in high mountain regions during daylight hours because of several factors increasing its damaging potential. UV exposure can cause significant short-term disability to military personnel through severe sunburn.

heading: Contributing Factors
text: Decreased UV filtering by the thinner atmosphere at high altitude causes an increased intensity of exposure (approximately 4 percent for every 1,000 feet of elevation increase) and a shift of the UV spectrum to more harmful short wavelengths. Reflection from snow and ice increases the intensity of exposure (approximately 75 percent of incident radiation is reflected). Soldiers vary greatly in their risk of sunburn based on their skin type and pigment.

heading: Symptoms
text: Symptoms of sunburn are painful, burning, red, or blistered skin with slight swelling. The skin may be warm to the touch. In severe cases, chills, fever, and headaches may occur.

heading: Treatment
text: Limiting skin exposure with clothes and sunscreen (sun protection factor 15 and above) will prevent most sunburns. Applying to skin areas that are normally shaded, such as the eyelids and under the chin, is necessary to reduce the likelihood of sunburn from light reflected off snow and rocks. Opaque agents, such as zinc oxide, red veterinary petrolatum, or titanium dioxide; can be used for high-risk body areas, such as the nose, lips, and tops of the ears. The agents should be used carefully in a tactical situation where they could make a Soldier more visible to opposing forces. Diagnosis, prevention, treatment, and prognosis of solar radiation injuries are the same as at low altitude. (See TB MED 505.)

heading: Snow Blindness
text: Snow blindness results when solar radiation "sunburns" the eyes. Snow blindness can occur in a few hours of exposure, and there is no sensation of abnormality other than brightness as a warning that eye damage is occurring.

heading: Snow Blindness
text: Using eyewear or goggles that block more than 90 percent of UV radiation will help prevent snow blindness. To prevent injury from reflected light, protective eyewear should have side shields. Additionally, eyewear should have a safety cord or strap to prevent it from being lost accidentally. If sunglasses are not available, opaque eye covering (for example, tape-covered eyeglasses) with narrow, horizontal slits provide adequate field-expedient eye protection.

heading: Symptoms
text: Eyes may feel painful and gritty, and there may be tearing, blurred vision, severe light sensitivity, and headache. Symptoms are worst for 6 to 8 hours after exposure and resolve in 48 to 72 hours.

heading: Treatment
text: Treating snow blindness involves patching the eye and controlling the pain. Cool compresses over the eyes help alleviate some discomfort. Dilating the pupil and using ocular antibiotics are helpful. Pain control may require oral analgesics, sedatives, or both. The prognosis is generally good, although snow blindness may take several days to resolve. The pain and visual decrements will require temporary, but significant, duty limitations. In severe cases, permanent damage can occur.

heading: BLISTERS
text: Blisters often only cause minor discomfort but can become severe enough to restrict a person's physical activity and mobility temporarily. In some cases, friction blisters have developed into serious complications and infections requiring antibiotics and medical treatment. As one of the most common injuries to the military mountaineer, blisters present a notable adverse impact to mobility and mission readiness.

heading: Contributing Factors
text: Rough and sloped terrain increases friction generated between the skin and footwear during foot movements, leading to a higher incidence of blister development.

heading: Symptoms
text: Blisters are raised, painful, fluid-filled protrusions.

heading: Treatment
text: Before a blister forms or when a Soldier first notices one, cover a hotspot with moleskin (over the area and beyond it). Use tincture benzoin to help the moleskin adhere to and toughen the skin. Once a blister has formed, cover it with a dressing large enough to fit over the blister, and then tape it. Never drain blisters unless they are surrounded by redness or if draining pus indicates infection. If this occurs, drain the blister from the side with a clean, sterile needle. After cleaning with soap and water, gently press out the fluid, leaving the skin intact. Make a doughnut of moleskin to go around the blister and apply to the skin. For toe blisters, wrap the entire toe with adhesive tape over the moleskin. (Toenails should be trimmed straight across the top, leaving a 90 degrees angle on the sides. This provides an arch, so the corners do not irritate the skin.)

heading: CARBON MONOXIDE POISONING
text: This is the replacement of oxygen in the blood with carbon monoxide, preventing adequate oxygenation of cells in the body.

heading: Contributing Factor
text: A contributing factor is inhaling fumes from burning fuel, such as fires, stoves, heaters, and running engines, without proper ventilation.

heading: Symptoms
text: Symptoms are like other common illnesses and include headaches, fatigue, excessive yawning, nausea, dizziness, drowsiness, confusion, and unconsciousness. Death may occur. Three visible symptoms are bright red lips, mouth, and inside of the eyelids.

heading: Treatment
text: Remove the victim from the source of contamination; administer oxygen, if available; and evacuate to a medical facility. Severe complications may develop even in casualties who appear to have recovered. If the victim is unconscious, administer rescue breathing and cardio-pulmonary resuscitation (CPR) as needed.

heading: COLD-WEATHER CONSIDERATIONS
text: Military mountain operations can occur in the coldest weather and with minimal logistical support, leaving troops under-equipped for hostile conditions. Individuals in these situations must rely on their prior training and strong leadership in cold stress management. This training can determine whether the mission will succeed or fail with either few or high casualty rates. Individuals in these situations often are not fully prepared, and, consequently, unit commanders and trainers must actively plan to prevent cold casualties. Soldiers need to be confident that they can master the environment by using preventive measures. Lessons learned from previous cold-weather deployments must be emphasized. Leaders must learn their unit's capabilities and manage cold exposure relative to the provided guidance. Soldiers must be prepared to survive, move, and fight in winter conditions. Intense cold affects the mind as well as the body. Simple tasks take longer to perform and take more effort than in a temperate climate. When weather conditions become extreme, the problems of survival become more significant. Warmth and comfort become top priorities. The effects of extreme cold and the probability of injury are magnified by a lack of proper diet and sleep. The most important measure in preventing cold-weather injuries is the education of personnel and their leaders.

heading: TYPES
text: Cold injuries may be divided into two types: freezing and non-freezing. The freezing type is known as frostbite. The nonfreezing type includes hypothermia, chilblain, and immersion foot. Cold injuries result from impaired circulation and from cold and ice forming upon the tissues of the body. Temperature alone is not a reliable guide as to whether a cold injury can occur. Low temperatures are necessary for cold injuries to occur, but freezing temperatures are not. Wind speed can accelerate body heat loss under both wet and cold conditions.

heading: PREVENTATIVE MEASURES
text:
Commanders should ensure the following measures are taken to prevent cold-weather injuries:
- Soldiers' uniforms are kept as dry as possible and are protected from the elements.
- Soldiers are educated on proper use of clothing systems to avoid the effects of overheating and perspiration (layer dressing and ventilation).
- The buddy system is used to watch for early signs of cold-weather injuries.
- All Soldiers waterproof their equipment.
- The rate of movement should be slow, deliberate, and careful. Soldiers should not move out at a force march pace and then be stationary after they have perspired heavily. Soldiers should not wear excessive cold-weather clothing while moving.

heading: RISK FACTORS
text: Several demographic, behavioral, and past history characteristics increase risk for cold-weather injuries.

heading: Body Composition
text: Individuals with a high amount of body surface area relative to their body mass (long and lean) lose more body heat in the cold than individuals with a small surface area relative to their body weight (short and stocky) do. The reason for this is that the principal means of heat loss in the cold is at the skin surface. This effect is somewhat reduced in short, stocky people because a large body mass maintains a constant temperature better than a small body mass.

heading: Sex
text: The peripheral (for example, hands and feet) cold-injury rate for female Soldiers is two times higher than the rate for males. Sex differences during cold exposure are almost entirely attributable to women's generally greater body fat content and thicker fat layer under the skin compared to men of comparable age and weight. Women typically have a greater surface area but smaller total body mass (thus lower total body heat content) than men do.

heading: Race
text: African-American male and female Soldiers are two to four times more likely to suffer a cold-weather injury versus their Caucasian counterparts. This increased risk is consistent across all career management fields, which suggests that occupational exposure does not account for the differences between African-Americans and Caucasians. Differences between races may be due to cold-weather experience, but more likely they are due to anthropomorphic considerations (longer, thinner digits) and perhaps greater surface-area-to-mass ratio.

heading: Fitness and Training
text: Overall, physical training and fitness levels appear to have only minor influences on cold management. Fitter individuals can sustain more physical activity at a higher intensity and longer duration; therefore, they produce more heat from exercise for longer periods when compared to less fit individuals.

heading: Fatigue
text: Physical fatigue can impair shivering and peripheral vasoconstriction responses during cold exposure. Therefore, physical fatigue can increase the Soldier's risk for hypothermia. Fatigued Soldiers cannot sustain sufficient activity levels to maintain body temperature during severe cold exposure.

heading: Age
text: Soldiers who are 45 years of age or older may be less cold tolerant than younger people, either because of a decline in physical fitness or because of reduced vasoconstriction and heat conservation in comparison to their younger counterparts.

heading: Dehydration
text: Dehydration can increase susceptibility to cold injury by decreasing the ability to sustain physical activity (particularly if accompanied by heat stress from exercising in heavy clothing) and, therefore, decreasing the ability to sustain thermal balance. In addition, dehydration might impair cognitive function and cause Soldiers to use poor judgment. Dehydration has not been shown to reduce peripheral skin temperatures and does not impair shivering.

heading: Sustained Operations
text: Exertional fatigue, sleep restriction, and underfeeding are common stressors during sustained operations and together impair a Soldier's ability to maintain thermal balance in the cold. The metabolic heat production response degrades and impairs the ability to sustain exercise performance. Soldiers engaged in sustained operations also may make more judgment errors when tired and increase their exposure and risk of injury. A given cold stressor is more likely to induce cold injury after a long period of sustained operations compared to earlier in the operation. This emphasizes the need for planned rest, sleep, feeding, and recovery before conducting stressful operations in the cold.

heading: Food and Nutrient Consumption
text: Consuming too little nutrients can result in hypoglycemia (low blood sugar), which can impair shivering. Hypoglycemia contributes to an inability to sustain physical activity and the associated exercise-induced heat production during cold exposure. No food for 48 hours, even in the absence of hypoglycemia, results in an impaired ability to shiver and increased risk of hypothermia.

heading: Alcohol
text: Although alcohol may impart a sense of warmth, any peripheral vasodilation increases heat loss and the risk of hypothermia. Alcohol can cause hypoglycemia, which will decrease shivering responses and the ability to sustain physical work. In addition, alcohol blunts the senses and impairs judgment, so the Soldier may not feel the signs and symptoms of a developing cold injury. Soldiers must not consume alcohol while exposed to cold weather.

heading: Nicotine
text: Smoking or chewing tobacco can increase susceptibility to frostbite by increasing vasoconstriction in the periphery (for example, the hands). Heavy smokers (two to three packs per day) have a 30-percent higher incidence of peripheral cold injury, perhaps because nicotine reduces the body's response to the cold. Smoking and chewing will be discouraged during cold-weather operations.

heading: Previous Cold Injuries
text: If Soldiers have had previous cold injuries, they are at higher risk for subsequent cold injuries.

heading: Associated Injury
text: Injuries resulting in shock or blood loss reduce blood flow to extremities and may increase the injured individual's susceptibility to cold injury, which, in turn, can accelerate shock.

heading: COLD-WEATHER INJURIES
text: A cold-weather injury is any preventable injury resulting from exposure to cold environmental conditions. Some of the most common nonfreezing cold-weather injuries are described in paragraphs 3-57 through 3-75.

heading: Hypothermia
text: Hypothermia is the lowering of the body core temperature at a rate faster than the body can produce heat. Hypothermia may be caused by exposure or by sudden wetting of the body, such as falling into a lake or being sprayed with fuel or other liquid. Hypothermia can occur even on moderate days with temperatures of 40 degrees F to 50 degrees F with little precipitation if heat loss exceeds heat gain, and the Soldier's condition can deteriorate. Hypothermia is classified as mild (core temperature above 90 degrees F or 32 degrees Celsius [C]) or severe (core temperature below 90 degrees F or 32 degrees C). An individual is considered "clinically hypothermic" when their core temperature is less than or equal to 95 degrees F.

heading: Hypothermia
text:
Methods of heat loss:
- Radiation--direct heat loss from the body to its surrounding atmosphere is called radiation heat loss. The head can radiate up to 80 percent of the total body heat output. On cold days, personnel must keep all extremities covered to retain heat. Heat loss from extremities accounts for the largest amount of heat lost from the body.
- Conduction--direct transfer of heat from one object in contact with another (being rained on or sitting in snow).
- Convection--loss of heat due to moving air or water in contact with the skin. Wind chill is convection cooling. Clothing that ventilates, insulates, and protects must control the layer of warm air next to the skin.
- Evaporation--evaporation of perspiration causes heat loss. Wet clothing can cause heat loss by conduction and evaporation. Dressing in layers allows Soldiers to remove or add clothing as needed.
- Respiration--when cold air is inhaled, the air is warmed, then exhaled, resulting in a significant source of heat loss.

heading: Contributing Factors
text:
Factors that contribute to hypothermia are--
- Dehydration.
- Poor nutrition.
- Diarrhea.
- Decreased physical activity.
- Accidental immersion in water.
- Change in weather.
- High winds.
- Inadequate types or amounts of clothing.

heading: Symptoms
text:
Body temperature refers to the core (rectal) temperature. Symptoms become progressively worse as the body temperature drops.
- 96 degrees F:
- Shivering (begins about 2 degrees below normal body temperature).
- Uncontrollable shivering (about 96 degrees F).
- Inability to care for self.
- Clumsiness (stumbling or falling).
- Slow reactions.
- Mental confusion.
- Difficulty speaking.
- 95 degrees F to 90 degrees F:
- Sluggish thinking.
- Irrational thought.
- Apathy.
- False sense of warmth.
- Cold skin.
- Pale or bluish skin.
- Inability to perform simple tasks.
- Amnesia.
- Hallucinations.
- Decreased heart and respiratory rate.
- Weak pulse.
- Dilated pupils.
- Slurred speech.
- Visual disturbance.
- 90 degrees F to 85 degrees F. Shivering may stop. In addition, a Soldier may experience--
- Irrationality.
- Incoherence.
- Loss of contact with the environment.
- Muscular rigidity.
- Disorientation.
- Exhaustion.
- 85 degrees F and below:
- Muscle rigidity.
- Unconsciousness.
- Comatose state.
- Faint vital signs.
- Faint or impalpable pulse.
- Breathing possibly too shallow to observe.

heading: Prevention
text: Prevent hypothermia by using the buddy system to watch each other for symptoms and consume adequate amounts of liquids, rest, and eat properly.

heading: Avoidance
text: Hypothermia can be avoided by dressing in layers, which permits easy additions or removal to prevent overheating, becoming too cold, or getting wet or windblown. If Soldiers are in a situation that precludes staying warm and dry, they should seek shelter. Eating sugary foods and physical activity helps to produce body heat.

heading: Treatment
text: Treatment methods vary based on the severity of the hypothermia. Mild cases--if Soldiers show symptoms of hypothermia, prevent additional heat loss by getting them into a shelter, if available; removing wet clothing; and replacing it with dry, insulated clothing. If they are capable, feed Soldiers fast energy food and hot liquids and increase their physical activity level to generate heat. If they are unable to move, insulate them from the ground, and consider directing warm Soldiers to share a sleeping bag (cover head) with injured Soldiers to transfer body heat. This method of warming can compromise warmer Soldiers' core temperatures as well if they are not sufficiently fed, warm, and healthy. Make a diagnosis (for example, by obtaining a rectal temperature). Rehydrate the Soldier with warm liquids, sweets, and food. If the tactical situation allows, build a fire. Above all else, keep Soldiers conscious until their vital signs are normal, and seek medical assistance.

heading: Treatment
text: Severe cases--if the victim is unconscious or appears dead without any obvious injury, prevent further heat loss. Avoid rapidly rewarming an unconscious victim, which can create problems. Evacuating as soon as possible is preferable. At all times, the victim should be handled gently so as not to cause the cold blood from the extremities to rush to the heart. Immediately transport the victim to the nearest medical facility. Field reheating is not effective and may be hazardous. Provide artificial respiration if breathing stops. If no pulse is detectable, be aware that in hypothermia there is often effective circulation for the victim's hypothermic state. In such a case, cardiac compression (such as CPR) may be fatal. The exception is acute hypothermia with near drowning.

heading: Treatment
text:
Use the following treatment methods based on the severity of the victim's hyperthermia:
- Breathing warm, moist air is the fastest way to warm the inside of the body. If breathing steam is not possible, place tubing under the rescuer's shirt so the victim will still breathe warm, moist air. This process can be done while on the move. In addition to breathing moist, warm air, the victim must be gradually rewarmed using external heat sources. Padded hot water bottles or heated stones should be placed in the armpits.
- If conscious, the victim can be given warm, sugary drinks.
- All bodily systems in hypothermia are brittle so treat the victim gently. While making these attempts, try to evacuate the victim. Severe complications may arise as the body temperature rises, which may result in cardiac arrest even though the victim seems to be doing well.

heading: Immersion or Trench Foot
text: The circulatory and nervous systems of the feet are damaged from prolonged exposure to cold and wet at above freezing temperatures. This can happen wearing boots or not. A Soldier may not feel symptoms until the injury has already begun.

heading: Contributing Factors
text:
Factors that contribute to immersion or trench foot are--
- Stepping into water that comes over the boot tops.
- Not changing socks often enough.
- Improper hygiene.
- Prolonged exposure (3 to 5 days).

heading: Symptoms
text: Symptoms of immersion or trench foot include the sensation of tingling, numbness, and then pain. The toes are pale and feel cold and stiff. The skin is wet and soggy with the color turning from red to bright red, progressing to pale and mottled, and then grayish blue. As symptoms progress and damage appear, the skin becomes red and then bluish or black. Swelling may occur. Because the early stages of trench foot are not painful, Soldiers must be constantly aware to prevent it.

heading: Treatment
text: To prevent this condition, keep the feet dry and clean. Change socks often, drying the insides of boots, massaging the feet, and using foot powder. Drying the feet for 24 hours usually heals mild cases. Moderate cases usually heal within 3 to 5 days. The feet should be handled gently?not rubbed or massaged. They should be cleaned with soap and water, dried, elevated, and exposed to room temperature. Victims must stay off their feet and seek medical attention. Severe cases, when feet are not allowed to dry, are evacuated as a litter casualty.

heading: Chilblain
text: Chilblain (also known as pernio or kibe) is a superficial cold injury typically occurring after approximately 1 to 5 hours in cold-wet conditions, at temperatures below 50 degrees F. A discolored rash or small red spots may appear on the skin, most often on the fingers but can commonly occur on the ears, face, and exposed skin. The lesions are swollen, tender, itchy, and painful. Upon rewarming, the skin becomes inflamed, red, and hot to the touch, and swollen with an itching or burning sensation that may continue for several hours after exposure.

heading: Frostbite
text: Frostbite is the freezing or crystallization of living tissues due to heat being lost faster than it can be replaced by blood circulation or from direct exposure to extreme cold or high winds. Exposure time can be minutes or instantaneous. The extremities are usually the first to be affected. Damp hands and feet may freeze quickly since moisture conducts heat away from the body and destroys the insulating value of clothing. Heat loss is compounded with intense cold and inactivity. Frostbite can be prevented with properly maintained and used clothing and equipment. The extent of frostbite depends on temperature and duration of exposure. Frostbite is one of the major nonfatal cold-weather injuries encountered in military operations but does not occur above an ambient temperature of 32 degrees F.

heading: Categories of Frostbite
text: Superficial (mild) frostbite involves only the skin. The layer immediately below usually appears white to grayish with the surface feeling hard, but the underlying tissue is soft. Deep (severe) frostbite extends beyond the first layer of skin and may include the bone. Discoloration continues from gray to black, and the texture becomes hard as the tissue freezes deeper. This condition requires immediate evacuation to a medical facility.

heading: Contributing Factors
text:
Factors that contribute to frostbite are--
- Dehydration.
- Below-freezing temperatures.
- Skin contact with super cooled metals or liquids.
- Use of caffeine, tobacco, or alcohol.
- Neglect.

heading: Symptoms
text: Symptoms of frostbite vary and may include a cold feeling, pain, burning, numbness, and, in the final stages, a false sense of warmth. The skin first turns red, then pale. The skin may be bluish in color and then may appear frosty or waxy white. The skin may feel hard, be immovable over the joints and bony prominences, or be frozen. Identifying deep versus superficial frostbite is difficult to determine and often requires 3 to 7 days after rewarming for medical personnel to diagnose. Blisters, swelling, and pain may occur after thawing.

heading: Treatment
text:
Using the buddy system is one of the primary ways to prevent frostbite. Buddies must watch each other for symptoms of frostbite and provide mutual aid if frostbite occurs. Frostbite should be identified early with prompt first aid care applied to prevent further damage:
- Treat early signs of frostbite by rewarming with skin-to-skin contact or by sheltering the body part under the clothing next to the body. Do this immediately. If tissues have frozen, evacuate the victim before they thaw. If the feet are involved, evacuate the victim as a litter patient.
- Thawing of a frostbitten victim is a hospital procedure. If the victim has frostbite with frozen extremities, protect the frozen parts and evacuate as a litter patient.
- If frostbite is not recognized before it thaws, do not let the area re-freeze since this causes more damage. The most often affected body parts are the hands, fingers, toes, feet, ears, chin, and nose. If evacuating victims as a litter case is not possible and the body part has not yet thawed, have the victims walk out on their own. Walking out on frozen feet is better than having them thaw and refreeze. Self-evacuation may be tactically necessary. Walking on frozen feet does less harm than walking on thawed feet.
- If reheating is inevitable, do not overheat the affected body parts near flame; the warming temperature should not be greater than normal body temperature. Do not rub the parts; the crystallized tissues may break internally and cause more damage. Do not pop blisters; cover them with a dry, sterile dressing. Keep the victim warm (apply loose, bulky bandages to separate toes and fingers).
- Once a part is rewarmed, it will become painful. Pain may be managed with narcotic analgesics.
- Once the foot is rewarmed, it will swell and putting the boot back on will not be possible.

heading: SECTION II - ALTITUDE EFFECTS, INJURIES, AND ACCLIMATIZATION
text: As altitude increases, the overall atmospheric pressure decreases. Decreased pressure is the underlying source of altitude illnesses. Whether at sea level or 20,000 feet, the surrounding atmosphere has the same percentage of oxygen. As pressure decreases, the body has a much more difficult time passing oxygen from the lungs to the red blood cells and thus to body tissues. This lower pressure means lower oxygen levels in the blood and increased carbon dioxide levels.

heading: ACCLIMATIZATION
text:
When the unit arrives at an operation area, all personnel require a period of conditioning and acclimatization. The schedule should allow for longer and more frequent periods of rest. The rigors of establishing an assembly area exhaust most personnel who are not acclimated. Water, food, and rest should be considered priorities, ensuring enough while individual metabolisms and bodies become accustomed to functioning at higher elevations. Since the acclimatization process cannot be shortened, and the absence of acclimatization hampers the successful execution of operations, planning for deployments to higher elevations should consider the following:
- Above 8,000 feet, a unit should ascend at a rate of 1,000 to 2,000 feet per day. Units can leapfrog, taking extended rest periods.
- Units should not resort to using pharmaceutical pretreatment with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, such as acetazolamide. These drugs have side effects that mimic the signs and symptoms of AMS. Inexperienced medics may have difficulty recognizing the differences between the side effects of the drug and a condition that could possibly be life threatening. Additionally, these drugs are diuretics, which results in higher hydration levels (at least 25-percent increase per Soldier per day). These higher hydration levels create a larger logistical demand on the unit by requiring more water, more time to acquire water, more water purification supplies, and, if in a winter environment, more fuels for melting snow and ice for water.
- Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, such as acetazolamide, are effective in treating mild and severe AMS. These drugs should accompany attached medical personnel because they can treat the Soldier suffering from AMS and, although rest may be required, evacuation may not be needed.
- Do not move troops directly to high altitudes even if allowances can be made for inactivity for the first 3 to 5 days before mission commitment. Moving troops directly to high altitude can increase the probability of altitude sickness. Even if inactivity follows deployment, the incidence of altitude sickness is more likely than with a gradual ascent.

heading: ACUTE MOUNTAIN SICKNESS
text: AMS is the body's response to physical distress from difficulty adjusting to lower oxygen levels at high altitude. AMS is a temporary illness that can affect any Soldier, regardless of mountaineering experience. Soldiers are subject to this sickness at altitudes as low as 5,000 feet. Incidence and severity increase with altitude and when quickly transported to high altitudes. Disability and ineffectiveness can occur in 50 to 80 percent of the troops who are rapidly brought to altitudes above 10,000 feet. At lower altitudes, or where ascent to altitudes is gradual, most personnel can complete assignments with moderate effectiveness and little discomfort.

heading: ACUTE MOUNTAIN SICKNESS
text: Personnel arriving at moderate elevations (5,000 to 8,000 feet) usually feel well for the first few hours; a feeling of exhilaration or well-being is typical. There may be an initial awareness of breathlessness upon exertion and a need for frequent pauses to rest. Irregular breathing can occur, mainly during sleep; these changes may cause apprehension. Severe symptoms--such as nausea, sluggishness, fatigue, headache, dizziness, insomnia, depression, uncaring attitude, rapid and labored breathing, weakness, and loss of appetite--may begin 4 to 12 hours after arriving at higher altitudes.

heading: ACUTE MOUNTAIN SICKNESS
text: A headache is the most noticeable symptom of AMS and may be severe. Even when a headache is not present, some loss of appetite and a decrease in tolerance for food occurs. Nausea, even without food intake, occurs and leads to less food intake. Vomiting may occur and contribute to dehydration. Despite fatigue, personnel are unable to sleep. The symptoms usually develop and peak by the second day. They gradually subside over the next several days so that the total course of AMS may extend from 5 to 7 days. In some instances, the headache may become incapacitating, and the Soldier should be evacuated to a lower elevation.

heading: ACUTE MOUNTAIN SICKNESS
text:
Treatment for AMS includes the following:
- Oral pain medications, such as ibuprofen or aspirin.
- Rest.
- Frequent consumption of liquids and light foods in small amounts.
- Movement to lower altitudes (at least 1,000 feet lower) to alleviate symptoms, which provides for a more gradual acclimatization.
- Realization of physical limitations and slow progression.
- Practice of deep-breathing exercises.
- Use of acetazolamide in the first 24 hours for mild to moderate cases.

heading: ACUTE MOUNTAIN SICKNESS
text: AMS is nonfatal, although if left untreated or further ascent is attempted, development of high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) or high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) can be seen. Severe persistence of symptoms may identify Soldiers who acclimatize poorly and, thus, are more prone to other types of mountain sickness.

heading: HIGH-ALTITUDE PULMONARY EDEMA
text:
HAPE is a swelling and filling of the lungs with fluid, caused by rapid ascent. HAPE occurs at high altitudes and limits the oxygen supply to the body. HAPE--
- Occurs under conditions of low-oxygen pressure, is encountered at high elevations (over 8,000 feet) and can occur in healthy Soldiers.
- Can cause death. Incidence and severity increase with altitude. Except for acclimatization to altitude, no known factors indicate resistance or immunity. Few cases have been reported after 10 days at high altitudes. For Soldiers who remain at the same altitude, the incidence of HAPE is less frequent than that of AMS. No common indicator dictates how a Soldier will react from one exposure to another.

heading: CONTRIBUTING FACTORS
text:
The following factors are associated with the development of HAPE:
- A history of HAPE.
- A rapid or abrupt transition to high altitudes.
- Strenuous physical exertion.
- Exposure to cold.
- Anxiety.

heading: SYMPTOMS
text:
The following symptoms are associated with the development of HAPE:
- Progressive dry coughing with frothy white or pink sputum (this is usually a later sign) and then coughing up blood.
- Cyanosis--a blue color to the face, hands, and feet.
- An increased ill feeling, labored breathing, dizziness, fainting, repeated clearing of the throat, and development of a cough.
- Respiratory difficulty, which may be sudden, accompanied by choking and rapid deterioration.
- Progressive shortness of breath, rapid heartbeat (pulse 120 to 160 beats per minute), and coughing (compared to others who arrived at the same time to that altitude).
- Crackling, cellophane-like noises (known as rales) in the lungs caused by fluid buildup. A stethoscope is usually needed to hear them.
- Unconsciousness, if left untreated. Bubbles form in the nose and mouth, and death results.

heading: PREVENTION
text: HAPE is prevented by good nutrition, hydration, and gradual ascent to altitude (no more than 1,000 to 2,000 feet per day to an area of sleep). A rest day, with no gain in altitude or heavy physical exertion, is planned for every 3,000 feet of altitude gained. If Soldiers develop symptoms despite precautions, immediate descent is mandatory to receive necessary treatment, rest, warmth, and oxygen. They should be quickly evacuated to lower altitudes. A descent of 300 meters may help; do not delay manual descent to await air evacuation. If untreated, HAPE may become irreversible and cause death. Cases that are recognized early and treated promptly may expect to recover with no aftereffects. Soldiers who have had previous attacks of HAPE are prone to second attacks.

heading: TREATMENT
text:
Treat HAPE with--
- Immediate descent (2,000 to 3,000 feet minimum), if possible. If not, then treat it in a hyperbaric chamber.
- Rest (litter evacuation).
- Supplemental oxygen, if available.

heading: HIGH-ALTITUDE CEREBRAL EDEMA
text: HACE is the accumulation of fluid in the brain, which results in swelling and a decrease in brain function that may result in death. HACE is caused by a rapid ascent to altitude without progressive acclimatization. Preventing HACE is the same as for HAPE. HAPE and HACE may occur in experienced, well-acclimated mountaineers without warning or obvious predisposing conditions. Both types of edemas can be fatal. When the first symptoms occur, immediate descent is mandatory.

heading: CONTRIBUTING FACTORS
text:
The following factors are associated with the development of HACE:
- Rapid ascent to heights over 8,000 feet.
- Aggravation by overexertion.

heading: SYMPTOMS
text: Symptoms include mild personality changes, paralysis, stupor, convulsions, coma, inability to concentrate, headaches, vomiting, decrease in urination, and lack of coordination. The main symptom of HACE is a severe headache. Another manifestation of HACE is a headache combined with any other physical or psychological disturbances. Headaches may be accompanied by a loss of coordination, confusion, hallucinations, and unconsciousness. These may be combined with symptoms of HAPE. Victims are often mistakenly left alone since others may think they are only irritable or temperamental; no one should ever be ignored. The symptoms may rapidly progress to death. Prompt descent to a lower altitude is vital.

heading: PREVENTION
text: HACE is prevented by good nutrition, hydration, and gradual ascent to altitude (no more than 1,000 to 2,000 feet per day to an area of sleep). A rest day, with no gain in altitude or heavy physical exertion, is planned for every 3,000 feet of altitude gained. If a Soldier develops symptoms despite precautions, immediate descent is mandatory to receive prompt treatment, rest, warmth, and oxygen. They should be quickly evacuated to lower altitudes. A descent of 300 meters may help; manual descent is not delayed awaiting air evacuation. If untreated, HACE may become irreversible and cause death. Cases that are recognized early and treated promptly may expect to recover with no aftereffects. Soldiers who have had previous attacks of HACE are prone to second attacks.

heading: TREATMENT
text:
Treat HACE with--
- Supplemental oxygen.
- Rapid descent and medical attention.
- Use of a hyperbaric chamber if descent is delayed. This page intentionally left blank.

heading: Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment
text: Units receiving mountain training show a marked advantage in harsh mountain environments than those that do not. Normal activities, such as navigating, communicating, and moving, require specialized techniques. To gain confidence and experience, Soldiers must conduct realistic mountain training. They should be expected to perform under any environmental conditions. Extended training exercises test the sustainment mechanisms in place for the unit and expose the Soldier to the isolation common to mountain operations. Training should reflect

heading: the harsh mountain environment and should focus on the following:
text:
- Fitness and nutrition.
- Ability to survive and operate in a cold-weather environment.
- Resupply methods.
- Soldier load management.
- Bivouac considerations.

heading: SECTION I - PHYSICAL TRAITS OF THE MILITARY MOUNTAINEER
text: Operations in mountainous terrain are extremely taxing on the human body. The combined effects of harsh weather, difficult dismounted movements, and elevation require Soldiers to be in superior physical condition. The more adapted Soldiers are to the conditions in which they fight, the greater chance they have of success in executing their mission. To adapt to the mountain environment, Soldiers must train in similar environmental conditions and simulate the physical workload of operations in mountainous terrain. Simulating the stresses of mountain warfare on the Soldier's body in a training environment allows necessary adaptations to be made.

heading: PHYSICAL TRAINING FOR THE MOUNTAIN ENVIRONMENT
text:
Physical fitness training considerations can be broken down into two categories:
- Fitness aspects, which are important to Soldiers' abilities to perform in mountainous terrain.
- Fitness training programs that should guide commanders in developing their unit's capability to perform effectively in mountainous terrain.

heading: INDIVIDUAL FITNESS CONSIDERATIONS
text: Operating in the mountains demands a higher level of fitness from the individual Soldier. Even basic movement techniques require a higher level of exertion and as the terrain becomes increasingly technical, so too does the physical demand. This; coupled with increased loads, adverse environmental conditions, and altitude effects; can render a Soldier with substandard fitness ineffective. The mountain Soldier must possess the capacity to reach the objective with the energy to fight while moving safely through hazardous terrain.

heading: INDIVIDUAL FITNESS CONSIDERATIONS
text: A Soldier must demonstrate proficiency in many facets of fitness to prepare for mountain operations. Soldiers must have a holistic approach to their workout programming and selection. They should not focus entirely on one aspect of fitness. Mountain Soldiers must train for their job with a level of dedication like that of professional athletes training to compete. There are many similarities between mountain Soldiers and athletes, but there are key differences as well. Athletes train to compete in a known sport, governed by rules. Mountain Soldiers may be faced with unknowns and have a less defined concept of how they will need to perform during mountain operations. These differences drive the well-rounded, holistic approach to fitness required for Soldiers who may fight in mountainous terrain.

heading: Aerobic Capacity
text: Aerobic capacity allows the mountain Soldier to move for long periods and helps determine potential capacity of endurance for long movements. Aerobic capacity refers to the Soldier's ability to use oxygen to create energy for extended periods. Dismounted movements and the carrying of a casualty in mountainous terrain are examples of tasks requiring endurance. Training in a low-intensity, high-volume manner conditions the aerobic energy system and develops the necessary levels of endurance. FM 7-22, table 6-2, covers training such as ability group runs, terrain runs, foot marches, and endurance training machines to help increase aerobic endurance for unit members.

heading: Anaerobic Capacity
text: Anaerobic capacity allows a Soldier to sprint or have high levels of exertion for a short period. Little oxygen is needed for this type of energy production. The anaerobic energy system can create large amounts of force for a short period. Mountain Soldiers require a high level of anaerobic capacity to move under fire and perform tasks that require a short burst of energy. Training in a high-intensity, low-volume manner conditions the anaerobic energy system and provides the necessary levels of explosive energy. FM 7-22, table 6-2, covers training such as 30:60s, hill repeats, and shuttle runs to help condition the anaerobic energy system of unit members.

heading: Resistance Training
text: Resistance training increases the performance of the muscle tissue found in Soldiers' bodies and increases bone density. Properly trained muscle tissue protects Soldiers' joints during mountain operations, leading to greater durability in this harsh environment. Resistance training can affect the body in different ways. Mountain Soldiers must use resistance training correctly. Soldiers who operate in mountainous terrain should avoid excess bulking of their muscle tissue as this decreases their endurance capabilities. Soldiers do not need large muscles to have strength; adequate strength can be developed using resistance training to gain lean muscle mass. Strength is primarily a function of the brain's connection to the muscles (neuromuscular pathways), not the size of the muscles. Soldiers should use resistance training to increase the function and durability of the body, not aesthetics. This training should be designed to increase muscular endurance, lean muscle mass, and strength. A master fitness trainer can design training programs to help individual Soldiers and commanders achieve their desired results. FM 7-22, table 6-2, covers training, such as the climbing drill, push-up and sit-up drill, and the strength and conditioning circuit, to guide Soldiers through types of resistance training.

heading: UNIT FITNESS CONSIDERATIONS
text: The commander should develop a conditioning or training program to bring a unit to a level where it can operate successfully in mountain conditions. Training priorities should be established. As with all military operations, training is a major influence on the success of mountain operations. Fitness is the foundation upon which all other mountain skills are built. Proper levels of fitness increase the lethality and durability of Soldiers operating in mountainous terrain.

heading: UNIT FITNESS CONSIDERATIONS
text: A physical training program for operations in mountainous terrain should not be taken lightly. This type of program is time-consuming and requires buy-in from all levels of the deploying unit's chain of command. Exercise equipment that allows for proper training should be obtained. Prior to conducting this training, Soldiers should assess their fitness levels. This assessment is an important tool for commanders and master fitness trainers to understand what is needed in the exercise program. Once an exercise program is generated, a unit may begin to train. The program should focus on increasing Soldiers' physical abilities to perform their job in a tactical and mountainous environment.

heading: UNIT FITNESS CONSIDERATIONS
text:
U.S. forces do not routinely train in mountainous terrain. Therefore, extensive preparations are needed to ensure individual and unit effectiveness. Units should be conditioned physically and psychologically before undertaking rigorous mountain operations. Units must work well as a team to cope with the terrain, environment, and enemy situation. Certain factors should be considered:
- What are the climatic and terrain conditions of the area of operations?
- How much time is available for conditioning and training?
- What additional personnel will accompany the unit? Will they be available for training and conditioning?
- What is the unit's current level of physical fitness?
- Does the unit have master fitness trainers creating exercise programs specific to the mountain environment?
- Is there an exercise facility that will allow Soldiers to physically train themselves using the master fitness trainer's program?
- What is the level of individual expertise in mountaineering?
- What type of operations can be expected?
- Which areas in the United States most closely resemble the area of operations?
- Are predeployment areas and ranges available?
- Does the unit have trainers with experience in mountain warfare?

heading: UNIT FITNESS CONSIDERATIONS
text: Physical capability is not solely gained during 1 hour per day in the gym. The participating Soldier must have the discipline to adhere to proper nutrition planning and get adequate rest. To maximize recovery during this period, Soldiers should sleep 8 to 9 hours during a 24-hour period to minimize the chance of injury and increase performance gains.

heading: NUTRITION FOR THE MOUNTAIN ENVIRONMENT
text: The food Soldiers eat directly correlates to the energy levels they expend, including their ability to recover from strenuous activity as well as many other factors. An understanding of how different types of nutrients affect the body will help the Soldier eat better. Soldiers participating in an intense physical training program should not diminish their gains from the training with poor nutrition. When physical training and proper nutrition are combined, Soldiers have more success in achieving and sustaining the fitness required for operations in mountainous terrain.

heading: HYDRATION IN THE MOUNTAIN ENVIRONMENT
text: Water is vital to the health and performance of the mountain Soldier. Dehydration decreases cognitive and physical performance. Soldiers commonly face conditions, such as cold weather and high elevations, in mountainous terrain. Both elements affect the body's ability to stay properly hydrated. A cold climate decreases the sensation of thirst and causes cold-weather diuresis (excessive urination). These both decrease fluid levels in the body and can lead to a performance-limiting state of dehydration. High elevation combined with cold temperatures can further dehydrate a Soldier. Less oxygen leads to an increased respiration rate. While breathing, Soldiers exhale water vapor. Rapidly breathing dry air decreases fluid in the body.

heading: HYDRATION IN THE MOUNTAIN ENVIRONMENT
text: Soldiers and leaders should ensure the availability and consumption of fluids. Hydrating before, during, and after periods of exertion allows for adequate levels of performance and acclimatization. Other factors necessary for maintaining fluid balance in the body include consuming appropriate levels of sodium, electrolytes, and other necessary nutrients. Bananas and other fruits are great examples of electrolyte rich snacks.

heading: MACRONUTRIENTS
text: Nutrients are compounds in foods essential to life that provide the body with energy and building blocks for repair and growth. Nutrients required in large amounts are called macronutrients. Proteins, fats, and carbohydrates are the three types of macronutrients that must be consumed in certain proportions to maintain a healthy body. These important nutrients allow the human body to perform and acclimate in mountainous environments.

heading: Proteins
text: Protein is a macronutrient responsible for maintaining and restoring muscles, providing key enzymes, and strengthening immunity. Protein also helps preserve lean muscle mass and increase strength and endurance. Protein serves many functions that support physical activity. Protein repairs muscle after exertion and creates energy during prolonged periods of submaximal exertion. The recommended requirement is 0.8 grams of protein for every 2.2 pounds of body weight, but this can fluctuate with activity levels. Protein requires water for digestion and may facilitate dehydration. Proteins provide the body with about 4 calories of energy per gram.

heading: Fats
text: Fats are critical to physical performance, recovery from exercise, and cardiovascular health. Fats are the body's natural and most concentrated source of stored food energy. Main sources of fats are meats, nuts, butter, eggs, milk, and cheese. Fats should comprise 25 to 30 percent of the total daily caloric intake. Fats require more water and oxygen to digest than protein. Fats provide the body with approximately 9 calories of energy per gram. Fat is the most energy dense of the three macronutrients. It is harder for the body to use fat in an efficient manner to produce energy during periods of exertion. Fats are harder to digest at higher altitudes.

heading: Carbohydrates
text: Carbohydrates are the chief energy source for high-intensity physical activity, and they are important for meeting overall energy needs. Carbohydrates are an important source of calories and provide the body with dietary fiber and a variety of micronutrients. Nutritionally, the most useful sources of carbohydrates are foods, such as unrefined grains, vegetables, and fruit. Carbohydrates should comprise up to 50 percent of the total daily caloric intake. Carbohydrates provide the body with around 4 calories of energy per gram.

heading: BALANCED DIET
text: Eating a balanced diet provides the energy needed to conduct daily activities and to maintain internal body processes. A balanced diet containing adequate amounts of macronutrients, vitamins, and minerals ensures an efficient metabolism. Since operations in mountainous terrain are strenuous and demand high-energy use, a balanced diet is necessary. A proper diet requires Soldiers to be aware of how many calories they must consume. Soldiers of different ages, weights, and sexes have different nutritional needs. Caloric requirements differ between Soldiers, especially when accounting for levels of activity.

heading: BALANCED DIET
text: Mountain Soldiers should take the time to understand their own caloric requirements. (See figure 4-1.) Individual variables coupled with a variety of environmental conditions, cold weather, or altitudes make it difficult to generalize a Soldier's daily requirement, and it could range from 4,500 to 6,000 calories a day.

heading: BALANCED DIET
text: Vitamins allow chemical reactions in the body to happen so that they may use the energy found in the three macronutrients. Without these reactions, the energy from the calories in the macronutrients cannot be turned into adenosine triphosphate that the cells in our body use for energy, allowing them to function. Vitamins and minerals are found in vegetables, fruits, and meats. There are many different micronutrients, and it can become hard to track ingestion of all types. Physically active Soldiers should pay special attention to consume adequate amounts of iron, vitamin D, and antioxidants through a balanced diet. If a diet deficient in fresh foods containing essential vitamins and minerals is not available during a deployment, vitamin supplements are a suitable substitute.

heading: Resting Energy Expenditure (Calories Used at Rest)
text:
- Each Soldier's resting energy expenditure is different.
- It is important to know one's resting energy expenditure to know how many calories to consume.
- Resting energy expenditures can be multiplied by activity factors to get total caloric requirements for different levels of exertion. This is important to know to ensure Soldiers get proper nourishment while operating in challenging terrain. (See the Special Operations Forces Nutrition Guide, pages 4 to 5, for detailed information on performing these calculations.)

heading: Resting Energy Expenditure (Calories Used at Rest)
text: Extra food should be carried in case resupply operations fail. Food should be lightweight, easy to digest, and be able to be eaten hot or cold. Meals, ready to eat meet these criteria and provide the basic food groups. Commanders may consider supplementing meals, ready to eat with breakfast bars, fruits, juices, candies, cereal bars, and chocolate. Bouillon cubes can replace the required salt intake, and it can warm cold bodies and stimulate the appetite. Hot beverages of soup, juices, powdered milk, and cider should also be considered. Since coffee, tea, and hot chocolate are diuretics, consuming these beverages should not be relied upon for hydration (see AR 40-25).

heading: Resting Energy Expenditure (Calories Used at Rest)
text: Calories from carbohydrates, protein, and fat digest, absorb, and metabolize at different rates in our body. The timing of nutrient intake will affect the individual's physical, behavioral, and cognitive well-being. High-energy snacks help maintain performance during long movements. Soldiers should also consume a high-carbohydrate snack to replenish energy stores and maximize recovery immediately following foot movements or hard physical work.

heading: Resting Energy Expenditure (Calories Used at Rest)
text: Certain drugs, medications, alcohol, and smoking have adverse effects on the circulation, perspiration, hydration, and judgment of Soldiers. They should be avoided, if possible, when operating in extremely cold conditions or at high altitudes.

heading: NUTRITION OF ELEVATION
text: Success in mountain operations depends on proper nutrition. Because higher altitudes affect eating habits, precautions must be taken. If possible, at least one hot meal each day should be eaten, which may require personnel to heat their individual rations. (See USARIEM TN-01/4 for more information on nutrition.)

heading: NUTRITION OF ELEVATION
text: Soldiers can experience physiological acclimatization with abrupt ascents to high altitudes. The circulatory system works to provide the needed oxygen to the body. Large meals require the digestive system to work harder than usual to digest food. Large meals may be accompanied by indigestion, shortness of breath, cramps, and illness. Therefore, relatively light meals that are high in carbohydrates are best while acclimatizing at higher elevations. Personnel should eat moderately and rest before strenuous physical activity. Since fats and protein are harder to digest, less digestive disturbances may occur if meals are eaten before resting. A diet high in carbohydrates is not as dense in energy and may require eating more often. Consuming carbohydrates, beginning in the morning and continuing through mid-afternoon, are important in maintaining energy levels.

heading: ACCLIMATIZATION
text:
The following elements are characteristic of nutritional acclimatization in mountain operations:
- Weight loss during the first 2 to 3 days at high elevation.
- Loss of appetite with symptoms of AMS.
- Loss of weight usually stops with acclimatization.
- At progressively higher elevations (greater than 14,000 feet), the tolerance of fatty or high-protein foods rapidly decreases. A high-carbohydrate diet may lessen the symptoms of AMS and may digest better than fat at high altitudes. (See USARIEM TN-01/4.)

heading: FATIGUE
text: Increased fatigue can cause Soldiers to become disinterested in eating properly. Decreased consumption can result in malnutrition because of the unpleasant taste of cold rations. Leaders should ensure that fuel tablets and squad stoves are available or that natural flammable materials are used, if possible. Although there is no physiological need for food to be hot, hot food does increase morale and a sense of well-being. Losing weight in the first few days can occur because of dehydration, metabolic changes, and loss of appetite. Carbohydrate-rich beverages, such as fruit juices and sports drinks, increase carbohydrates, energy, and liquid intake when the normal appetite response is blunted at altitude.

heading: SECTION II - COLD-WEATHER SUSTAINMENT
text: The ability to operate for extended periods in cold weather is an essential skill if a unit wishes to be successful in mountainous terrain. Individual skills and collective unit skills required for cold weather must be practiced before deploying to a cold region of the world. The skills required for survival in the cold must be known so they do not become the sole focus once the unit is faced with harsh conditions. For a unit to accomplish its mission in cold, unforgiving weather, it must have the equipment necessary to live and operate in extreme conditions. Cold weather can affect many facets of daily life, from nutrition to clothing.

heading: CLOTHING
text: The clothing system refers to every piece of clothing placed against the skin (base layer), the insulating layers, and the outermost garments (shell), which protect the Soldier from the elements. When clothing is worn properly, the Soldier can function better; when clothing is worn improperly, Soldiers can develop hypothermia or frostbite. Wearing cold-weather clothing provides a barrier against weather and heat retention, moves moisture away from skin, dries quickly, and allows for adequate dexterity.

heading: CLOTHING
text: Clothing for the cold-weather environment must manage Soldiers' temperatures and control moisture. Clothing must be able to vent and breathe so a Soldier does not become overheated and perspire excessively. The clothing must also create insulation to shelter the Soldier from extreme temperatures. Clothing must manage moisture that comes from external sources, such as rain, or from internal sources, such as perspiration.

heading: CLOTHING
text: One of the most effective ways to manage moisture from perspiration is to set a pace that limits exertion. In a cold-weather environment, patrols should move at a pace that will not saturate Soldiers' insulating layers with sweat. Rest halts allow Soldiers an opportunity to adjust layers and control their own individual temperatures.

heading: CLOTHING
text: Fitness, load, body composition, and metabolism all affect individual clothing needs. There should be room for individual variation in the wear of cold-weather clothing, but clothing decisions should be based on the principles of moisture management, trapped air spaces, and protection from the elements. The components of any clothing system can be broken down into the following general categories to match those principles.

heading: BASE LAYER
text: The base layer is a thin, lightweight moisture-wicking layer worn against skin and moves moisture away from the skin to prevent heat loss from conduction. Base layers should be constructed of wool, synthetic, or silk fabrics.

heading: INSULATING LAYERS
text: Insulating layers are those layers worn over the base layer and under the shell. Insulating layers provide additional warmth by resisting the transfer of heat.
