Modern insulating layers allow moisture to move easily, and they trap air to increase the insulating factor. Several thin layers of insulation provide more warmth than one thick layer. Insulating layers should be constructed from wool, synthetic, or down fabrics. Insulating layers help Soldiers retain heat and not lose heat through convection.

heading: SHELL
text: The shell is the outermost layer worn. The shell is the primary barrier between the elements and the body and prevents outside moisture from getting in, while allowing inside moisture out. Shells must have some ventilation capacity to prevent overheating. There are two types of shells.

heading: SHELL
text: A hard shell is generally more moisture and wind repellant and provides better protection against the elements at the cost of breathability. Soldiers cannot ventilate their bodies as well with a hard shell. The hard shell is a good outer layer to be worn in extreme conditions or static environments.

heading: SHELL
text: A soft shell is a more breathable option. The soft shell is not as moisture and wind repellent as hard shells but is more breathable. The soft shell is a good outer layer to be worn when active as it provides better ventilation and breathability. Note. Cotton layers should NEVER BE WORN as any layer during operations in a cold environment.

heading: GAITERS
text:
Gaiters protect the lower leg from snow, ice, mud, twigs, and stones. Using waterproof fabrics or other breathable materials laminated to nylon makes the gaiter an integral component of the cold-weather clothing system. Gaiters are not presently fielded in the standard extended cold-weather clothing system and, in most cases, will need to be locally purchased. Gaiters are available in four styles:
- Trail gaiters are short, typically extending just above the boot. They keep snow and debris out of boots in the spring and summer.
- Alpine gaiters extend up to the knee and keep deep snow out of boots in the winter.
- Expedition gaiters are thicker, designed to fit around a larger plastic mountaineering boot, and sometimes have added built-in insulation.
- The integrated gaiter is a boot with a built-in gaiter, eliminating the need for a second piece of equipment.

heading: HAND WEAR
text: Even during the summer months, temperatures in the mountains can dip below the freezing point. While mittens are warmer than gloves, the finger dexterity needed to do most tasks makes gloves the primary cold-weather hand wear.

heading: HAND WEAR
text: The principles that apply to clothing also apply to gloves and mittens. A modular approach should be taken when wearing hand wear. (See figure 4-2, page 48.) They should provide moisture transfer from the skin to the outer layers?the insulating layer must insulate the hand from the cold and move moisture to the shell. The outer layer must be weather resistant and breathable. Both gloves and mittens should be required for all Soldiers during mountain operations, as well as replacement liners for both. This will provide enough flexibility to accomplish all tasks and keep the users' hands warm and dry.

heading: HAND WEAR
text: Just as the clothing system is worn in layers, gloves and mittens work best using the same principle. Soldiers should have multiple sets of hand wear. They should have multiple thin liner gloves, intermediate climbing gloves, thicker gloves for working with carabiners in the extreme cold, trigger-finger mittens for using their personal weapon in the extreme cold, and thick mittens to protect their hands in the extreme cold. When outer layer gloves are removed, they can be placed in the jacket to keep warm.

heading: HEADWEAR
text: Headwear in mountainous environments should take a modular approach as well. A single hat does not perform well in every condition; several hats should be available to mountaineers: a thin moisture-wicking hat to wear under the helmet or during active movements; an intermediate fleece cap for protection in cold, dry environments; and a heavy thick cap for extreme cold. For colder climates, a neck gaiter can be added. The neck gaiter is a tube of synthetic material that fits around the neck and can reach up over the ears and nose. For extreme cold, a balaclava can be added. This covers the head, neck, and face, leaving only a slot for the eyes. Worn together, the combination is warm and provides for moisture movement, keeping the wearer drier and warmer.

heading: FOOTWEAR
text: Soldiers may encounter various environmental conditions within relatively short distances in mountainous, plateau, and other highland areas. (See CTA 50-900.) In such places, clothing allowances that are adequate for adjacent lower areas may not provide sufficient protection for diverse highland areas; therefore, in these higher or more rugged areas, commanders may authorize, at their discretion, additional clothing items and special mountaineering equipment, as required.

heading: FOOTWEAR
text: Mountain climates are colder than surrounding areas. Even in summer months, it may be necessary to equip troops with cold-weather boots. The intermediate cold-weather boot provides adequate protection for summer conditions in most mountain ranges with high elevation (2,500 to 4,000 meters) located in temperate regions. It can be appropriate footwear for Soldiers whose mission only requires mobility in easy terrain. (See figure 4-3, page 50.)

heading: FOOTWEAR
text: Leather mountaineering boots are designed to provide more capability in mountainous terrain. They are typically warmer and more water resistant than combat boots are. Rigid leather mountaineering boots provide better edging while climbing alpine rock. They also perform better when kicking steps in firm snow or wearing crampons. In general, a leather mountaineering boot with moderately stiff soles and upper section works well for most military mountaineering tasks. Although they are not available through the supply system, they can be a commercial, off-the-shelf purchase. (See figure 4-3, page 50.)

heading: FOOTWEAR
text: During the winter months, most mountain ranges experience periods of extreme cold (-26 degrees F to - 40 degrees F). The extreme cold-weather boot (with vapor barrier [VB]) provides adequate protection from the extreme cold, but it is not an adequate platform for mountaineering tasks in these conditions. Plastic mountaineering boots provide a more versatile platform for any condition encountered in the mountains, while keeping the foot dryer and warmer. Plastic mountaineering boots are a double boot, consisting of a hard, plastic shell, and an inner insulating boot. The stiffness of the shell makes it compatible with crampons, snowshoes, and skis. The hard, plastic shell provides waterproofing, while the inner liner remains free of snowmelt, making it an ideal boot in wet conditions. Plastic mountaineering boots are the optimal footwear for extended operations in cold mountainous environments. (See figure 4-3, page 50.) Note. Maintenance of all types of footwear must closely follow the manufacturers' recommendations.

heading: SOCKS
text:
Socks cushion the foot, remove excess moisture, and insulate from cold temperatures. Improper wear and excess moisture can cause hot spots and blisters. Socks can be worn as a layered system:
- The first layer should be a moisture-wicking material that moves moisture from the foot surface to the outer sock.
- The outer sock should also be made of moisture-wicking materials but should be complemented with materials that provide cushioning and abrasion resistance.
- A third layer can be added depending upon the climatic conditions:
- In severe wet conditions, a waterproof-type sock can be added to reduce the amount of water that would saturate the foot. This layer would be worn over the first two layers if conditions were extremely wet.
- In extremely cold conditions, a VB sock can be worn either over both original pairs of socks or between the moisture-wicking layer and the insulating layer. If the user is wearing VB boots, the VB sock is not recommended.

heading: EXTENDED COLD-WEATHER CLOTHING SYSTEM
text:
The extended cold-weather clothing system is the currently issued cold-weather clothing system. (See figure 4-4.)
- Level 1: Base layer--a crewneck shirt constructed with a lightweight material that is highly breathable and has moisture-wicking properties. Kit includes two sets.
- Level 2: Grid fleece (waffle)--a midweight long-sleeve shirt and elastic waistband drawers constructed with a heavyweight material, which offers stretch for increased comfort during movement, is highly breathable, and has moisture-wicking properties. Kit includes one set.
- Level 3: Fleece jacket--a zipper jacket with raglan sleeves constructed with a material that creates air pockets that trap air and retain body heat, providing outstanding warmth without weight. This material also offers excellent breathability and the ability to dry quickly. However, this layer is not recommended as an outer garment for use during inclement or windy weather. Kit includes one piece.
- Level 4: Wind jacket--a nylon or spandex jacket. It offers wind protection and environmental comfort with low weight and bulk and is quick drying. Kit includes one piece.
- Level 5: Soft-shell jacket and trousers--constructed with a waterproof fabric, is quick drying, highly durable, and breathable. Kit includes one piece.
- Level 6: Wet weather jacket and trousers--constructed with a two-layer waterproof and windproof fabric with sealed seams and is extremely breathable. Kit includes one piece.
- Level 7: Extended cold-weather parka and trousers--three-layer construction that is fabricated with an outer layer, an insulation layer, and an inside layer of lightweight rip-stop material. They are water resistant, highly durable, and breathable. Kit includes one piece.

heading: SECTION III - SMALL GROUP MOUNTAIN SUSTAINMENT AND SUBSISTENCE
text: There is no one standardized way to plan for sustainment in mountain operations. Each mission has its own set of complications. Layers of contingencies should be built into the plan for sustainment. If one method fails due to any number of unforeseen circumstances, another method of sustainment must be ready to provide Soldiers with what they need. Gear that Soldiers carry must not be so heavy it makes them vulnerable. Methods to procure water must be available. Detailed coordination must be made with air assets to provide aerial resupply.

heading: SOLDIER LOAD MANAGEMENT
text: Operations in mountainous terrain require Soldiers to carry only mission-essential items as they move through challenging terrain. Individual Soldiers, small teams, and large units must be able to adjust their equipment. They must understand the fundamentals of cross-leveling essential equipment to avoid excess gear. Understanding and practicing these simple, yet often overlooked, skills can make a unit lighter, faster, and more lethal in mountainous terrain. No amount of training can change the body's reaction to carrying excessive loads. Analyzing the situation and the level of risk are the keys to determining what is mission essential. All leaders should familiarize themselves with ATP 3-21.18, where they can access table 3-4, which is a helpful guide for leaders when planning loads for dismounted movements. (See chapter 6 for detailed information on load management to maximize mobility.)

heading: CHOICE OF EQUIPMENT
text: Mission requirements and unit standard operating procedures (SOPs) will influence the choice of gear carried, but the following lists provide a sample of what should be considered during mission planning.

heading: Personal Gear
text: Personal gear includes an emergency survival kit with signaling material, fire-starting material, and water procurement material. Pocket items should include a knife, whistle, pressure bandage, notebook with pen or pencil, sunglasses, sunblock and lip protection, map, compass, and altimeter.

heading: Standard Gear
text: Standard gear that can be individually worn or carried includes cushion-soled socks; combat or mountain boots, combat uniform and cap; load-carrying equipment with canteens, magazine pouches, and first aid kit; individual weapon; a large rucksack containing hard-shell top and bottom; insulating layers; helmet; poncho; and sleeping bag.

heading: Mountaineering Equipment and Specialized Gear
text: The element's leadership should scrutinize mountaineering equipment. The equipment should allow Soldiers to move safely through any known technical terrain. Identifying hazards and obstacles during the planning phase is a crucial step to help determine the appropriate gear for the given mission. Required mountaineering equipment is never set in stone, and each patrol or mission may require different equipment.

heading: Daypack
text:
When Soldiers plan to be away from the bivouac site for the day on a patrol or mountaineering mission, they carry a light daypack. This pack should contain--
- Extra insulating layer.
- Hard-shell layer, such as a waterproof jacket and pants or poncho.
- First aid kit.
- Flashlight or headlamp.
- Canteen or water bottle.
- Cold-weather hat or scarf.
- Rations for the time away from the base camp.
- Survival kit.
- Improvised harness materials or climbing harness.
- Necessary mountaineering equipment for technical terrain.
- Gloves.

heading: TEN ESSENTIALS
text: Regardless of what equipment is carried, the individual military mountaineer should always carry 10 essentials when moving through the mountains.

heading: Navigational Tools
text: Knowledge of the terrain and a well-developed route plan are the two most important tools for avoiding issues in the mountains. A map should be carried along with appropriate navigational aids like a compass, altimeter, and Global Positioning System (GPS) device.

heading: Headlamp and Night Vision Devices
text: Night vision devices are powerful tools for target identification and discrimination and are critical tools in the mountains. However, their narrow focal plane at close ranges is minimally helpful when scrambling in rough terrain. Light enables faster and safer movement and scrambling. Preventing enemy observation should always be a primary concern, but for maneuver in terrain that is masked from observation where risk of a fall is a greater threat, a light is valuable. Headlamps are also important for camp tasks, planning, and map work.

heading: Sunglasses and Sunscreen
text: In alpine or snow-covered terrain, sunglasses are vital for preventing snow blindness. Side shields, which minimize light entering from the side, permit ventilation to help prevent lenses from fogging. Each independent climbing team should carry at least one extra pair of sunglasses.

heading: Extra Clothing
text:
Clothing is the primary protection from the environment and needs to match the conditions and the pace of a movement. Extra clothing includes the additional layers needed for static operations or enduring the long, inactive hours of an unplanned bivouac, such as the following:
- Waterproof, breathable shells to protect from unexpected wind or precipitation.
- Extra underwear to replace sweat-soaked underwear.
- Extra hats or balaclavas.
- Extra pair of heavy socks.
- Extra pair of insulated mittens or gloves.
- Extra insulation for the upper body and the legs (winter or severe mountain conditions).

heading: Extra Clothing
text: To back up foul weather gear, bring a poncho or extra-large plastic trash bag. A reflective emergency space blanket can be used for hypothermia first aid and emergency shelter. Insulated foam pads prevent heat loss while sitting or lying on snow. Finally, a bivouac sack can help by protecting insulating layers from the weather, cutting the wind, and trapping essential body heat.

heading: Water and Water Containers
text: These include wide-mouthed water bottles for water collection, hands-free backpack hydration systems, and a small length of plastic tubing for water procurement at snowmelt seeps and rainwater puddles on bare rock. Wide-mouth containers are easy to fill, easy to clean, and easy to clear out if ice forms. Hydration bladders are convenient, but they can break and have freezing issues in the tube.

heading: First Aid Kit
text: Small teams in the mountains often operate independently. In addition to the improved first aid kit, each Soldier should carry first-aid supplies to address common mountaineering injuries, such as punctures and abrasions with severe bleeding, broken bones, serious sprains, and blisters. Splinting material for stabilizing orthopedic injuries is an important addition.

heading: Lighter and Fire Starter
text: Lighters are handy for starting fires, but they should be backed up by matches stored in a waterproof container with a strip of sandpaper. Fire-starting material is key to igniting wet wood for emergency campfires. Candles, heat tabs, and canned heat all work. These can also be used to quickly warm water or soup in a canteen cup. In alpine zones above the tree line with no available firewood, a stove works as an emergency heat source.

heading: Knife
text: A small folding knife is a helpful tool for its weight. It can be useful for cutting rope or cordage or for food preparation and shelter construction. A knife is important for first aid when improvising interventions with limited medical supplies. A multipurpose pocket tool is also helpful.

heading: Repair Kit
text:
A repair kit should include--
- Stove tools and spare parts.
- Duct tape.
- Patches.
- Safety pins.
- Heavy-duty thread or dental floss.
- Sewing kit.
- Cord or wire.

heading: Extra Food
text: Soldiers should carry one day's extra worth of food in case of delay caused by bad weather, injury, or navigational error.

heading: SMALL UNIT CROSS-LEVELING
text: A small team of Soldiers must analytically look at the packing and choice of team gear. Everyone must be aware of essential-item locations. They must also ensure there is no unnecessarily redundant equipment. In challenging terrain, unnecessary weight slows Soldiers and reduces situational awareness.

heading: SQUAD OR TEAM EMERGENCY PACK
text:
When a squad-sized element leaves the bivouac site, squad safety gear should be carried in addition to individual daypacks. This can be either loaded into one rucksack or cross-leveling among squad members. In the event of an injury, CASEVAC, or unplanned bivouac, these items may make the difference between succeeding and failing the mission. Squad safety gear comprises the following items:
- Sleeping bag.
- Sleeping mat.
- Squad stove.
- Fuel bottle.
- Litter or packaging material.

heading: SQUAD OR TEAM EMERGENCY PACK
text:
The following mnemonic, DROP, can help leaders ensure an appropriate load plan is achieved:
- D--Determine level of mobility.
- R--Reduce redundant or nonessential equipment.
- O--Organize resupply.
- P--Police Soldiers.

heading: WATER PROCUREMENT
text: Supplying adequate water to maintain hydration is a sustainment challenge. Fluids lost through respiration, perspiration, and urination must be replaced. However, water is heavy, and even a few days' supply will overburden Soldiers. If the water supply is insufficient, then physical activity must be reduced. However, Soldiers cannot adjust permanently to a decreased water intake.

heading: WATER PROCUREMENT
text:
Individual loads and support requirements can be reduced if small units can procure water from the environment. Water found in mountain streams and pools is often clean, but it cannot be assumed potable. Soldiers should be educated to drink water only from safe sources. Emphasis must be placed on the three rules of water discipline:
- Only drink treated water.
- Conserve water for drinking. Potable water in the mountains may be in short supply.
- Do not contaminate or pollute water sources.

heading: WATER SOURCES
text: Water is scarce above the timberline. After setting up a perimeter, such as a patrol base, assembly area, or a defense; a watering party should be employed. Mountain streams, springs, rain, and lakes provide good sources of water. In areas where water trickles off rocks, a small piece of tubing can be used to fill canteens, or a shallow reservoir may be dug from which to collect water (after the sediment settles).

heading: WATER SOURCES
text: Snow may be melted to procure water, which is a time-consuming process that requires significant fuel. Water should be collected at midday when the sun thaws the snow. In glaciated environments, fine particulate can be found in the runoff and should be filtered. After sundown, high mountain areas freeze. Storing water next to a Soldier or placing it in a sleeping bag at night can protect water from freezing.

heading: BIOLOGICAL CONTAMINANTS
text: Virtually all surface waters are microbiologically contaminated. There are three types of disease-causing microorganisms: protozoa, bacteria, and viruses.

heading: BIOLOGICAL CONTAMINANTS
text: Protozoa are the largest of waterborne bugs measuring in the 1-micron range. Giardia and cryptosporidium are the most infamous of the group. The infective cysts and oocysts of protozoa are extremely robust and can survive for months in a water source. They thrive in domestic and wild animals, as well as humans. Cryptosporidium oocysts are known for their resistance to chemical treatment. Most disinfectants are ineffective, and the few that require long dwell times to do the job.

heading: BIOLOGICAL CONTAMINANTS
text: Bacteria are an order of magnitude smaller than protozoa measuring in the 0.2-micron range. The most well-known bacteria are Escherichia coli (commonly referred to as E. coli); others include campylobacter, salmonella, and shigella. Bacteria are not as hearty, surviving in water for weeks instead of months. However, unlike protozoa and viruses, which require a host to multiply, some bacteria grow in water and are found in higher numbers than protozoa and viruses. Both animals and humans often carry bacteria, such as protozoa; as a result, many water sources are contaminated with bacteria. Beware of water sources near agricultural operations.

heading: BIOLOGICAL CONTAMINANTS
text: Viruses--some notorious waterborne viruses are poliovirus, hepatitis, and norovirus. Waterborne viruses are very resilient and can survive for months in water. Viruses are generally species-specific; in other words, those that infect animals do not infect humans and vice versa. Because of this and the modern sanitation measures taken in developed countries, not as many water sources are contaminated with viruses. In developing countries with little or no sewage control, the opposite is true. However, as more people are becoming active outdoors, more rivers, lakes, and streams are at risk of viral contamination.

heading: CHEMICAL CONTAMINANTS
text: Filters and purifiers provide microbiologically safe drinking water. The carbon in the filters and disinfectant of the purifiers will adsorb or react with chemical contaminates, such as herbicides, pesticides, and volatile organic compounds. However, filters or purifiers will not protect from high chemical concentrations or heavy metal contamination. It is best to avoid water sources such as mining tailing ponds or those near agricultural operations.

heading: WATER PURIFICATION
text: Water should always be treated. No matter how clean the snow or water may appear, it should always be considered contaminated. There are many techniques to purify water, each with inherent advantages and disadvantages.

heading: WATER PURIFICATION
text: Boiling kills biological contaminants but does not eliminate chemical contaminants. Filtration should also be used if chemical contaminants are suspected. To ensure all biological contaminants have been killed, let the water boil for 1 minute. This method requires time and fuel while allowing water to be treated away from the source.

heading: WATER PURIFICATION
text: Chemical treatment can be accomplished with iodine or chlorine dioxide. These treatments are available commercially and come with instructions for proper use. Chemical treatment will kill almost all biological contaminants but are ineffective against cryptosporidium. It requires time for these chemical treatments to be effective, and, in cold temperatures, it takes longer. This method allows water to be treated away from the source and on the go.

heading: WATER PURIFICATION
text: UV lights are an effective way to kill all biological contaminants but do not treat for chemical contaminants. They require batteries and in cloudy debris-filled water, it may not kill all contaminants. Ensure water is filtered if it is cloudy before use. This method can be used away from the source.

heading: WATER PURIFICATION
text: Filters are compact and lightweight. They work by filtering out particulate, chemicals, and biological contaminants. Filters are not capable of removing any chemical contaminants that are dissolved in the water. Certain filters may not be able to filter out smaller biological contaminants as the pores of the filter are too large to remove them. These types of filters are designed to remove waterborne protozoa and bacteria but not viruses. The benefit of these types of filters is that water moves more rapidly through them. Filters that can filter smaller contaminants are often referred to as water purifiers. Water purifiers are designed to remove protozoa, bacteria, and viruses, offering a higher level of defense by combating all three. The drawback to these types of filters is that they filter water at a slower rate and may clog when filtering very cloudy water. Be sure to read the capabilities of the filter and treat the water with multiple methods, if necessary. Filters can freeze in cold temperatures if they are not properly cleared after use. In extreme temperatures, they may not operate at all. Filters require treating water at the source.

heading: AERIAL RESUPPLY
text: Movement of supplies by air is often the preferred method for remote, hard to reach locations. This is only possible when assets are available and the weather, terrain, and situation allow it. Air distribution in the mountains requires detailed planning, effective liaison, and a habitual relationship between the aviation crew and the ground unit. Direct communication between the unit and the air delivery asset is coordinated early in the planning process to help ensure proper delivery.

heading: AERIAL RESUPPLY
text: Aerial resupply, though effective, is limited by weather, which must be permissive from the point of origin to the point of delivery, and all stops in-between. Fog, cloud cover, sudden storms, ice, and unpredictable air currents can shut down air support. Higher elevations will decrease aircraft lift capabilities. Temperature and air density at altitude restrict an aircrew's ability to carry loads into the high mountains. Erratic weather conditions in the mountains will frequently prevent rotary- and fixed-wing aircraft from flying; this may last for multiple days.

heading: AERIAL RESUPPLY
text: Suitable drop zones in the mountains are difficult to find. A common resupply delivery is accomplished by helicopters flying at a low altitude above the mountain terrain delivering unit-configured loads. Supplies should be packaged for immediate Soldier transport upon delivery. (For more information on options, see ATP 3-21.50, ATP 4-48, and supporting aviation assets.)

heading: SECTION IV - BIVOUAC CONSIDERATIONS
text: Mountainous regions often have strong turbulent winds, cold temperatures, and a general lack of concealment above the timberline. The wind overhead creates an extensive lee near the mountain. An inland wind blowing 50 miles per hour (mph) may not strike the ground for several kilometers after passing the edge of a cliff or a very steep slope. Such a lee is an attractive bivouac site from the standpoint of wind protection. Note that such a lee area is often an area of maximum snow deposit. Frequent requirements to dig out vehicles, walkways, and weapons positions may offset the wind-free advantages of a lee site during snowfall or snow-blowing weather. Avalanche hazard areas must be avoided. Cold air is heavier than warm air and frequently settles in valleys. If tactically feasible, it is better to establish a bivouac up the hillside above the valley floor and below the timberline.

heading: BIVOUAC SITE LOCATION
text:
The following are considerations for selecting a bivouac site in the mountains:
- Cover and concealment--cover and concealment from air and ground observation is essential for the bivouac area. Forested areas pose few problems in comparison to areas above the tree line. Operations above tree line or at altitude may offer less cover and concealment. Bivouac may need to be established below tree line to support operations conducted above tree line.
- Wind protection--protection from the wind is a prime consideration. Depending on the area of operations, bivouac site selections may vary due to the unpredictability of winds at elevation.
- Ground condition--the condition of the ground is important. In warm conditions, bivouac should be located on hard ground. In snow-covered terrain, avoid digging to the ground, as this may collect water due to the thawing of the snow, or rain. A layer of snow should be left for ground insulation, comfort, and water absorption. The depth that is dug in will vary depending on the site selection and snow depth.
- Construction materials--construction materials play an important part in selecting a bivouac. When reconnoitering an area, consider such things as the availability of firewood, water procurement, and snow for snow shelters.
- Hazard awareness--bivouac sites must be protected from mountain-specific hazards that are not commonly encountered, such as rockfall, icefall, flooding, and avalanche-runout zones. These hazards are not always obvious so good awareness and vigilance must be used when selecting these sites in mountainous terrain.

heading: GLACIER BIVOUAC PROCEDURES
text: When locating a bivouac site or a gathering area where the team might need or want to unrope, at least one person will need to probe the area for hidden crevasses. (See chapter 14, section II, for detailed information on probing a potential bivouac site.)

heading: GLACIER BIVOUAC PROCEDURES
text: Once an area is determined to be safe, it must be marked to keep personnel within that area. Typically, wands are carried as flagging material specifically for this purpose. Water procurement sites (uphill) and latrines (downhill) must be determined for safety to avoid contamination.

heading: GLACIER BIVOUAC PROCEDURES
text: Multiple tent sites can be connected, which keeps tents closer together. Probe all areas between the tents if planning to move in those areas. Closer tents will make communicating between tent groups and rope teams easier.

heading: GLACIER BIVOUAC PROCEDURES
text: If there is a chance for severe storms with high winds, snow walls may be constructed to protect the tent site from wind. The walls can be constructed from loose snow piled on the perimeter, or blocks can be cut from consolidated snow layers. In deep, soft snow, digging 3 or 4 feet to find a consolidated layer will result in enough snow moved to build up decent walls around the tent site. For block construction, move the soft snow from the surface into the wall foundation areas (down to a consolidated layer of snow).

heading: SHELTERS
text: Operations in mountainous terrain require Soldiers to be familiar with a variety of bivouac shelter construction techniques. Ideally, purpose-designed shelters should be used. However, given the erratic nature of weather in mountainous terrain, Soldiers should also be prepared to improvise survival shelters for emergency bivouac situations that occur when carrying manufactured shelters is not feasible.

heading: TENTS
text: When selecting a tent, the mission must be defined to determine the number of people the tent must accommodate. The climate should also be taken into consideration. A tent used for warmer temperatures will greatly differ from tents used in colder, harsher environments. Tent manufacturers offer many designs of different sizes, weights, and materials. Mountaineering tents are made of breathable or weatherproof material. A single-wall tent allows for moisture inside the tent to escape through the tent's material. A double-wall tent has a second layer of material (referred to as a fly) that covers the tent. The fly protects against rain and snow, and the space between the fly and tent helps moisture to escape from inside. Before using a new tent, the seams should be treated with seam sealer to prevent moisture from entering through the stitching. The frame of a tent is usually made of an aluminum or carbon fiber poles. The poles are connected with an elastic cord that allows them to extend, connect, and become long and rigid. When the tent poles are secured into the tent body, they create the shape of the tent. Tents are rated by a relative strength factor; the speed of wind a tent can withstand before the frame deforms. Temperature and expected weather for the mission should be determined before choosing the tent.

heading: FLOORLESS SHELTERS
text: Floorless shelters are lighter and more packable than conventional tents. Soldiers can enter and exit the tent with boots on without bringing dirt into the tent or ripping the floor of a conventional tent. They can be pitched in many different types of terrain for many different uses. They can provide overhead cover while staying in a static position for a long period. They offer much more ventilation, allowing the use of a stove inside and no worry of spilling fuel onto the tent floor. Because floorless shelters are lightweight and easier to pack than conventional tents, it is possible to carry a much larger shelter. A tarp, poncho, or piece of house wrap makes a clean and dry floor area near the sleeping bags if the ground is damp. Floorless shelters do have some drawbacks. They are not suitable above the tree line due to the lack of anchoring and potential high winds. They need soil into which to drive the stakes. If extreme cold temperatures are encountered, they have much more ventilation and are inherently colder than a conventional tent. (See figure 4-5.)

heading: EMERGENCY BIVOUAC SHELTERS
text: The equipment that a Soldier carries, and the environment determine the type of shelter that can be built. Shelters can be built in wooded areas, open country, and barren areas. Wooded areas usually provide the best location, while barren areas have only snow as building material. Wooded areas provide timber for shelter construction, wood for fire, concealment from observation, and protection from the wind. Note. In extreme cold, do not use metal, such as an aircraft fuselage, for shelter. The metal conducts away from the shelter what little body heat the Soldier can generate.

heading: EMERGENCY BIVOUAC SHELTERS
text: Shelters made from ice or snow usually require tools, such as ice axes or saws. Significant time and energy must be expended to build these shelters. Be sure to ventilate an enclosed shelter, especially if the intent is to build a fire for warmth. Always block a shelter's entrance, if possible, to keep the heat in and keep out the wind. Use a rucksack or snow block. Construct a shelter no larger than needed. This will reduce the amount of space to heat. A common error in cold-weather shelter construction is making the shelter so large that it steals body heat rather than helping conserve it.

heading: EMERGENCY BIVOUAC SHELTERS
text: If possible, avoid sleeping directly on the ground. Lay down some pine boughs, grass, or other insulating material to keep the ground from absorbing body heat.

heading: EMERGENCY BIVOUAC SHELTERS
text: Never fall asleep without turning off the stove or lamp. Carbon monoxide poisoning can result from a fire burning in an unventilated shelter. Carbon monoxide is a great danger. It is colorless and odorless. Any time there is an open flame, it may generate carbon monoxide. Always check for proper ventilation. Even in a ventilated shelter, incomplete combustion can cause carbon monoxide poisoning. Usually, there are no symptoms. Unconsciousness and death can occur without warning. Sometimes, however, pressure at the temples, burning of the eyes, headache, pounding pulse, drowsiness, or nausea may occur. The one visible sign of carbon monoxide poisoning is a cherry red coloring in the tissues of the lips, mouth, and inside of the eyelids. Soldiers must immediately be moved to fresh air if they begin to exhibit any of these symptoms.

heading: Poncho Lean-To
text: A poncho lean-to takes only a short time and minimal equipment to build. (See figure 4-6.) Material requirements are a poncho, 6 to 9 feet of rope or cord, 3 stakes about 12 inches long, and 2 trees or 2 poles that are 6 to 9 feet apart. Before selecting the trees or the location of the poles, check the wind direction to ensure that the back of the lean-to is facing into the wind.

heading: Poncho Lean-To
text: When using the lean-to for more than one night or if rain is expected, make a center support for the lean-to. Make this support with a line. Attach one end of the line to the poncho hood and the other end to an overhanging branch. Ensure there is no slack in the line.

heading: Poncho Lean-To
text: Another method for creating a center support is to place a stick upright under the center of the lean-to. However, this method restricts space and movement in the shelter.

heading: Poncho Lean-To
text: For additional protection from wind and rain, place some brush, a rucksack, or other equipment at the sides of the lean-to. To reduce heat loss to the ground, place some type of insulating material, such as leaves or pine needles, inside the lean-to. (See ATP 3-50.21 for more information.) Note. When at rest, Soldiers lose as much as 80 percent of their body heat to the ground.

heading: Field Expedient Lean-To
text: In a wooded area that has enough natural materials, a field-expedient lean-to can be constructed with only a knife. It takes longer to make this type of shelter than it does to make other types, but it protects against the elements. It requires two trees (or upright poles) about 6 feet apart, one pole about 6 feet long and 1 inch in diameter, 5 to 8 poles about 9-feet long and 1 inch in diameter for beams; cord or vines for securing the horizontal support to the trees; and other poles, saplings, or vines to crisscross the beams. (See ATP 3-50.21.)

heading: NATURAL SHELTERS
text: Do not overlook natural formations that provide shelter. Examples are caves, rocky crevices, clumps of bushes, small depressions, large rocks on leeward sides of hills, large trees with low-hanging limbs, and fallen trees with thick branches. When selecting a natural formation, stay away from low ground, such as ravines, narrow valleys, or creek beds. Low areas collect the heavy cold air at night and are therefore colder than the surrounding high ground. Thick, brushy, low ground also harbors more insects. Check for ticks, mites, scorpions, stinging ants, and venomous snakes. Look for loose rocks, dead limbs, or other natural growth that could fall on the shelter. (See ATP 3-50.21.)

heading: Snow-Cave Shelter
text: The snow-cave shelter is an effective shelter because of the insulating properties of snow (See figure 4-7.) A snow-cave shelter requires significant time and energy to build, and during construction, clothing can become quite wet. Find a drift about 3-meters (the length of an avalanche probe) deep that can easily be dug into. While building this shelter, keep the roof arched for strength and allow melted snow to drain down the sides. Build the sleeping platform higher than the entrance. Separate the sleeping platform from the snow-cave's walls or dig a small trench between the platform and the wall. This platform and a smooth ceiling will prevent the melting snow from dripping on clothing and equipment. The construction is especially important to ensure an efficient means of retaining heat. Ensure the roof is high enough to sit up on the sleeping platform. Block the entrance with a snow block or rucksack. The walls and ceiling should be at least 12-inches thick. Install a ventilation shaft. If there is no drift large enough to build a snow cave, a variation can be built by piling snow into a mound large enough to dig out. (See ATP 3-50.21.)

heading: Snow-Trench Shelter
text:
The snow trench is a hasty shelter designed to allow Soldiers to sleep below the snow and wind level while using the snow's insulating qualities. To build a snow-trench shelter, follow the following steps:
- Cut snow blocks about 1 foot by 1 foot by 2 feet and construct the walls by interlocking the snow blocks with overlapping placements. The walls should be slightly higher than the tent. At a minimum, build walls on the windward side of the tent site. Snow walls can also provide shelter from wind for food preparation and when using latrines.
- In areas of compacted snow, cut snow blocks and use them as overhead cover. If not, use a poncho or other material. Build only one entrance and use a snow block or rucksack as a door.

heading: LIGHTWEIGHT STOVES
text: Lightweight stoves should be used during mountain operations to reduce Soldier load and as a cold-weather emergency risk mitigation measure. They should be issued at the team level and provide 3 to 4 Soldiers with the ability to rehydrate rations, melt snow into water, heat water to warm Soldiers with cold weather or other injuries, and generate heat in small shelters during emergencies.

heading: LIGHTWEIGHT STOVES
text: Soldier load can be greatly reduced by carrying lightweight stoves and fuel in winter environments. This is because they can create far more water by volume for the same carried weight than just carrying water. The actual amount varies dependent on altitude, temperature, and fuel type.

heading: LIGHTWEIGHT STOVES
text: Factors that should be considered when choosing lightweight stoves for mountain operations are weight, altitude, operational temperature, fuel availability, and reliability.

heading: STOVE TYPES
text:
Most mountaineering stoves are either canister-fuel or liquid-fuel:
- Canister-fuel stoves are simpler to operate than liquid fueled stoves. The gas, already pressurized, flows from the fuel canister into the burner, where it ignites, in the same manner as a domestic kitchen stove. Canister-fuel stoves are generally accepted as being more efficient for weight carried than liquid fuel. However, canister-fuel stoves are unreliable in cold temperatures. They are not recommended for use in freezing temperatures or at high altitudes.
- Liquid-fuel stoves are more complex because the liquid fuel must be vaporized prior to burning. In many stoves, the priming pressure is generated by a small hand pump that forces air into the fuel container. Liquid-fuel stoves are typically capable of burning multiple types of fuel. They generally operate well in cold weather and at high altitude. Liquid fuel costs less than canister fuel. Some forms of fuel, such as kerosene or diesel, are readily available worldwide. Liquid-fuel stoves are the most widely used for mountaineering due to their wide versatility.

heading: STOVE USE
text: Stoves should be tested and maintained prior to operational use. Soldiers should be familiar with stove disassembly, cleaning, and troubleshooting prior to operational use. A repair kit and the tools needed to fix these stoves should always be packed together. The reliability of the stove has a huge impact on the success of the mission and the morale of personnel.

heading: STOVE USE
text: When in use, hot stoves must be kept away from equipment and ammunition. At higher elevations, the heating times may be doubled. To conserve fuel, stoves, fires, and fuel tablets should be protected from the wind.

heading: Avalanche
text: World War I is remembered for the brutal fighting in the trenches in France and Belgium. However, in the fighting between Italy and the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Soldiers saw some of the most intense mountain fighting in human history. After the Italians checked the Austrian offensive through the passes of the Alps, both sides fought higher and higher into the mountains. Small, light units of mountaineers clashed over new ground high in the peaks, while the armies dug in on the peaks they had secured. Positions and paths were blasted out of the rock and carved through the glaciers to move personnel and materiel to the fighting in the heights. By the winter of 1916, the line had mostly stabilized, and both armies were hunkering down for winter. Both sides had established extensive networks of trails and camps to support their forward positions; however, much of the infrastructure had been built in avalanche paths. In the second week of December, a major snowstorm blew in, loading the slopes and causing massive avalanches across the range. Both nations suppressed the number of casualties they received, and no official Italian records exist, but what evidence did survive paints a grim picture. The lowest estimates place casualties at around 4,000 during the storm. Some records support numbers as high as 10,000. Today, their bodies are still melting out of the glaciers below.

heading: SECTION I - AVALANCHE HAZARDS
text: During winter months and throughout the year, snow covers the slopes. Steep, snow-covered terrain, in addition to mobility challenges and fall hazards, present the risk of avalanches. This hazard is easy to underestimate. It is not clearly visible, and, due to the complexity of the factors involved, there is a high degree of uncertainty, but the consequences of ignoring the hazard are high. Avalanches have taken the lives of more troops engaged in mountain warfare than all other terrain hazards combined.

heading: SECTION I - AVALANCHE HAZARDS
text: An avalanche is an unstable snowpack, located on particularly angled terrain, where the bonds between layers or several layers of snow have broken, causing a mass of snow to slide downhill. When operating in the mountains during the winter, these instabilities in the snowpack may make large areas too dangerous for travel. These snow slopes may appear unthreatening but may have weak layers buried in the snowpack that can be easily triggered. Military elements may gravitate into avalanche terrain to avoid steeper technical terrain or enemy observation. Avalanches can generate incredible destructive force, destroying equipment, killing or burying Soldiers, and blocking key roads. Whether operating dismounted in high alpine terrain or as a mounted force in valley bottoms, units must be aware of avalanche hazards. They must incorporate the evaluation of avalanche danger into the planning process and learn to recognize and avoid hazardous terrain. (See figure 5-1, page 64.)

heading: AVALANCHE ELEMENTS
text: Avalanches occur when the weight of accumulated snow on a slope exceeds the cohesive forces that hold the snow in place. There are three elements needed to create an avalanche: an unstable snowpack, terrain steep enough to slide, and a trigger that initiates the failure of bonds holding the snow in place.

heading: SNOWPACK
text: Layers of snow accumulate with each new snow or wind event. Variation in temperature and atmospheric conditions form layers with different types of snow crystals. These layers are subject to changes in texture and strength throughout the winter, as they are exposed to sun, wind, and temperature changes. Each layer in the snowpack will have distinct characteristics. Strong layers are made up of well-bonded, small, rounded grains. Weak layers are made up of larger, angular, poorly bonded grains.

heading: Snowpack Concerns
text:
Instabilities are weaknesses within the snowpack as described below (see figure 5-2):
- Weak layers--weak layers may collapse under load, initiating an avalanche. Poorly bonded crystals can act like ball bearings between stronger layers. Weak layers can change over time, becoming stronger, denser layers. This happens more quickly in temperatures above freezing. However, many avalanche cycles are due to weak layers that resist this change and retain their large grain size and angular shape for long periods. These types of layers are known as "persistent" weak layers. These are common in prolonged colder temperatures.
- Weak bonds between layers--differences in the size and compositions of crystals between layers inhibit bonding. Large differences between layers are the primary source of instability.
- Bed surface--the bed surface is the surface over which a fracture and subsequent avalanche release occurs. Smooth, uniform sliding surfaces provide less friction to hold the snow in place. Examples are firm old snow layers, rain crusts, and sun crusts.

heading: Loading
text:
When instability exists in the snowpack, another important factor is the load placed on top of the weak layer. With the added weight of accumulated snow, it increases the shear forces within the snowpack:
- New snow--during snowstorms, snowfall will rapidly increase the forces placed on the snowpack. Snowfall of more than 2.5 centimeters (cm) (1 inch) of snow an hour or more than 30 cm (1 foot) of snow in 24 hours is considered critical loading. Avoid traveling in avalanche terrain during critical loading.
- Wind loading--sustained winds will transport snow from windward slopes and ridge tops, depositing it in sheltered features on leeward aspects. With high winds, even small deposits of new snow can produce significant loading. Top loading occurs when wind deposits snow over the top of a ridge. Side loading (or cross loading) occurs when snow is blown across the slope and deposited in gullies or on the leeward sides of ridges.
- Rain--rain rapidly increases the load on the snowpack and erodes bonds between snow crystals and layers. After a period of sustained cold where weak layers have been preserved in the snowpack, rain can produce dense, wet avalanches that are very destructive.

heading: TERRAIN FACTORS
text: Terrain is the second factor that determines if an avalanche can occur. The character of a snowpack and opportunities for whether instabilities develop are determined by its elevation and aspect. A slope's characteristics--slope angle, shape, and physical characteristics--determine the likelihood of a slide. Recognizing and avoiding avalanche terrain are the keys to managing avalanche risk.

heading: Elevation
text: Precipitation, temperature, and wind often vary significantly at different elevations. This results in differences in the snowpack, all of which influence the type, size, distribution, and sensitivity of avalanches.

heading: Elevation
text: Increased precipitation--as weather systems are lifted over mountains (orthographic lift), the air cools and can hold less moisture, causing additional precipitation at elevation. Increased precipitation causes increased loads on the snowpack.

heading: Elevation
text: Temperature--warming in the snowpack temporarily increases instability as bonds melt but improves stability when it re-freezes. Cooler temperatures at higher elevations inhibit stabilization. Instabilities can persist for much longer.

heading: Aspect to Wind
text: Sustained winds of 15 mph or higher transport snow from the windward aspect of the slope and deposit it in the form of wind slabs on the leeward slopes. Leeward slopes can accumulate three to five times the amount of snow that falls in sheltered locations. Slopes on the windward side have much of their new snow "scoured" off by the wind and are generally more stable than leeward slopes. Leeward slopes tend to form dangerous cornices and large, unstable slabs of snow.

heading: Aspect to Sun
text: Solar radiation causes drastic temperature swings in the snowpack. South-facing slopes can be dangerous on warm, sunny days immediately following storms. However, over time, these slopes stabilize as the added heat promotes bonding between layers. Snow on north-facing slopes does not stabilize as quickly and is more hazardous through most of the winter. Note. This effect is reversed in the Southern Hemisphere.

heading: Start Zone Characteristics
text: The steepness of a slope, or its slope angle, is the primary factor that determines if an avalanche will occur. Most large avalanches occur on slopes between 30 degrees and 45 degrees . Slopes above 60 degrees often do not build up significant quantities of snow because they are too steep. Snow will slide off as frequent, small sloughs. Under most conditions, slopes below 25 degrees do not slide. (See figure 5-3.)

heading: Start Zone Characteristics
text:
The shape of the slope will also affect the forces within the snowpack, concentrating tension in specific areas where it requires less force to trigger an avalanche. (See figure 5-4, page 68.)
- Profile or shape--
- Convex slopes. Slabs are most likely to fracture just below the bulge where stress is greatest. Convex rollovers have little support and are often steeper than the surrounding slope, making them a likely trigger point.
- Planar slopes. On these broad, smooth slopes, avalanches can happen anywhere. Slabs often fracture below cliff bands.
- Concave slopes. These slopes provide a certain amount of support through compression at the base of the hollow, but they are still capable of avalanching, especially on large slopes.
- Anchoring--
- Boulders, trees, and ledges act as anchors and help hold the snow in place until they are buried.
- Anchors can be areas of stress concentration because the snow upslope is held in place while the snow below or to the sides are pulled downhill by gravity. For this reason, anchors can be starting points for initial failure to occur, and fractures often run from tree to tree or rock to rock.

heading: Terrain Traps
text: Terrain traps are features that increase the consequences of being caught in an avalanche. Examples include cliffs, gullies, creeks, lakes, trees, benches, or roads where debris will pile up, crevasses, or bergschrunds. Some terrain traps increase trauma during an avalanche. Others increase burial depth, making survival more unlikely.

heading: TRIGGERS
text:
All avalanche triggers, whether caused by natural forces or human actions, are due to overloading the cohesive strength of the snowpack:
- Natural--avalanches may be triggered by new snow, falling rock, snow, ice, or smaller avalanches. Solar warming erodes bonds and can trigger avalanches. Naturally occurring avalanches are a critical warning sign that the conditions for an avalanche exist on similar slopes. If natural avalanches are possible, human triggered avalanches are likely.
- Human--most victims trigger the avalanches that kill them. People apply significant force to the snowpack. The impact of that force depends on snow density and distribution of force. A Soldier traveling on skis will not stress the snowpack as deep as a Soldier on foot will. Vehicles apply even more force. When a collapse occurs in a weak layer, it can propagate long distances up or across the slope.

heading: TYPES OF AVALANCHES
text: Avalanches can be categorized into two broad categories: loose snow and slab avalanches. (See figure 5-5, page 70.) Loose snow slides start with less snow and pick up more snow as they descend. Slab avalanches occur when one or more layers of cohesive snow break away as a unit and are generally more destructive.

heading: TYPES OF AVALANCHES
text: There are many variations of these types, each with distinct characteristics. These characteristics are defined by the structures within the snowpack, how an avalanche is released, and where it is found in the terrain. These avalanche problems guide group discussions, route planning, terrain choices, and the observations made during snowpack evaluation.

heading: LOOSE-DRY AVALANCHES
text: A loose-dry avalanche is a release of dry, unconsolidated snow. These avalanches occur within layers of soft snow near the surface of the snowpack. Loose-dry avalanches start at a point and entrain snow as they move downhill, forming a fan-shaped avalanche. Other names for loose-dry avalanches include point-release avalanches or sluffs. Loose-dry avalanches can trigger slab avalanches that break into deeper snow layers. Loose-dry avalanches are usually less dangerous than other avalanche problems but can be hazardous when combined with terrain traps, such as gullies, rocks, dense timber, cliffs, or crevasses. (See figure 5-5, page 70.)

heading: STORM SLAB AVALANCHES
text: A storm slab avalanche is a release of a soft cohesive layer (a slab) of new snow that breaks within the storm snow or on the old snow surface. Storm-slab problems last between a few hours and a few days but often stabilize quickly. (See figure 5-5, page 70.)

heading: WIND SLAB AVALANCHES
text: A wind slab avalanche is the release of a cohesive layer of snow (a slab) formed by the wind. Wind transports snow from the upwind sides of terrain features and deposits snow on the downwind side. Wind slabs are often smooth and rounded, sound hollow sometimes, and can range from soft to hard. Wind slabs form in specific areas and are confined to lee and cross-loaded terrain features. They can be avoided by sticking to sheltered or wind-scoured areas. (See figure 5-5, page 70.)

heading: PERSISTENT SLAB AVALANCHES
text: A persistent slab avalanche is a release of a cohesive layer of soft to hard snow (a slab) in the middle to upper snowpack, when the bond to an underlying persistent weak layer breaks. Persistent weak layers can continue to produce avalanches for days, weeks, or even months, making them challenging to manage. As additional snow and wind events build a thicker slab on top of the persistent weak layer, this avalanche problem may develop into a deep, persistent slab. They can be triggered by light loads and last weeks after the last storm. The slabs often propagate in surprising and unpredictable ways, making this problem difficult to predict and manage, and require a wide safety buffer to handle the uncertainty. The best ways to manage the risk from persistent slabs are to make conservative terrain choices. (See figure 5-5, page 70.) Note. Storm slabs and wind slabs formed over persistent weak layers are also considered persistent slabs.

heading: DEEP, PERSISTENT SLAB AVALANCHES
text: A deep, persistent slab avalanche is a release of a thick, cohesive layer of hard snow (a slab), when the bond breaks between the slab and an underlying "persistent" weak layer, deep in the snowpack or near the ground. Deep, persistent slabs are difficult to trigger but are very destructive and dangerous because of the large mass of snow involved. Once developed, they can persist for months or an entire winter season. They are often triggered from areas where the snow is shallow and weak and are difficult to forecast and manage. (See figure 5-5, page 70.)

heading: WET-LOOSE AVALANCHES
text: A wet-loose avalanche is a release of wet, unconsolidated snow or slush. These avalanches occur within layers of wet snow near the surface of the snowpack but may quickly gouge into lower snowpack layers. Like dry-loose avalanches, they start at a point and entrain snow as they move downhill, forming a fan-shaped avalanche. They often carve channels or paths through the snowpack to which subsequent avalanches are constrained. They move slowly but can contain enough mass to cause significant damage to trees, cars, or buildings. To avoid wet-loose avalanches, travel when the snow surface is colder and stronger. Plan movements to avoid crossing on or under very steep slopes in the afternoon. Move to colder, shadier slopes once the snow surface turns slushy. Avoid steep, sunlit slopes above terrain traps, cliffs, and long steep slopes. (See figure 5-5.)

heading: WET SLAB AVALANCHES
text: A wet slab avalanche is a release of a cohesive layer of wet snow (a slab) when the flow of liquid water weakens the bond between the slab and the surface below (snow or ground). They often occur during prolonged warming events or rain-on-snow events. Wet slabs can be very destructive. Avoid terrain where and when wet slab avalanche activity is expected. Give suspect slopes a wide safety buffer to handle the uncertainty. (See figure 5-5.)

heading: CORNICE FALL
text: Cornice fall is the release of an overhanging mass of snow that forms as the wind moves snow over a sharp terrain feature, such as a ridge, and deposits snow on the downwind (leeward) side. Cornices range in size from small wind lips of soft snow to large overhangs of hard snow that are 10 meters (30 feet) or taller. They can break off suddenly. Even small cornices can have enough mass to be destructive and deadly. Cornice fall can entrain loose surface snow or trigger slab avalanches. Cornices can never be trusted and avoiding them is necessary for safe travel. Stay well back from ridgeline areas with cornices. They often overhang the ridge edge; they can be triggered remotely. Avoid areas underneath cornices, especially during periods of significant warming. (See figure 5-5.)

heading: GLIDE (FULL DEPTH) AVALANCHES
text: A glide avalanche is a release of the entire snow cover at the ground surface. Glide avalanches can be composed of wet, moist, or almost entirely dry snow. They occur in very specific paths, where the slope is steep enough and the ground surface is smooth. They often occur on south-facing slopes during periods of strong sun and warm temperatures. They may be proceeded by full depth cracks (glide cracks), though the time between the appearance of a crack and an avalanche can vary between seconds and months. Predicting the release of glide avalanches is very challenging. Because they only occur on very specific slopes, avoidance is key to safe travel. Glide cracks and other glide avalanches are indicators. (See figure 5-5.)

heading: FORECASTS
text: In areas with extensive avalanche terrain and conditions, there are regional offices with staff members that monitor weather and snowpack conditions and produce forecasts to warn the public of avalanche hazards. Forecasts are created using a combination of weather models, remote weather stations, snowpack data, and field observations. Forecasts use the North American Avalanche Danger Scale and add additional information regarding specific avalanche problems, location in the terrain, likelihood of triggering, and expected size.

heading: NORTH AMERICAN DANGER SCALE
text: The North American Avalanche Danger Scale is a tool used by avalanche forecasters to communicate the potential for avalanches to cause harm or injury to backcountry travelers. It converts the forecasters' projections of the size and distribution of avalanches and likelihood of triggering into travel advice. (See figure 5-6.)

heading: AVALANCHE PROBLEM
text: In addition to the danger rating, forecasters publish a more detailed discussion of the avalanche problem. The avalanche problem describes the types of potential avalanche, the expected location based on aspect and elevation, the likelihood of triggering, and the expected size. Specific avalanche problems with similar ratings on the danger scale may present differently and require different terrain choices. (See figure 5-7, page 72.)

heading: USING THE FORECAST
text: The forecast is a starting point to guide planning for patrols or missions. In addition, planners should consult a record of the season's conditions and current weather. Group discussion, identifying the hazard, communicating recent observations, and planning routes with clear decision points are all part of the decision-making framework used to manage avalanche risk.

heading: SECTION II - AVALANCHE RISK MANAGEMENT
text: More than any other hazard faced in the mountains, avalanches pose the most significant threat of a catastrophic accident for an entire element. There is inherent uncertainty in any forecast, even those produced by avalanche professionals, and the consequence of being caught in an avalanche are high. The best control measure is avoiding all avalanche terrain. However, this is not always possible. In some mountain ranges, even valleys, roads, and railways are threatened by avalanches when dangerous weather conditions are present. Key terrain and approaches to it may be in avalanche terrain. Much of the time, the snowpack may be stable and safe for travel, but without an understanding of specific hazards and their locations in the terrain, units can be dangerously exposed.

heading: SECTION II - AVALANCHE RISK MANAGEMENT
text: Education is the greatest tool for managing avalanche hazard. Unit commanders are responsible for implementing avalanche training. They must understand the hazards that Soldiers may be exposed to and ensure that subordinate leaders and Soldiers are prepared for those threats. Units should have designated unit members with formal avalanche training and education.

heading: UNIT-LEVEL RESPONSIBILITIES
text: Avalanche hazard shuts down large areas to maneuver. As part of their intelligence preparation of the battlefield, units need to analyze terrain, snowpack, and weather factors to develop a forecast for subordinate elements. Route planning, terrain selection, and risk decisions are all driven by a forecast.

heading: UNIT-LEVEL RESPONSIBILITIES
text: When training in the United States, units may have access to avalanche forecasts being generated at avalanche centers in our geographic regions. These forecasts identify the avalanche problems and locations in the terrain and assign them a danger rating based off the likelihood of triggering them and their size. These forecasts guide route planning and help to evaluate the overall risk. To develop an operational capability, units must identify and develop key personnel that can evaluate the hazards using weather data and snowpack observations within their area of operations.

heading: MILITARY MOUNTAINEER RESPONSIBILITIES
text:
Route planning and decision making are the primary tools to reduce exposure and avoid avalanche prone terrain and being caught in an avalanche. The following skills are critical for travel in avalanche terrain:
- Terrain analysis--military mountaineers must be able to use information from an avalanche forecast to identify and inform commanders of hazardous slopes and safe corridors within their area of operations. They must also recognize terrain traps. To travel safely below avalanche terrain, they must estimate run-out zones (how far an avalanche may travel before it stops). This can vary and is determined by snow cover and snow depth.
- Route selection--routes with terrain angles that are less than 30 degrees and greater than 45 degrees should be identified, and care must be taken to ensure routes are not threatened by overhead avalanche hazard. The safest routes are on ridge tops, slightly on the windward side. Valley bottoms can provide safe routes, but lines of travel must be far from the bottom of slopes, clear of any run-out zones. Avoid cornices from above or below. Take advantage of dense timber, ridges, or rocky outcrops as islands of safety. Use them for rest stops.
- Critical weather analysis--changes in the following weather factors that increase loads on the snowpack or erode bonds will directly contribute to increasing avalanche danger:
- Rain.
- Snowfall of more than 2.5 cm (1 inch) an hour or more than 30 cm (1 foot) in 24 hours.
- New or recent wind loading.
- Rapid rise in temperature.
- Stability analysis--direct signs of instability, such as those noted below, should be viewed as clear evidence of immediate danger to Soldiers traveling in similar terrain:
- Evidence of avalanching and recent avalanches on similar slopes.
- Shooting cracks--a shooting crack is evidence of a slab or weak layer combination.
- Whoomphing sounds--hollow sounds when moving through the snow. These are evidence of the collapse of a weak layer. On a steeper slope, a whoomph could trigger an avalanche.
- Deliberate triggering:
- Types--avalanches can be triggered using explosives. Soldiers can use recoilless rifles, artillery, and mortars to trigger avalanches. Small charges of C4 explosive (1 to 2 kilograms) with a time fuse are effective if Soldiers can drop the charge to a point in the slope that triggers an avalanche.
- Uses--deliberate triggering can be used for force protection. Soldiers can trigger small avalanches so that larger avalanches do not threaten key positions and infrastructures. Soldiers can use avalanches to deny key terrain to the enemy, and to block roads and narrow passes. Mountaineer Soldiers can use deliberate triggering of avalanches offensively to isolate elements that they desire to engage with direct fire and indirect fire assets.
- Principles--understanding what cause avalanches and where they are likely to occur are useful for selecting the best triggering locations. Choose a point of maximum tension in the snowpack to detonate the charge.
- Planning and supervising avalanche training--leaders must ensure that all Soldiers operating in avalanche terrain practice and rehearse individual avalanche protective measures. They must be capable of coordinating and leading the rescue if someone is caught in an avalanche.

heading: INDIVIDUAL RESPONSIBILITIES
text:
All Soldiers operating in avalanche terrain must be proficient in basic avalanche tasks. They must be able to travel in the terrain, be proficient with all equipment, and well drilled in tasks for companion rescue.
- Travel techniques--just as battle drills are rehearsed for tactical movement, troops moving in avalanche terrain must practice and rehearse movement techniques for limiting exposure to avalanche hazard by--
- Having a planned and rehearsed communication strategy. Be deliberate when passing through pockets of increased hazard.
- Zipping up clothing and other layers.
- Posting a spotter to observe the entire element as it passes through. Send one person across at a time. Stop on islands of safety. All Soldiers should travel in the same track. Set the track high, above potential start zones.
- Avalanche safety equipment--every Soldier operating in avalanche terrain should be equipped with the three basic items of avalanche rescue equipment. They should be trained and rehearsed in their use.
- Shovel--to dig out the victim. It should be constructed of aluminum and collapsed or disassembled in a pack where it is protected and will not be lost but easily accessed. E-tools are insufficient for this purpose.
- Transceiver--an active radio-beacon transceiver designed for finding people buried under snow. When turned on, it broadcasts a signal that other transceivers can locate with a range of about 30 meters.
- Probe--a long pole used to confirm the location of an avalanche victim and to measure how deeply they are buried.
- Survival--try to escape quickly out of the side of the avalanche. An alternative for if or when Soldiers are caught in the start zone and before debris gains speed is to arrest in the bed surface and let the snow flow past. If Soldiers are caught, they should discard equipment and attempt to swim to stay closer to the surface. If their head goes under the snow, they should shut their mouth and use their elbow to form an air pocket in front of their face by reaching across the body and grabbing the opposite shoulder strap of the rucksack. Many avalanche victims suffocate because their mouth and nose are plugged with snow. The opposite arm can be used to attempt to reach for the surface. Although often difficult to tell surface direction when tumbling, many victims have been quickly found when a rescuer found a hand or body part sticking out of the snow. When the snow stops, try to relax. If Soldiers feel themselves about to pass out, they should not fight it. Once unconscious, respirations are shallower, pulse rates slower, and body temperature lower, all of which help to conserve oxygen.
- Companion rescue--a fast, efficient transceiver search and shoveling are key to the survival of an avalanche victim. Avalanche rescue is covered in-depth in section III.

heading: SNOWPACK EVALUATIONS
text:
Snowpack stability evaluation can be difficult in the absence of direct evidence, such as recent avalanches, whoomphing, or shooting cracks. It is also especially difficult when it has been several days since new loading has occurred (rain, new snow, wind-transported snow), several days without significant temperature changes, or in situations where a "persistent" weak layer exists in the snowpack. During these times, experienced Soldiers may use a multitude of tests to help determine stability and identify particularly dangerous terrain. These tests are limited, because their accuracy is localized to the vicinity and should only be used to determine where not to go. Typically conducted by master mountaineers, these tests require a high degree of skill and training both to perform and interpret; therefore, specific procedures are not covered in detail in this manual. Most of these tests require the digging of snow pits in safe locations that are specifically representative of terrain that is in question (same aspect and elevation). These snow pits can have a range of dimensions that can be modified depending upon the types and quantities of tests to be conducted; however, they are typically 2-meters across the slope by 1.5-meters up slope and dug to below the depth of any weak layers in question.
- Layer identification--used to identify specific areas of concern within the snowpack, for example, layers with major differences in characteristics. This could be major differences in hardness, softness, gain size, and shape.
- Shovel tilt--used to evaluate bonding between the most recent storm snow and the old snow surface. Also used to identify thin weak layers not found during layer identification. Limited to the top 45 cm of the snowpack.
- Compression test--used to locate weak layers in the top 1 meter of snow and to provide an indication of triggering potential on nearby slopes with similar conditions.
- Extended column test--used to test for the potential of crack propagation of a pre-identified slab or weak layer combination in the upper 1 meter of the snowpack.
- Propagation saw test--used to test for the potential of crack propagation of a pre-identified slab or weak layer combination that is greater than 1-meter deep.
- Rutschblock--used to test stability of pre-identified weak layers up to 1-meter deep with skis.
- Explosives--used to test slopes and trigger slides in the top layers of the snowpack. Placement in the sensitive regions of the start zone is critical for getting a reaction.
- Hasty tests (hand shear, pole plants, test slopes)--nonstandardized tests that can be used quickly while traveling in the terrain to determine signs of instability or to recognize when conditions are changing.

heading: SNOWPACK EVALUATIONS
text: Avalanches pose a significant threat to Soldiers operating in mountainous terrain. Unlike fall hazards, or weather conditions, avalanche hazard is not easily observed. If units wish to maintain the ability to conduct operations during winter months or in regions of the world with the possibility of snow throughout the year, they must develop the capability to assess avalanche hazard. This means identifying individuals for further training and education, incorporating avalanche forecasts into the planning process, and ensuring that all Soldiers operating in the terrain are equipped and trained for the avalanche threat.

heading: SECTION III - AVALANCHE SEARCH AND RESCUE
text: The primary risk mitigation tool in avalanche terrain is avoidance. In the planning phase, Soldiers should make every effort to patrol routes that avoid avalanche hazards. The planning phase includes having clear decision points from which to evaluate conditions and viable alternate routes. However, when evaluating an avalanche hazard, there is often a high degree of uncertainty. When mistakes are made, the consequences are high. Avalanches produce incredible energy. Soldiers caught in an avalanche may be injured or killed by blunt force trauma from collisions with rock, ice, and trees. If they come to rest with an intact air pocket, they may succumb to hypothermia or shock. However, most avalanche victims die from asphyxiation. Without an air pocket, unconsciousness may come in minutes, followed rapidly by permeant brain injury and death. Evidence has shown that after 15 minutes, the chances of surviving complete burial decreases from 90 percent to 30 percent. It is critical that all Soldiers operating in avalanche terrain are equipped with avalanche safety equipment and are drilled in companion rescue.

heading: AVALANCHE SEARCH
text: All individuals traveling into terrain in which avalanches could possibly occur must be familiar with and carry the following equipment: avalanche transceiver, lightweight shovel, and collapsible probe. Soldiers must be adequately trained in their use during avalanche rescue.

heading: TRANSCEIVER
text: Avalanche transceivers (beacons) are radio transceivers that emit a pulsed signal. (See figure 5-8, page 76.) When turned on, they broadcast a signal that other transceivers can locate within a range of approximately 30 meters. Other transceivers can be switched into a search mode to receive that signal and find transceivers buried under the snow. Soldiers should wear their transceiver over the top of their base layers but underneath insulating layers that may be removed or added throughout the course of the day. Soldiers should always wear their transceiver below a layer to protect it in case of an avalanche.

heading: TRANSCEIVER
text: Electronic interference has been shown to interfere with the range and accuracy of avalanche transceivers, especially in search mode. Manufacturers recommend that transceivers are worn 30 cm (12 inches) away from any radios, cell phones, and GPS devices to ensure that there is no metal or reflective material (such as meals, ready to eat wrappers) in the area around where the device is worn. This may not be possible when wearing combat equipment, but in a training environment, every effort should be made to adhere to manufacturer recommendations. In search mode, manufacturers recommend that Soldiers turn off all other devices and keep the transceiver at least 50 cm from other devices. If possible, Soldiers with radios and active electronic equipment should delegate transceiver searches to those without electronic equipment and radios.

heading: SHOVEL
text: Shovels suitable for avalanche rescue are lightweight and made of aluminum. They are durable enough to cut through dense avalanche debris but light enough to for Soldiers to carry while skiing or mountaineering. Soldiers can collapse or disassemble their shovel to carry it inside their pack. Soldiers should pack their transceiver, so it is quickly accessible. (See figure 5-8, page 76.)

heading: PROBE
text: Probes are used to confirm the location of a burial before digging. Probes are approximately 3-meters long. They collapse to fit disassembled inside a pack but deploy quickly with a pull of the connecting cable. They should lock into place automatically. Soldiers should carry their probes inside their pack in a location where it is protected and immediately accessible.

heading: GROUP CHECKS
