text: All Soldiers must be familiar with the group avalanche equipment functions check process before movement into avalanche terrain. All leaders must be familiar with conducting these functions checks to ensure that their unit is prepared to respond to an avalanche burial event. All Soldiers must be familiar with avalanche response actions. SOPs and rehearsals should be conducted in the same manner as battle drills.

heading: PRECOMBAT CHECKS
text:
Soldiers must be trained and familiar with each equipment item and how it functions. Individual and team rehearsals, transceiver checks, and rescue drills are necessary:
- Check that individual rescue equipment is functional and stowed appropriately.
- Conduct verbal rehearsals of all avalanche tasks, movement through danger areas, and avalanche rescue.

heading: TRANSCEIVER CHECK
text:
A group check confirms that each member of the element knows how to turn on the device and switch between modes, ensures that every device can receive and search for a signal, and that every device transmits a signal. Manufacturers recommended procedures for group checks might vary.
- Locate an area away from other groups that may cause conflicting signals. Stand in a half circle an arm's length or more apart, with the leader a few meters away in the middle of the group.
- Turn transceivers on. As the transceivers power on, each individual confirms that the transceiver runs a self-check, and the display is ok. Note battery strength and report it aloud to the group. For patrols or missions lasting less than 24 hours, battery life should be a minimum of 50 percent. For multi-day missions, each Soldier should begin with fresh batteries.
- Switch all transceivers to search mode. Silence indicates that everyone is ready and ensures that no transmitting units are in packs or sleds.
- The leader then switches to transmit/send and checks that each group member can receive a signal by walking toward each group member one by one while group members read their display aloud.
- Turn all units to transmit. The leader ensures that group members stow their unit for the day, secured under an outside layer, and 30 cm from a cell phone or radio.
- The leader returns to Search mode and confirms all group members are transmitting. The check-leader then switches to transmit mode and confirms to at least one group member, who also verifies that the leader's device is transmitting and properly stowed.

heading: AVALANCHE RESCUE
text: Units must be prepared to conduct avalanche rescue when operating in avalanche terrain. Avalanches, especially those involving Soldier burial, will significantly affect tactical operations. Commanders must provide clear guidance regarding subordinate unit response to avalanche burial events during tactical operations. This guidance should cover avalanche victim rescue priority in relation to mission conduct, affected unit response SOPs, higher unit response capabilities and SOPs, and reporting expectations. Maneuver units must be capable of finding and digging out victims quickly. Unit commanders must plan for and be prepared to organize rescue operations for avalanche mass casualty events, as well as deliberate body location and recovery.

heading: ORGANIZING THE RESCUE
text:
The normal chain of command may be broken if a leader is buried or separated. Everyone should be prepared to organize and take charge of a rescue. Every Soldier must be prepared to make critical decisions and tasks for an efficient and successful rescue.
- Assess safety--determine if there is further avalanche hazard. If there is risk of secondary avalanches (hangfire), limit the number of personnel exposed to further hazard. Post a watch and a relay to maintain communications.
- Headcount--get an accurate headcount to find out how many Soldiers are buried.
- Report or call for help--do not waste time; report the accident to get resources moving if a Soldier needs them. If possible, delegate and leave a relay up high to maintain communications. Do not let radio operators in the rear or at a dispatch delay or interfere with the rescue.
- Switch all transceivers to Search mode--physically ensure that all unit members have switched their transceivers to Search mode to avoid disrupting the searchers. Just one rescuer still transmitting will confuse the searchers and waste precious time.
- Assign roles--in small teams, everyone may need to help with the transceiver search. In a larger group, assign some to search and others to prepare probes and shovels.
- Determine where to search--the spotter should have been able to observe a point last seen. Search the fall line below the point last seen. Search the run-out zone and other areas of deposition, such as terrain traps. Search in line with equipment clues if they exist.

heading: TRANSCEIVER SEARCH
text:
Transceiver searches involve three distinct phases: signal search, course search, and fine search.
- Signal search--begin searching for a signal. Get all the searchers online with 40-meter spacing to ensure that the search ranges overlap across the entire search area. If alone, or covering a very wide search area, use a search pattern that covers the entire path. Movement should be rapid but deliberate. Keep eyes up, searching for physical clues. (See figure 5-9, page 78.)
- Course search--once a signal is found, the transceivers change tones and light up with a distance and direction. Slow down and follow the arrow. Communicate with the other searchers, calling out the distance reading. At 10 meters, slow down even further. Ensure the transceiver aligns with the direction arrow. Continue moving slowly and bring the transceiver lower and closer to the surface of the snow. Avoid sudden movements or changes in orientation.
- Fine search--inside 3 meters, transition to a fine search. The transceiver should be moving in a plane just above the surface of the snow. Maintain orientation throughout the rest of the search. Do not twist or turn it. Continue the azimuth of approach until the numbers start to rise. Return to the low point, and search side to side, far enough to see the numbers rise, returning to the point with the lowest number.

heading: PROBING
text: Mark the lowest point with a foot or hand. Probe at the low point, perpendicular to the snow surface. Probing must be conducted with both hands. (See figure 5-10.) If no strike is felt, probe again 2 cm uphill and continue to probe in a spiral search pattern. Once a probe strike is achieved, do not remove the probe. This probe is a valuable reference point that must be visible to ensure Soldiers do not waste effort and energy during shoveling.

heading: SHOVELING
text: Upon probe strike, take 1 large step downhill, 2 steps for a deep burial (greater than 2 meters). Rescuers should excavate snow from the side so that they are not lifting snow out of a hole. They should dig towards the probe and throw the snow far away while shoveling as fast and hard as possible. If there is a large group, rotate personnel often. Those who are not shoveling in the hole should continue to move snow out of the way and widen and improve the platform the others are creating. Everyone must prepare to switch out often so that those shoveling are doing so at maximum capacity. (See figure 5-11, page 80.)

heading: PATIENT CARE
text: Work to clear the victim's airway as soon as possible. Provide first aid and CPR as required. With long burials where there is a risk of hypothermia, move the patient gently. Move the patient to safe terrain and begin planning for evacuation.

heading: PROBE SEARCHES
text: Avalanche burials longer than 15 minutes can result in permanent brain damage and death. If victims are going to be saved, it is critical that it is done quickly. If the Soldier is not wearing a transceiver, the likelihood of finding them in time for survival is small.

heading: PROBE SEARCHES
text:
If transceivers are unavailable, it is likely there are no probes available either. Soldiers can use their ski poles with the basket removed to begin initial probing attempts. If there is any hope of success, searchers must focus their efforts on the most probable locations.
- Start the search from the point last seen.
- Look for equipment clues. Gloves, hats, ski poles, packs--all may give clues to the trajectory of the victim or may still be attached. Pull each out of the snow to confirm.
- Most buried victims are carried to the place of greatest deposition, usually the toe of the slide. Any terrain features that catch and hold avalanche debris, such as outside curves, are also likely locations.
- Vegetation, rocks, and other obstacles act as strainers and may catch or slow the victim.

heading: PROBE LINES
text: For body recovery of individuals without transceivers, it may be necessary to locate them using a probe line. A probe line is a systematic search, online, through the entire debris field. It is a slow process and requires many rescuers. A probe line is not appropriate when there is still an overhead avalanche hazard.

heading: PROBE LINES
text: There are two distinct probing methods: coarse probe and fine probe. Coarse probing is intended to be fast, with wide spacing of probe insertions. Fine probing involves close-spaced probing with an emphasis on thoroughness. The coarse-probe technique has about a 70-percent chance of locating the victim on a given pass, while the fine probe has closer to a 100-percent chance of locating the victim. This page intentionally left blank.

heading: Mountain Mobility
text: A unit's ability to maneuver through difficult and hazardous terrain provides it with access to the most tactically advantageous areas in the mountains. Units with Soldiers trained to a high level of mobility can move further, faster, and more safely through all levels of terrain. Mobility skill is the primary tool to manage risk when there is a fall hazard. Rope systems and belays can be used to mitigate fall risk during movement but require more time to complete, more technical training to accomplish, and can result in increased exposure to enemy attack. By far, the greatest combat multiplier in the mountains is high mobility skill. Units anticipating combat operations should focus on building individual movement skills over nearly all other special technical or tactical skills.

heading: SECTION I - INDIVIDUAL MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES
text: The speed at which the unit can move, the complexity of terrain they can negotiate unroped, and the violence of action they can muster as a team on the objective are all determined by the mobility of the unit's weakest members. Properly equipped units with mobility skills are more likely to outmaneuver the enemy in physically demanding and hazardous terrain. Soldiers who have been trained in mobility techniques can take advantage of terrain above operational level 2. This provides commanders with access to the highest and most difficult to reach points of domination in their areas of operation. For those untrained in mountaineering, such terrain can prove too hazardous to move in. However, units well-trained to maneuver here can take advantage of reduced combat risks during all types of combat operations by owning ground that most enemy forces cannot access, granting them overwhelming tactical advantage. As a result, individual mobility skills training should always be a high priority for units anticipating these operations.

heading: MOBILITY
text: Individual mobility comprises many factors, the most important of which are fitness and movement techniques. Soldiers can increase their mobility by practicing the movement techniques specific to negotiating rough terrain. Soldiers build proficiency by approaching movement from a skill-building perspective, whether the movement is walking, scrambling, or climbing, and regardless of whether the surface is dirt, rock, snow, or ice. The hallmarks of mobility are balance, surefootedness, and net endurance. The results are reduced likelihood of slipping or falling, reduced energy expended, increased speed, and the ability to focus on other critical tasks. A reasonable goal for Soldiers is the ability to move confidently through 3rd-class terrain unroped, even when exposed to fall hazards that would result in significant injury or death.

heading: BALANCE
text: The most important aspect of mobility is balance. Soldiers who learn to move in such a way that their body is rarely out of balance will display a higher level of surefootedness and endurance than ones who have not mastered this skill.

heading: BALANCE
text: Moving in balance requires a basic understanding of how the human body moves, how gravity and other forces act upon it, and how to counteract them. In the beginning of skills development, Soldiers can build knowledge by paying attention to when they feel out of balance, such as when they are stepping around, over, or under small obstacles in their path. Carrying a pack or heavy tactical equipment high on the body will increase the effort required to stay in balance.

heading: BALANCE
text: As Soldiers begin to identify when movements put them out of balance, they should begin to experiment with adjusting body position, or foot placement, to maintain the feeling of being in balance. Early in training, achieving a less out-of-balance feeling may be the best a Soldier can achieve. Through practice, this will improve.

heading: BALANCE
text: The complexity or severity of the terrain will determine the difficulty of the movement techniques and body positions required. Techniques for 5th-class rock climbing are much less intuitive than those necessary for hiking, but the principles for building skill are the same for both, and across the spectrum of difficulty.

heading: BALANCE
text: With enough focus and practice, Soldiers will develop enough skill that moving becomes natural and requires little effort. At that point, they can focus on other mission critical tasks, such as navigation, security, communicating, firing weapon systems, moving casualties or any other complex tasks without the distraction of trying not to fall.

heading: FITNESS
text: Soldiers develop and improve their mountain fitness through strengthening muscles that move and stabilize the body. Although strength in some large muscle groups is useful to move the body uphill against the pull of gravity, muscles used in maintaining balance are far more important. Recovering from a slip or stumble requires far more energy than just maintaining balance and footing in the first place. Well-developed supporting and stabilizing muscles prevent these slips and stumbles and reduce the burden on large muscle groups. In this way, mountain Soldiers are better at controlling corrective movements and conserving energy, which reduces fatigue and results in greater endurance over the course of a movement. (See FM 7-22 for more information on training specific muscle groups.)

heading: FITNESS
text: Flexibility is another important aspect of fitness. Soldiers who are flexible have a greater range of movement. Soldiers with low flexibility may not be able to perform movements necessary to negotiate some obstacles. Soldiers should develop flexibility along with strength when training for mobility in the mountains.

heading: FITNESS
text: General combat fitness does not translate to mountain fitness. Ruck marching, especially over relatively level ground, does not develop the balance and flexibility necessary for movement over rough, broken, and steep terrain. Upper body mass developed through heavy body building regimens does nothing for dismounted mobility and little for scrambling and climbing. A holistic approach to fitness is necessary. Physical training plans must balance combat fitness and mountain fitness requirements to best prepare Soldiers for combat action.

heading: FITNESS
text: A Soldier's role within the unit should be considered when training for the physical requirements of the mountains. An advanced military mountaineer who will be responsible for regular movement in 4th- and 5th-class terrain requires a higher level of mobility than a machine gunner does.

heading: MOUNTAIN WALKING
text: Most terrain negotiated during combat operations in mountainous terrain requires only well-developed walking skills. However, this terrain is typically undeveloped, broken, steep and covered by loose dirt, rock, or snow. Surfaces are often slick. Heavy loads, nonuniform stride, and unpredictable footing challenge Soldiers moving in any of these conditions. Half of the battle for mountaineers is knowing where to step under these variable conditions to gain maximum traction, and the other half is knowing how to position their body to ensure their footing holds.

heading: TYPES OF TERRAIN
text: Typically, mountain-walking terrain is considered class 1 and 2 terrains, but these skills are equally important in terrain that is more difficult. Mountain-walking techniques provide the foundation for higher-level skills, such as climbing. They require the same level of focus and practice to master.

heading: MOBILITY EQUIPMENT
text: Quality footwear, such as mountaineering boots, reduces many risks associated with moving in mountainous terrain. Quality boots increase both mobility and security of footing and can reduce orthopedic injuries. Boots designed for mountaineering range in weight, breathability, flexibility, and in how well they interface with other equipment. The rand helps protect the toe area from sharp rock and standing water. They have a high enough upper boot to protect the wearer's ankles from sharp rock and provide joint support against rolling. They have recessed soles made of softer rubber, a protective band around the forefoot, at least a partial shank, and are constructed with abrasion and water-resistant materials. Mountain boot soles are designed for traction on dirt and slick rock alike. Their stiffer, stickier rubber soles provide a significant advantage when climbing.

heading: MOBILITY EQUIPMENT
text: Quality socks are more durable, help reduce blisters, better manage moisture, and dry faster than other materials.

heading: MOBILITY EQUIPMENT
text: Good quality insoles are critical to reducing minor foot injuries, such as blisters, during movement in rough, rocky terrain that can interfere with mission completion if they progress untreated.

heading: MOBILITY EQUIPMENT
text: Most Soldiers do not require special packs in walking terrain if they assemble their packs neatly and do not overload them.

heading: MOBILITY EQUIPMENT
text: The rucksack is the issued, modular lightweight load-carrying equipment (MOLLE) pack. The carry harness should be adjusted to the body of the Soldier carrying it. Soldiers should place heavier items close to the frame. Heavy items attached to the outside of, or higher on the pack, increase strain on the Soldier and raise the Soldier's center of gravity, increasing the effort required to stay in balance. Soldiers should remove large pouches that they usually attach to the outside of MOLLE packs to streamline the pack and reduce its likelihood of being caught on obstacles. Soldiers should use compression straps to prevent loads from shifting and throwing them off balance. They should use waist belts to support the weight on their hips and lower their center of gravity.

heading: MOBILITY EQUIPMENT
text: Mountaineering packs are designed to be slimmer, taller, and lighter than Army packs. Typically, mountaineering packs are not designed with organization and accessibility in mind but rather to consolidate loads close to the body and to make movement and balance easier. They are generally less durable than Army packs; however, crossover packs, designed for remote mountain hunting, provide an excellent middle ground. The drawback of crossover packs is the high expense.

heading: MOBILITY EQUIPMENT
text: Using assault packs when walking terrain can reduce the negative impact on Soldier mobility if loads are not too heavy. Their lack of a rigid frame means that they provide less support. If lashing items to the outside of the assault pack becomes necessary to carry all required items, then carrying a properly loaded MOLLE pack is probably less detrimental to the Soldier's mobility.

heading: GRASSY SLOPES
text: Grassy slopes are usually composed of small tussocks of growth rather than one continuous field. When ascending, step on the upper side of each hummock or tussock, where the ground is more level. When descending a grassy slope, climbers should use the traverse technique because of the uneven nature of the ground. A climber can easily build up too much speed and fall if a direct descent is attempted. When traversing, the climber's uphill foot points in the direction of travel. The downhill foot points about 45 degrees off the direction of travel (downhill). This maintains maximum sole contact and prevents possible downhill ankle rollout.

heading: MOUNTAIN WALKING
text:
Two critical skills in mountain walking are selecting foot placements and moving the body in a way that maintains balance with each step. (See figure 6-1, page 86.) These skills increase the security of foot placements and decrease slips. Surface characteristics vary greatly in mountains, and Soldiers should experiment with various features and surfaces in their operational environment. To obtain maximum traction on a given feature, Soldiers must position their bodies so that their weight pushes perpendicularly against the feature. Soldiers must reposition their body with each step to do this and should try to gain as much sole contact as possible to achieve maximum friction. As Soldiers become familiar with surface characteristics in their area of operation, they learn just how much friction is necessary for the footing to hold on various features such as the following:
- Common microfeatures that can provide greater footings are flat spots, small divots, or depressions, the uphill side of stable rocks and tussocks, rough rock features, dry spots, rough or heavily featured rock, and stable compact dirt.
- Common microfeatures that make traction more difficult to achieve and that should be avoided if possible are smooth features, loose dirt or small rocks, wet spots, and any surface covered with loose debris, such as leaves or small sticks.

heading: MOUNTAIN WALKING
text: Selecting reliable foot placements is even more difficult while descending. This is primarily because they must be made dynamically (while stepping down) and often out of their ideal body position. This prevents the Soldier from testing the placement before committing weight. If a slip occurs, momentum increases the likelihood of a fall or tumble.

heading: MOUNTAIN WALKING
text:
General techniques for ascending:
- As terrain becomes steeper, routes should adopt a traversing or switchback pattern. This involves moving diagonally up and across a slope, then turning back and doing the same in the opposite direction as necessary. This switchback pattern reduces the intensity and demand on large muscle groups, slows the onset of fatigue, and allows Soldiers to maintain situational awareness. Charging in a straight line up a steep hill is more demanding, results in more extreme fatigue and longer recovery time, and increases the likelihood of slips, falls, and injury. This technique should be avoided unless speed is critical, and all members of the group are highly fit and experienced moving this way.
- The rest step technique involves locking out the rear leg briefly with each step. This gives muscles a micro rest with each step and results in greater endurance over long movements. (See figure 6-2, page 88.)
- Pressure breathing--this technique involves breathing all the way out on the exhale to empty the lungs of air. This does two positive things. First, it ensures all carbon dioxide is pushed out of the lungs, reducing the likelihood of cramping, and making more space for oxygenated air. Second, the negative pressure created in the lungs makes it easier to pull lower pressure air into them when moving at higher altitudes.

heading: MOUNTAIN WALKING
text:
General techniques for descending:
- Whenever Soldiers must use a questionable foot placement, they should identify a quick plan for how they will react prior to stepping down.
- Soldiers should ensure they bend their knees when stepping down to reduce impact on their joints. Prolonged descents often prove painful, and they could sustain long-term damage if they do not take measures to protect their joints under heavy loads.
- Poles are helpful when descending. They make it easier to stay in balance and allow the arms to absorb or reduce much of the impact on lower extremity joints. Even one pole can be very helpful.
- When Soldiers are new to walking in the mountains, it takes more focus to do so effectively. They move slower, but they benefit by moving at a rate that allows them to remain in balance without slipping and stumbling. Additionally, they improve mountain walking skills when allowed to move a little slower during training, becoming faster and more efficient in the end. Leaders should look at every dismounted movement in training as an opportunity to improve.

heading: MOUNTAIN WALKING
text: When a moderate pace is set, the need for rest halts decreases and the chance of personnel overheating lessens. Typically, shorter breaks taken more often are better than long breaks, especially in colder weather. However, leaders should consider fitness level, difficulty of the terrain, length of movement, speed, load, and level of fatigue when determining rest durations.

heading: MOUNTAIN WALKING
text: During the first half-hour of movement, an adjustment halt should be taken. Soldiers will loosen or tighten bootlaces as needed, adjust packs, and add or remove layers of clothing.

heading: Brush
text: Brush is both a help and a hindrance. Brush-filled gullies can provide routes and rally points concealed from observation; on the other hand, steep, brushy terrain is hazardous to negotiate. Cliffs and steep ravines are hidden traps, and blow downs and thickets can obstruct travel as much as manmade obstacles. When brush must be negotiated, take the most direct route across the obstacle; look for downed timber to use as raised paths through the obstacle; or create a tunnel through the obstacle by prying the brush apart, standing on lower branches, and using upper limbs for support.

heading: Dirt and Rocky Terrain
text: Surfaces comprised of mixed dirt are very common in mountainous terrain. As the terrain gets steeper and rockier, it typically becomes rougher and looser. This may require slowing the rate of movement to one that is maintainable by the less fit and skilled or overburdened members of the group. If this is not done, they are at risk of falling out or injury while struggling to catch up.

heading: Dirt and Rocky Terrain
text: Hard ground is firmly compacted, rocky soil that does not give way under the weight of a Soldier's step. It is usually found under mature forest canopy, in low brush or heather, and areas where animals have beaten out multiple trails. When ascending, employ the rest step to rest the leg muscles.

heading: Dirt and Rocky Terrain
text: Scree fields are comprised of loose rock approximately fist-sized or smaller, that are common in the mountains and are a challenge to ascend. The experience is like climbing sand, except that the loose rock can be rough on ankles and lower legs. Climbers should avoid ascending scree fields, if possible, as they demand the expenditure of much more energy than other surfaces. Soldiers should kick in with the toe of the upper foot so that a step is formed in the loose scree. After determining that the step is stable, the Soldier transfers weight to the upper leg, then steps up, and repeats the process with the lower foot. Traversing scree is very difficult, as the loose stones slide out from under the foot downslope with each step. On the other hand, they are often a good option for descent routes. Greater focus on maintaining balance is required since foot placements are invariably unstable. The best method for descending scree slopes is to come straight down the slope using a short shuffling step with the knees bent, back straight, feet pointed downhill, and heels dug in. When several climbers descend a scree slope together, they should be as close together as possible (one behind the other at single-arm interval) to prevent injury from dislodged rocks. Avoid running down scree as this can cause a loss of control.

heading: Dirt and Rocky Terrain
text: Talus fields are comprised of larger rocks. Often these rocks are loose and present a hazard to Soldiers moving through them. Soldiers must choose their foot placements carefully, often testing rocks to ensure they are stable. Typically, talus is easier to ascend than scree or loose dirt, but it is still demanding physically. Often it requires occasionally using hands for balance on steeper slopes. If a talus field is particularly unstable, then the switchback travel technique may not be appropriate for larger groups to use, as the risk of Soldiers higher on a slope knocking off a rock that hits Soldiers lower on the slope is potentially high.

heading: SCRAMBLING
text: Scrambling is the act of moving over difficult or broken terrain, characterized by using mostly walking techniques but requires some use of the hands for balance or other specific climbing techniques. It is perhaps the most dangerous means of mobility in which snow and ice are not present. At the lowest level, scrambling involves simply placing a hand or hands on features periodically to help maintain balance and improve efficiency during movement. At the higher level, scrambling involves Soldiers making multiple easy rock-climbing moves, followed by several steps walking, and repeating that sequence throughout an ascent.

heading: SCRAMBLING
text: Typically, 3rd-class terrain is where Soldiers begin scrambling, but just exactly what terrain and terrain features require is determined largely by the mobility skill of the individual Soldier. Soldiers with low-mobility skill will need to use hands more often, especially if a fall risk is present, which will slow their movement. Soldiers with higher mobility skills need to use their hands less often for balance enabling them to move faster even when a fall risk is present.

heading: SCRAMBLING
text: The higher the rock-climbing skill, the more quickly, efficiently, and safely Soldiers can scramble. The best way to train Soldiers to be better at scrambling is to provide rock-climbing training. Rock climbing is easier to protect with ropes and forces Soldiers to use better movement techniques even though rock-climbing training involves steeper and more difficult terrain.

heading: SCRAMBLING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS
text: Scrambling terrain can be some of the most dangerous terrain through which Soldiers can move. Often it is the low ground between higher terrain features or cliffs, subjecting it to falling object hazards and significant tactical disadvantage. Additionally, it can be exposed to fall hazards below.

heading: SCRAMBLING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS
text: Good reconnaissance and route planning are critical for movements through scrambling terrain. Whenever possible, small teams of advanced military mountaineers should be sent to find the best route ahead of the main body.

heading: SCRAMBLING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS
text: Maneuvering is incredibly difficult in terrain that requires a lot of scrambling. If enemy contact is a possibility, bounding overwatch must be used to ensure security during movement. Small teams may need to be sent forward to clear points of domination over the route. Sniper or machine gun overwatch positions may need to be established to cover movement through sections of terrain that is particularly exposed to enemy attack. All these security measures increase movement times significantly. (See ATP 3-21.50 for VDA-crossing TTP.)

heading: SCRAMBLING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS
text: Two-point slings should be used to secure rifles close to the body. Heavier weapon systems, such as sniper rifles and machine guns, may need to be secured to rucksacks close to the body during sustained scrambling to allow Soldiers to use their hands freely for assistance.

heading: SCRAMBLING CONSIDERATIONS
text: There are no scrambling specific movement techniques, but greater care in selecting hand and footholds is often necessary given the nature of the terrain. Possessing rock-climbing skills (discussed later in the chapter) increases the efficiency with which Soldiers can scramble. Vegetation may appear to provide good handholds but may easily pull free. Large boulders or masses of loose rock may be knocked free without warning. Groups should move in such a way that Soldiers further back in the formation are not subject to rockfall from those above. Some scrambling terrain may require simple fixed lines to aid movement. This is even more likely during descending. These sites must be identified, planned for, and established prior to the main body arriving for efficiency. (See chapter 11 for more techniques for moving on ropes.)

heading: CLIMBING ROCK
text: Climbing rock, typically 4th- and 5th-class terrain, requires a very high level of skill, especially when done for sustained periods. The probability and consequence of falls are high, even under the best conditions. Rope systems are usually necessary to protect climbers from injury or death, slowing movement and reducing tactical maneuverability.

heading: CLIMBING ROCK
text: Building rock-climbing skill increases the confidence and speed at which Soldiers can move unroped in easier terrain, even when subjected to higher fall consequence. Soldiers who possess moderate rock-climbing skills can maneuver more safely and efficiently unroped in easy terrain. This should be the goal for level 1 mountaineers. Soldiers with high rock-climbing skills can do the same in moderate terrain. This should be the goal for level 2 mountaineers.

heading: CLIMBING ROCK
text: The basic principles of rock climbing are the same as walking in rough terrain; they are just more difficult to achieve, and the required movements less intuitive. Selecting hand and foot placements can be much more difficult, and the movements and body positions required for them to hold can be challenging to perform. Experience built through climbing terrain more difficult than would need to be accessed in military operations is the path to building rock-climbing skill.

heading: CLIMBING EQUIPMENT
text: Climbing shoes are small, lightweight, close-fitting shoes with a smooth, soft, rubber sole used by recreational climbers, which increase the precision in which weight can be applied to small rock features. They contain hook-and-loop fasteners or laces to secure to the foot, and they are designed for various levels of climbing difficulty. The tighter, stiffer, and more downcurved the toe is, the more difficult the terrain (YDS 5.9 and higher) for which they are designed. Typically, climbing shoes are not appropriate for military applications because they are much more uncomfortable to wear for long periods and unsuitable for walking even short distances. However, these are an excellent choice for advanced military mountaineers looking to improve their skills using established routes off military installations, where climbing with muddy boots may be frowned upon. A moderate climbing shoe that is comfortable for the Soldier to wear for long periods is sufficient in training and (rarely) operationally. Operationally, climbing shoes are only appropriate to small, assault climber teams that must guide or establish routes for others in the most difficult operational terrain. (See figure 6-3.)

heading: CLIMBING EQUIPMENT
text: The issued advanced combat ballistic helmet provides sufficient protection from head impacts during a fall and from small falling objects. However, it is not designed to absorb large impact from above, and its weight introduces substantial additional fatigue during sustained climbing. Rock-climbing helmets are very lightweight and are designed to protect the wearer against impact from falling objects but do not provide a means of mounting night vision devices. Plastic, tactical bump helmets offer a reasonable compromise for military rock climbers as they provide the best combination of top- and side-impact protection, the ability to mount night vision devices, and weight savings. Commanders must consider risks when determining headgear requirements for Soldiers during rock climbing. It is recommended that lead climbers use, at a minimum, a lighter-weight helmet. (See figure 6-4, page 92.)

heading: CLIMBING EQUIPMENT
text: The issued MOLLE pack is not suited for rock climbing. Its size, empty weight, and width interfere with movements necessary for even moderate climbing. When loaded, climbing may not even be possible. Soldiers climbing sustained rock routes may require a smaller lightweight pack to carry required items (for example, water, sensitive items, communications equipment) during the climb. Whatever packs are worn should be snugged to the body, and waist straps as well as chest straps worn to reduce the load from shifting during climbing and throwing the climber out of balance.

heading: ROCK CLIMBING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS
text: Sustained climbing in 5th-class terrain during conventional military operations is impractical. However, routes through easier terrain are often blocked by shorter sections of 4th or easier 5th-class terrain. These routes may be the only or most tactically sound approaches to points of domination for properly trained units. Small teams of advanced military mountaineers can be used to establish fixed-rope routes for lesser-trained Soldiers to use for protection during movement. Accessing these points may be required to reach enemy defensive positions, establish observation posts, or position small teams conducting reconnaissance or forward observation of fires.

heading: ROCK CLIMBING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS
text: Soldiers climbing 4th- and 5th-class terrain are typically unable to provide themselves sufficient local security during movement. Bounding overwatch in vertical terrain by small-specialized teams or VDA-crossing procedures must be performed by a larger unit to provide adequate security for climbing Soldiers. (See ATP 3-21.50 for more on VDA.) Small reconnaissance and surveillance teams may have to rely on careful technical route selection that provides concealment throughout the approach and the climb. Fortunately, 4th-class and easier 5th-class terrain often provide such opportunities for teams with the technical and mobility skills necessary to negotiate them.

heading: CLIMBING ROUTE SELECTION
text: Before climbing, Soldiers should scan the rock for features that indicate that climbing the route is possible. With experience, Soldiers can determine how difficult a section of rock will be for them to complete. Climbers should begin to form a plan for climbing the route and a plan to protect themselves with a rope system (when necessary) before leaving the ground. (See chapter 10 on how to protect climbers from fall hazards.)

heading: CLIMBING ROUTE SELECTION
text: During military operations, the least difficult routes possible should be selected for travel. (See chapter 7 for more information on planning technical movement routes.)

heading: ROCK-CLIMBING TECHNIQUES
text: The basic principles for rock climbing are the same as those for walking in rough terrain. They are finding and selecting suitable holds and positioning the body to achieve sufficient friction for continued movement. Due to the vertical nature of the terrain, hands must be used to aid Soldiers in maintaining balance and preventing them from tipping backward off the rock.

heading: ROCK-CLIMBING TECHNIQUES
text: Suspect rock-climbing holds should be tested to ensure they are secure by tapping with a hand or foot. Holds that move or shift should be avoided. This is common in undeveloped 4th- and 5th-class terrain.

heading: Maintaining Balance
text: Balance is the most important aspect of rock climbing and footwork is the foundation of balance. Good use of the feet saves energy and makes staying in balance easier. A relaxed, comfortable stance is essential. The body should be centered over the feet as much as possible. On lower angle sections of climbing, it should be positioned away from the rock face. Alternatively, it should be positioned closer to the rock face on steeper sections. This puts downward pressure on footholds, increasing their security. Smaller lower body movements are often less strenuous than larger ones, which take more effort to stay in balance.

heading: Maintaining Balance
text: Rock climbing usually requires the use of handholds to maintain balance. Handholds can be large jugs that allow climbers to hold nearly their whole weight or tiny crimpers that only hold a fraction of their weight. Specific handhold techniques are discussed throughout this section. New climbers commonly overuse their arms to pull themselves up the rock and burn out quickly. Tired or pumped forearms are a sign of bad footwork.

heading: Maintaining Balance
text: Whenever possible, three points of contact should be maintained while moving the fourth to the next hold. This can reduce the likelihood of a fall should one point of contact fail.

heading: Types of Contact
text: Though counterintuitive, often pushing rather than pulling is required during climbing. Using downward pressure involves pushing down on a feature with the hands to allow unweighting of the other hand or one foot for movement to the next hold. Using counterpressure involves pushing away from features to allow a hand or foot to be unweighted for movement. (See figure 6-5, page 94.)

heading: Types of Contact
text: Occasionally, the holds available put the climber out of balance, but repositioning the body (usually by extending a leg to the left or right) improves the climber's balance. This technique is called counterbalancing and often allows the climber greater reach. (See figure 6-6.) Often the climber can find a microfeature to touch or apply slight pressure to with the foot improving the security of the move.

heading: Types of Contact
text: Occasionally, the climber must switch hands or feet on a hold to make the next move. Sometimes the hold can be shared temporarily by two hands or feet, even if they are unsecure, while the lead hand or lead foot moves. Other times, the second hand or foot may need to use a temporary, perhaps less desirable hold, while the lead one moves.

heading: Types of Contact
text: Dynamic moves are sudden, explosive moves where climbers throw themselves out of balance, potentially even losing contact with the rock, to reach another hold. These moves must be calculated carefully because failing to execute them perfectly usually results in a fall.

heading: Slab and Face Climbing
text: Slabs are typically smoother, lower angle rock features. They can be large or small. Comparatively, they provide the climber with few hands and footholds and require good footwork and balancing to climb. The primary technique used to climb them is smearing with the feet. This involves placing the sole of the boot or shoe on the rock with toe facing uphill to obtain maximum contact and friction. The body is then positioned away from the rock so that the foot does not slip. The closer climbers can get to pushing perpendicular to the rock, the more friction they will create. (See figure 6-7, page 96.) Hands are usually used to help balance by pushing against the rock. Any microfeature that can be found will improve the security of climbing slabby terrain. Climbing slabby rock helps build confidence in footwork and good balance skills.

heading: Slab and Face Climbing
text: Face climbing is what is commonly associated with rock climbing. Face climbs are typically suitably featured rock faces (cliffs) where climbers employ a wide variety of basic moves to ascending. Climbers spend most of their time facing the rock, like climbing a ladder. Many footholds are small or sloped and require edging or smearing to be effective; others are larger. (See figure 6-8.) Many techniques for using handholds exist. (See figure 6-8.) Using knees should be avoided because they are more likely to slip than good footwear.

heading: Slab and Face Climbing
text: Most slab or face climbing terrain appropriate to military operations can be climbed in combat boots, mountaineering boots, or approach shoes. Moderate to difficult climbs require climbing shoes. (See figure 6-9.)

heading: Resting During Climbing
text: Resting is critical during sustained rock climbing. Any opportunity to stand up and let go or lightly hold on with the hands should be taken. Sometimes the body or a body part can be wedged into a large crack, allowing the climber to relax. Often, the only rests available are between moves while looking for the next hold. When not actively moving, climbers should keep their weight on their skeletal system as much as possible. This means locking out legs or arms and providing muscles with a brief rest. Doing this is particularly important to preserve arm strength. Often one arm and the climbers' feet can support their weight while they shake out the other arm and hand. (See figure 6-10, page 98.)

heading: Specific Moves
text: Mantling involves pulling down with both arms on the edge of a ledge type feature until the chest is ledge height, then transitioning to pushing down on the ledge while walking the feet up the face below. This move is common to climbing out of a swimming pool. (See figure 6-11.)

heading: Specific Moves
text: Stemming involves placing the feet on features to the left and right of the body so that force is applied outward as well as down. Stemming is typically very stable and requires a relatively low amount of energy to maintain. (See figure 6-12, page 100.)

heading: Specific Moves
text: Underclinging involves gripping an overhanging rock feature with the hands, palm up, and pushing against a lower rock face with the feet. Underclings can be very stable but can be quite strenuous and tiring. Occasionally, underlings are the only means of getting through a section of climbing. (See figure 6-13, page 101.)

heading: Specific Moves
text: Liebacking involves using counterforce by pulling hard on a vertical or diagonal feature (such as a large flake) while pushing hard against the face of the rock. These moves are very strenuous because little or none of the climbers' weights is supported by their feet. In fact, leg muscles are being used to push away from the rock, so they are very taxing to the upper body. The climber's hands are then walked up the feature while the feet are walked up the face. Footholds on the face, however small, can be used to make liebacking easier and more secure. (See figure 6-14, page 102.)

heading: Crack Climbing
text: Crack climbing requires a specific set of nonintuitive techniques that take quite a bit of practice to build proficiency in. While some climbs involving cracks can be climbed with weak or no crack technique, more difficult crack climbs require climbing shoes and good technique to be climbable. Mixed crack climbing involves using features on the rock face for footholds while using a prominent crack for handholds. (See figure 6-15.) Classic crack climbing involves moving up a prominent crack by alternately jamming hands or fingers and feet or toes and walking them up the crack. Often, one foot is placed out of the crack to the side for balance, even on a featureless face. Off-width crack climbing is the term for climbing cracks that are larger than fist and foot sized but not large enough to fit the entire body. These climbs are difficult.

heading: Jamming
text: A critical technique in climbing cracks involves placing a hand or foot into a crack and turning, twisting, or otherwise manipulating them so that they become temporarily jammed in the crack. A good jam can be achieved in a variety of ways depending on crack size, whether it has constrictions in it or not, and its position in relation to other holds on the climb. Jams can provide solid hands or footholds but are often uncomfortable or even painful. Crack size determines which jam technique to use for a given hold. Constrictions in the crack make jam holds more secure.

heading: Types of Hand Jams
text: Hand-sized jams are the easiest to perform. The hand is inserted open into the crack and then the fingers bent exert pressure against the walls of the crack. Often turning one hand thumb down is useful. Typically, leaning to the same side adds security to a thumb up hand jam. (See figure 6-16, page 104 for variations of hand jamming.)

heading: Types of Hand Jams
text: Fist jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are larger than those that work for hand jams. The same jamming principles apply, but climbers just insert their entire fist into the crack. (See figure 6-17 for variations of fist jamming.)

heading: Types of Hand Jams
text: Finger jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are smaller than those that will accept a hand. The same jamming principles apply, but the climber only inserts their fingers, or parts of their fingers into the crack. Finger jamming is more difficult and can be painful for the joints. It is important to strengthen finger muscles prior to attempting to support substantial weight with finger jams to prevent joint strain. (See figure 6-18.)

heading: Types of Foot Jams
text: Foot jams involve turning the foot so that it fits into the crack and then twisting it so that the width of the foot wedges into the crack. This can be uncomfortable but can provide very secure footholds. (See figure 6-19.)

heading: Types of Foot Jams
text: Toe jams are used in the same manner as foot jams, but in smaller cracks. (See figure 6-20, page 106.)

heading: Types of Arm Jams
text: Arm bars is a technique used for off-width cracks and involves inserting an entire arm into the crack and bending at the elbow to create a jam. (See figure 6-21, page 106.)

heading: Types of Arm Jams
text: Chicken wing is a technique also used for off-width cracks and involves inserting an entire arm into the crack bent at the elbow and pushing against one wall of the crack with the hand to create a jam. (See figure 6-21, page 106.)

heading: Dihedral and Chimney Climbing
text: Climbing dihedrals and chimneys involves positioning the body inside a feature and using counterpressure or stemming to make upward movement. These features can often make for less strenuous climbing due to the counterpressure positions allowing for more rests. A dihedral is two rock faces that meet to form a corner, like an open book. Often there is a crack where the two faces meet. Chimneys are roughly parallel-sided features. They could be like a vertical shaft or crack large enough to accept a whole body.

heading: Dihedral and Chimney Climbing
text: Dihedrals can usually be climbed with a combination of stemming and either crack or face climbing. Dihedrals are easier and less strenuous to climb when the two faces have multiple and large features.

heading: Dihedral and Chimney Climbing
text: Chimneys are often unpleasant features to climb but provide a lot of security during movement. The basic technique for climbers is to position their body in the chimney and use counterpressure by pushing with arms, legs, and back against opposing sides. (See figures 6-22 through 6-24, pages 107 through 109, for variations in chimney climbing techniques.) Often during chimney climbing, it is necessary to attach climbing packs to the harness hanging below the climber.

heading: Traversing
text: Traversing is moving laterally on the rock. This is often necessary because the features that make up a rock route are not always continuous or travel straight up a face. Traversing often involves a series of placement exchanges. Most traversing is done facing the rock.

heading: Traversing
text: Hand traversing requires a ledge, flake, other horizontal feature, or a series of horizontally oriented large handholds. Climbers' hands walk their way across the features while their feet walk their way across a face below. (See figure 6-25, page 110.)

heading: Traversing
text: Steep traverse is a technique often used when handholds are not as good, but decent footholds are present. Climbers lean heavily in the direction they want to move and place hands on available holds, and then walk their feet in the same direction using available footholds. Sometimes a crossover step is helpful. This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and counterforce skills. (See figure 6-26.)

heading: Topping Out or Gaining Ledges
text: Topping out or gaining a ledge can be one of the more challenging parts of climbing. Often low holds located near where climbers want to put their feet need to be used to get over the edge. Often, a mantling technique is effective. Most importantly, climbers should avoid laying on their belly on the edge when moving because it may be difficult to get their feel back on the rock, and they may slide off on sloped ledges. A crossover step is helpful. This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and counterforce skills. (See figure 6-26 for the proper technique.)

heading: Down Climbing
text: Down climbing is far more difficult than climbing up and takes much practice to gain proficiency. This is largely because rock features are often difficult to identify from above. They are easily obscured by other features above them or even the climber's body parts. However, down climbing is an important skill to practice, as it is often necessary to do in 3rd- and 4th-class terrain.

heading: Down Climbing
text: Facing out is a technique used on low angle rock. Climbers face out and use their hands for stability behind and below their body while moving their feet down to the next hold. (See figure 6-27, page 112.)

heading: Down Climbing
text: Walking down a slab is a technique that involves simply walking down slabby rock while maintaining maximum friction and balance. (See figure 6-27, page 112.)

heading: Down Climbing
text: Facing sideways involves climbers facing to the side and side stepping down to lower footholds while controlling and balancing their movement using handholds above. Climbers use this technique on steeper rock. (See figure 6-27, page 112.)

heading: Down Climbing
text: Facing the rock involves climbing down in the same position as the climber would use to move up the rock. Climbers lower themselves down with their arms, keeping their body away from the rock so they can see footholds below, and then transition their weight onto the next foothold. (See figure 6-27, page 112.)

heading: TRAINING FOR ROCK CLIMBING
text: Beginner rock-climbing training is typically conducted at established climbing areas using top rope belay techniques (see chapter 10). When supervised by qualified mountaineers, this kind of rock climbing is relatively low risk and has a high payoff for developing mobility skills. One restriction is that sites do not often allow large groups to be actively engaged. Thus, climbing training should be planned along with concurrent training for smaller groups to rotate through. Route difficulty should be challenging to climbers but easy enough that they can be successful. This motivates climbers to build skills. A motivational rather than critical atmosphere is most effective when building climbing skills.

heading: TRAINING FOR ROCK CLIMBING
text: Climbing training for more advanced military mountaineers can be conducted the same way, just on more challenging routes, but should also be conducted in a multipitch setting that more accurately reproduces conditions of climbing during military operations. This setting requires the development of lead climbing and route-finding skills, which are critical to the advanced military mountaineer.

heading: TRAINING FOR ROCK CLIMBING
text: Leaders should try to learn the etiquette associated with climbing before using civilian climbing areas.

heading: SECTION II - MOVEMENT OVER SNOW AND ICE
text: Deep snow, steep powdery slopes, glare ice, and frozen waterfalls all present significant challenges to movement. The basic individual movement principles and skill development necessary for movement under other surface conditions also apply to movement over snow and ice. However, additional skills are necessary for efficiency and safety. Specialized equipment is required in even the easiest snow or ice-covered terrain.

heading: MOBILITY OVER SNOW AND ICE
text: Fitness and movement techniques are the foundation of moving through snow or up steep ice. However, identifying and selecting secure foot placements can be difficult because traction is drastically reduced. Movement without specialized equipment, such as crampons or skis, is difficult under almost all conditions above 1st-class terrain. Even when it is possible, deep snow requires a substantial amount of energy to move through unaided. Anything deeper than calf-deep snow will impede movement in even easy terrain, and a few inches of snow or a glaze of ice will make steeper terrain treacherous. Soldiers must develop the same level of skill using snow and ice equipment, which requires proficiency in an additional set of skills. Like moving over broken rocky terrain, these skills can only be developed through experience and repetition. Units that train their Soldiers to proficiency in these conditions can move faster, safer, and access terrain that others cannot.

heading: EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE
text: Skis provide substantial floatation in deep snow and require the least amount of energy for movement. This is especially true for downhill movement where much energy can be saved over walking. There are varieties of ski systems available for movement over snow, but those most suited to military mountaineering are called alpine touring skis. The ski itself is like a downhill ski, but the binding allows the heel to release for movement over flat or uphill terrain. It can also be locked down for greater control when skiing downhill. Climbing skins are used in conjunction with skis to climb uphill. Skins are designed to slide in only one direction, providing traction in deep snow and on steep slopes. At a minimum, a stiff mountaineering boot is necessary for use with skis. In the steepest terrain, a dedicated rigid plastic ski boot may be required. Compatibility between boots and bindings must be considered. (See figure 6-28, page 114.)

heading: EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE
text: Snowshoes are another tool available to Soldiers for moving over deep snow. Modern snowshoes provide sufficient floatation and traction for moving through snow on fairly steep (class 2) slopes and should be small and light enough to pack, if necessary. Snowshoes work with any boot. (See figure 6-29.)

heading: EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE
text: Ski poles are typically used with snowshoes and skis to provide more lateral stability and balance. Ski poles can be used to provide excellent support for weapons systems during firing from the prone, kneeling, and standing positions.

heading: EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE
text: Sleds are useful for carrying large amounts of equipment, such as bivouac equipment, heavy weapons, food and water, or other supplies. They range in size, shape, and weight, all of which should be considered before selection for military operations. Four- and ten-Soldier Ahkio-style sleds are available through the military supply system. These are designed to carry all group sustainment equipment (for example, tents, stoves, fuel) for a four- or ten-Soldier group. These come with a cover and rigid poles, convenient for dragging up and downhill. (See figure 6-30, page 116.)

heading: EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE
text: Crampons attach to the Soldier's boot to provide traction on ice and snow. There are two basic types: general mountaineering crampons and ice climbing crampons. Mountaineering crampons have less aggressive points. They are designed for use in steep snow and on low-angle ice and can be used for ice climbing but are not ideal. Ice climbing crampons have points that are more aggressive and are typically more rigid. They are designed for steep ice climbing but can be used in snow and low angle ice as well. Crampons work best when paired with a stiff leather or rigid plastic mountaineering boot. They do not work well with issued cold-weather combat boots. (See figure 6-31.)

heading: EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE
text: Mountain axes are important tools for movement over steep snow and occasional low-angle ice. The two types of axes usually used in alpine terrain are general mountain axes and hybrid mountain axes. General axes are designed for steep snow and hybrid axes are designed for steep snow and low-angle ice climbing. Ice axes have an adze to the rear of the pick for chopping snow and ice. (See figure 6-32.)

heading: EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE
text: Ice tools are modified ice axes designed for steep ice climbing. They are much more aggressive and curved to help obtain solid sticks in hard vertical ice and over bulges. They are less effective in snow than general or hybrid axes because of their short length. Ice tools can include an adze or a hammerhead. Hammers are used for placing pitons during mixed climbing. (See figure 6-33, page 118.)

heading: MILITARY OPERATIONS IN SNOW- AND ICE-COVERED TERRAIN
text: Snow and ice present many additional challenges for units that need to move in mountainous terrain. Specialized equipment, training, and experience are necessary to move in it safely and effectively. Whether the challenges are deep snow, slick slopes, or steep sections of vertical ice, they will prove substantial obstacles for unprepared units. Units anticipating operating in such terrain and conditions should train in them prior to engaging in combat operations.

heading: MILITARY OPERATIONS IN SNOW- AND ICE-COVERED TERRAIN
text: Even with proper equipment and training, it is unlikely that larger units can move in terrain steeper than 2nd-class terrain without ropes due to the high risk of long sliding falls. Small teams of advanced military mountaineers should be trained to move over ice and snow and tasked with finding routes and establishing rope systems for larger units. (See chapter 11 for establishing fixed-rope systems for troop movement in steep terrain and ATP 3-21.50 for crossing VDA TTP.)

heading: MOVEMENT OVER SNOW
text: Low- to moderate-angle snow slopes found on or adjacent to valleys are primary avenues of movement for military units operating in winter conditions. Steeper slopes in gullies and passes are often the easiest routes through even steeper rocky features around them. Though challenging to move over, these often provide the best access to points of domination in alpine terrain.

heading: MOVEMENT OVER SNOW
text: Techniques for moving over snowy surfaces change IAW slope and surface conditions. Some soft snow increases physical strain but can increase the security of foot placements. During movement, breaks should be taken more frequently and for shorter durations in cold weather to assist with moisture management. This helps prevent overheating, which can cause problems once movements stop. Snow deeper than calf-height makes movement difficult without skis or snowshoes. Hard-packed snow slopes requiring special techniques and equipment or falls that could result in serious injury or death are likely.

heading: MOVEMENT OVER SNOW
text: A thorough analysis of avalanche threat should be conducted prior to moving over slopes that could be exposed to avalanche risk. Terrain at any risk for avalanche should be avoided. All Soldiers moving in potential avalanche terrain must be equipped with avalanche protective equipment and trained in its use, as well as avalanche response procedures. (See chapter 5 for more information on avalanche considerations.)

heading: BOOT PACKING
text: The boot-packing method requires the least amount of training and special equipment. The same techniques can be used in mountain walking; however, there is often less traction. During the boot-packing method, Soldiers move slower and minor slips and falls should be expected. In deeper soft snow, Soldiers should step in the tracks left by the Soldier in front of them. This packs them into hard steps and makes movement less difficult. Rotate lead Soldiers to prevent fatigue.

heading: BOOT PACKING
text: Crampons are strongly recommended for moving on hard-packed slopes. However, if crampons are not available, there are a few techniques to use to improve the security of foot placements. Step kicking involves kicking the toe or edge of the boot into the surface with each step creating a small depression, which improves traction. Mountain axes can be used as a third point of contact, allowing the body to gain more traction. The axe is typically held by its head in the uphill hand, with the pick to the rear (cane position). Steps can be cut into the slope using the axe's adze to improve foot placement security. (See figure 6-34, page 120.) This technique is effective for short distances but is very time-consuming.

heading: GLISSADING
text: Glissading is a technique used to descend low to moderate angle slopes by sliding in the seated position and using a mountain axe as a brake. (See figure 6-35.) Glissading allows Soldiers to descend appropriate slopes very quickly and efficiently, thereby saving significant time and energy. Specific conditions are required for glissading to be appropriate. The slope should not have any obstacles (such as trees, rocks, drop offs, crevasses) in the slide path, and it should have sufficient soft snow on the surface to allow Soldiers to control the speed of the slide. Glissading should never be done on hard-packed snow or ice surfaces. Crampons should be removed prior to glissading to ensure injuries to lower extremities are not caused by a crampon becoming caught on something during the slide.

heading: GLISSADING
text: Glissading is conducted by sitting in the snow and positioning the midpoint of a mountain axe shaft against one hip with the spike in the snow. The hand on the same side as the axe holds its shaft to the hip at the midpoint. The other hand holds the top of the axe where pick, shaft and adze meet. The mountain axe pick should always face forward (away from the Soldier) to prevent injury. Soldiers then initiate the slide on their buttocks using the axe spike as a brake. To slow down, Soldiers rotate the spike downward, pressing it deeper into the snowpack and increasing friction. To speed up, Soldiers rotate the spike away from the snowpack, decreasing friction. Adequate time should be allowed between Soldiers sliding in the same glissade path to ensure a collision does not occur should a Soldier stop shortly mid-slide.

heading: FLATFOOTING
text: Flatfooting is the term for numerous techniques that increase security and efficiency of movement over snow and ice slopes. These techniques involve the use of both crampons and a mountain axe. The key principle of flatfooting is to position the body so that all crampon points are embedded in the snow surface. This provides maximum security for foot placements. These techniques are particularly critical to safe movement over steep, hard-packed snow. Flatfooting with heavy loads requires greater proficiency. Flatfooting techniques are much more difficult to perform in flexible boots or with loose sloppy crampons. (See figure 6-36, page 122.)

heading: FLATFOOTING
text: Crampons substantially increase the security of foot placements when used properly. However, walking in them forces the Soldier's gait to change and can take some practice getting used to. They must be sized properly and snugged tight to the boot, so Soldiers' boots do not slide around in the crampon introducing instability to their foot placements.

heading: Ascending
text: Lower-angle slopes can be ascended using a diagonal traverse or switchback technique. More security can be gained from pointing the toe downhill some when placing the foot. Mountain axes or an ice tool can also be used in cane position the same way previously mentioned. (See figure 6-37.)

heading: Ascending
text: As terrain gets steeper, maximizing crampon point contact with the surface becomes more difficult. Footwork techniques used in rock climbing, such as edging, are very insecure when wearing crampons. They should not be used. Ankles must be rolled somewhat downhill to ensure crampon points are embedded in the surface. Turning the downhill foot so that the toe points downhill increases security by making it easier to engage the crampon points on the outside edge of the foot.

heading: Ascending
text: To obtain secure foot placements, lean the body away from the slope to increase pressure on crampon points. This becomes more important as surface conditions get firmer. Generally, it is easier to stay in balance and achieve solid foot placements by taking smaller steps. Moving diagonally up slope makes this easier to execute.

heading: Ascending
text: Flatfooting, using a mountain axe in a cross-body position. To perform this technique, the Soldier stands sideways to the slope. The mountain axe head is held in the downhill hand and the shaft held low in the uphill hand. The uphill foot is placed perpendicular to the slope and the downhill foot is placed similarly, but with the toe pointed downhill as much as comfort demands. The axe spike is then forced into the snowpack uphill from the feet far enough so that most of the Soldier's weight is transitioned onto it. This provides balance and security during foot movement. The downhill foot is moved across and placed above the uphill foot. If the crossover step is too awkward, it can be moved to a position just below the uphill foot, but this method is less efficient. The Soldier's weight is then transitioned onto the newly placed foot so that the uphill foot may be moved upslope. The process is then repeated, starting with replacing the axe uphill and the Soldier moves in a generally diagonal path up the slope. (See figure 6-38.)

heading: Ascending
text: Flatfooting using a mountain axe in anchor position. The footwork is the same for this technique as when using the axe in a cross-body position. However, the axe is held by the shaft like a hammer and swung so that the pick is embedded into the uphill slope. The axe can then be "climbed" by walking the hands up the shaft while the feet work their way up the slope. (See figure 6-39.)

heading: Ascending
text: Front pointing involves kicking into the slope with the toe of the boot so that all front crampon points become embedded in the surface. The Soldier leans forward slightly locking the ankle so that the sole of the foot is held perpendicular to the slope. If the heel is too low or too high, or only the large front points are embedded, then the foot placement will be less secure and may fail. The Soldier stands up on the placement using hands or mountain axe for balance and repeats kicking in with the other foot higher on the slope. This process is repeated as the Soldier generally moves straight up the slope. The front-pointing technique is very effective and allows for faster movement in steep terrain but is more physically taxing. The Soldier's calf muscles become fatigued quickly using this technique. The front-pointing technique is most effective for ascending short, steep sections of terrain. (See figure 6-40.)

heading: Ascending
text: Front pointing with a mountain axe in dagger positions involves Soldiers holding the axe by the head with the adze and thumb facing them. The pick is then forced into the slope in a hammer-fist motion (high dagger). Once placed, Soldiers walk their feet up the slope, using front pointing as high as they can go. A low dagger technique can be used to allow climbing higher than a high dagger allows by transitioning the hand to the top of the axe head and pushing down on it for balance. The process is then repeated, moving straight up the slope. (See figure 6-41.)

heading: Ascending
text: Front pointing with mountain axe in anchor position involves holding the axe by the shaft and swinging it like a hammer so that the pick is embedded into the slope higher above the Soldier. The axe is then used as holds for both hands as Soldiers climb the slope with their feet using front pointing. (See figure 6-42.)

heading: Ascending
text: Front pointing using mountain axe as in ice climbing involves holding the axe by the shaft and swinging it like a hammer so that the pick is embedded into the slope as with anchor position. However, in this technique the Soldier only uses the axe for holds with one hand. The other hand is placed to push against the slope for balance. (See figure 6-43.)

heading: Descending
text: Slips and slides should be considered very likely on moderate to steep terrain, especially if surface conditions are hard. Rope systems may be used to mitigate the risk of injury, but they do not make movement faster or easier. Efficient movement requires good flatfooting skills.

heading: Descending
text: Moderately steep slopes can be descended by simply using a diagonal traverse or switchback pattern down the slope. This may require rolling the ankle more than usual to force all crampon points into the snow. The downhill foot can be turned so that the toe points downhill to reduce strain and add security during movement. The mountain axe is used in any of the positions described above to aid with balance and prepare the Soldier for self-arrest. Edging technique is ineffective; Solders should not attempt this technique. (See figure 6-44, page 128.)

heading: Descending
text:
Steeper slopes require descent facing downhill and relying heavily on a mountain axe for balance and security. Soldiers must bend their knees to lower their center of gravity and position their weight over their crampons. Depending on the slope angle and surface hardness, the mountain axe should be used in one of the positions described below:
- Using the mountain axe in cross body position, while driving the spike into the slope behind the feet is a very secure method of moving down steep slopes when executed properly. During movement, most of the weight is supported by the mountain axe and the feet are moved forward in short deliberate steps. In hard surface conditions, crampons need to be stomped into the ground to ensure points are set. Weight is then transitioned over the feet, the axe moved down and reset. (See figure 6-44, page 128.)
- In addition to the positions already discussed, the mountain axe can be used in support position while descending. This is when it is carried in one hand, head oriented uphill and pick facing down, while the Soldier moves down the slope facing downhill. The axe is held in this position so that the Soldier can quickly plant the pick into the snowpack for security, as necessary. If this is done, the axe provides a handhold to assist in making one or two moves that are more difficult. This can be repeated for longer sections that are more difficult than necessary. (See figure 6-44, page 128.)
- If more security is needed, then the Soldier can transition to using the axe in the anchor position, allowing both hands to grip the axe and a more secure pick placement. (See figure 6-44, page 128.)

heading: Descending
text: Using the mountain axe in cross body position, while driving the spike into the slope behind the feet is a very secure method of moving down steep slopes when executed properly. During movement, most of the weight is supported by the mountain axe, and the feet are moved forward in short deliberate steps. In hard surface conditions, crampons need to be stomped into the ground to ensure points are set. Weight is then transitioned over the feet; and the axe moved down and reset.

heading: Descending
text: In addition to the positions already discussed, Soldiers can use the mountain axe in its support position while descending. Soldiers carry the axe in one hand, head oriented uphill and pick facing down, while moving down the slope, facing downhill. The axe is held in this position so that the Soldier can quickly plant the pick into the snowpack for security, as necessary. Carrying the axe this way provides a handhold to assist in making one or two moves that are more difficult. This can be repeated for longer sections that are more difficult, as necessary. (See figure 6-44, page 128.)

heading: Descending
text: If more security is needed, the Soldier can transition to using the axe in the anchor position, allowing both hands to grip the axe for a more secure pick placement.

heading: SELF-ARREST
text: Self-arrest is a technique intended to stop a short fall before it turns into a long, sliding, tumbling fall. Soldiers that will be moving on moderate to steep snow slopes unroped must be issued a mountain axe at a minimum and trained to proficiency in self-arrest techniques. There is little margin for error in executing self-arrest on steep slopes with firm surface conditions. Self-arresting should not be considered an adequate protective measure when slipping and falling risk is determined to be likely. Good movement skills are still the primary risk mitigation for moving unroped.

heading: SELF-ARREST
text: Soldiers should carry the axe in the cane position with the pick to the rear in the uphill hand. The instant Soldiers fall, they must commit to self-arresting immediately. The technique is executed by bringing the mountain axe into position at the center of chest, with the hand on its head and pick facing away. The lower hand moves to a position low on the axe shaft. The Soldier then uses body weight and violence of action to drive the pick into the snowpack. This must be done in seconds and if the axe is not centered under the body, it is difficult to apply adequate force to achieve this. The less aggressive and curved design of the ice axe pick is meant to prevent it from biting into the surface too well, where momentum would cause it to be ripped out of the falling Soldiers' hands. Rather, it is designed to stop the Soldier gradually. For this reason, picks that are more aggressive like those found on tools meant for ice climbing are less effective for this. If crampons are not worn, the Soldier can also dig toes into the snowpack to assist stopping the slide. Careful attention must be paid not to allow the spike of the axe to dig into the snow while sliding. If this happens, the Soldier could be flipped over backwards and thrown into a tumble. Recovering from a tumbling is unlikely. (See figure 6-45.)

heading: SELF-ARREST
text: When self-arresting with crampons on, Soldiers must bend their knees during the slide, so the crampon points do not catch and cause a tumble. Legs must remain bent until sliding has stopped. Front points can then be planted to reduce the likelihood of a slide resuming.

heading: SELF-ARREST
text: To self-arrest while sliding on the back, the Soldier must bring the axe into position at the center of the chest, then roll in the direction of the axe head until on the stomach, and then drive the pick into the snow.

heading: SELF-ARREST
text: To self-arrest headfirst face down, the Soldier must reach downhill to the same side as the axe head, plant the pick, pivot the body around the pick, and swing the legs downhill.

heading: SELF-ARREST
