- STEP 2. With the overhand loop formed, tie a figure-eight knot around the standing part.
- STEP 3. When dressing the knot down, the running end and the bight must be together.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- The loop should be large enough to accept a carabiner but no larger than a helmet-size loop.
- The tail and bight must be together.
- The figure eight is tied tightly.

heading: ALPINE BUTTERFLY
text: The alpine butterfly knot forms a single, fixed loop in the middle of the rope. (See figure 8-13, page 164.) The knot can be loaded in either direction or is easy to untie after use.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie an alpine butterfly knot:
- STEP 1. Take a bight of rope and twist it 360 degrees .
- STEP 2. Using the end of the bight, bring it up and back toward the two standing ends that exit at the back of the twisted bight just created. Careful to avoid untwisting the bight while doing this.
- STEP 3. Bring the bight back through the portion of the twisted bight that created a hole where the first twist in the bight is located. Pull the bight through that hole.
- STEP 4. Next dress down and tighten the knot.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- The knot should have a bight of rope exiting two opposing bights of rope.
- The opposing bights should be clean and untwisted.

heading: FIGURE-EIGHT BEND
text: The figure-eight bend is used to join the ends of two ropes of equal or unequal diameter up to a 5-mm difference. (See figure 8-14.) This joining knot should be the primary knot used to join cord. It can be untied after loading, which allows the material to be used for other applications.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a figure-eight bend:
- STEP 1. Form a bight in the running end of the rope.
- STEP 2. With the other hand, grasp the running end (short end) and make a 360 degrees turn around the standing end.
- STEP 3. Place the running end through the loop just formed creating an inline figure eight.
- STEP 4. Route the running end of the other rope back through the figure eight starting from the original rope's running end. Trace the original knot to the standing end.
- STEP 5. Remove all unnecessary twists and crossovers. Dress the knot down.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- There is a figure eight with two ropes running side by side.
- The running ends are on opposite sides of the knot.
- There is an approximate 4-inch tail.

heading: WATER KNOT
text: The water knot is used to attach the ends of webbing. (See figure 8-15.) The water knot is also known as a ring bend or tape knot.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a water knot:
- STEP 1. Tie an overhand knot in one of the ends.
- STEP 2. Feed the other end back through the knot, following the path of the first strand in reverse.
- STEP 3. Draw tight and pull all the slack out of the knot. The remaining tails must extend at least 4 inches beyond the knot in both directions.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- There are two overhand knots, one retracing the other.
- There is no slack in the knot, and the working ends come out of the knot in opposite directions.
- There is an approximate 4-inch tail.

heading: FLAT OVERHAND
text: The flat overhand is used for joining two ropes that are being used to rappel. (See figure 8-16.) Additionally, it is used as a stopper knot at the end of the ropes to prevent Soldiers from rappelling off the end of the ropes.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a flat overhand:
- STEP 1: Hold both strands 24 inches from the end of the ropes.
- STEP 2: Tie an overhand knot with both strands.
- STEP 3: Dress the knot down, ensuring there are no twists in the knot, and it is hard to touch.
- STEP 4: Lastly, ensure that there is a minimum 18-inch tail for both strands of rope.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- A double overhand dressed without twists.
- Minimum 18-inch tails.
- Knot should be hard to the touch, not loose, or sloppy.

heading: DOUBLE FISHERMAN'S KNOT
text: The double fisherman's knot is used to join the ends of a rope of the same diameter. (See figure 8-17.) Once loaded, it can become very difficult to untie. Avoid using this knot if it must be untied after use.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a double fisherman's knot:
- STEP 1. With the working end of one rope, tie two wraps around the standing part of another rope.
- STEP 2. Insert the working end (step 1) back through the two wraps and draw it tight.
- STEP 3. With the working end of the other rope, which contains the standing part (steps 1 and 2), tie two wraps around the standing part of the other rope, routing the wraps in the opposite direction as the first knot (the working end in step 1). Insert the working end back through the two wraps and draw tight.
- STEP 4. Pull on the opposing ends to bring the two knots together.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- Two double overhand knots securing each other as the standing parts of the rope are pulled apart.
- Four rope parts on one side of the knot form two X patterns; four rope parts on the other side of the knot are parallel.
- Ends of rope exit knot opposite each other with approximately 4-inch tails.

heading: SQUARE KNOT
text: The square knot is used to join the ends of rope of equal diameter while under tension. (See figure 8-18, page 170.) This joining knot should only be used when it is impossible to tie a more secure joining knot like the figure-eight bend or double fisherman's knot.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a square knot:
- STEP 1: Holding one working end in each hand, place the working end in the right hand over the one in the left hand.
- STEP 2: Pull it under and back over the top of the rope in the left hand.
- STEP 3: Place the working end in the left hand over the one in the right hand and repeat step 2.
- STEP 4: Dress the knot down and secure it with an overhand knot on each side of the square knot.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- There are two interlocking bights.
- The running end and standing part are on the same side of the bight formed by the other rope.
- The running ends are parallel to and on the same side of the standing ends with 4-inch minimum tails after the overhand safeties are tied.

heading: BOWLINE
text: The bowline is used to tie the end of a rope around an anchor. It may also be used to tie a single fixed loop at the end of a rope. (See figure 8-19.)

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a bowline:
- STEP 1. Bring the working end of the rope around the anchor, from right to left (as the climber faces the anchor).
- STEP 2. Form an overhand loop in the standing part of the rope (on the climber's right) toward the anchor.
- STEP 3. Reach through the loop and pull up a bight.
- STEP 4. Place the working end of the rope (on the climber's left) through the bight and bring it back onto itself. Now dress the knot down.
- STEP 5. Form an overhand knot with the tail from the bight.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- The bight is locked into place by a loop.
- The short portion of the bight is on the inside and on the loop around the anchor (or inside the fixed loop).
- There is an approximate 4-inch tail after tying the overhand safety.

heading: TRIPLE BOWLINE (THREE-LOOP BOWLINE)
text: The triple bowline is used to tie the middle or a bight of rope around an anchor. (See figure 8-20.)

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a triple bowline:
- STEP 1. Form a bight. Route the bight around the anchor.
- STEP 2. With the right thumb facing toward the body, form a doubled loop in the standing part by turning the wrist clockwise. Lay the loops to the right.
- STEP 3. With the right hand, reach down through the loops and pull up a doubled bight from the standing part of the rope.
- STEP 4. Place the running end (bight) of the rope (on the left) through the doubled bight from left to right and bring it back on itself. Hold the running end loosely and dress the knot down by pulling on the standing parts.
- STEP 5. Safety it off with a double overhand knot.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- There are two bights held in place by two loops.
- The bights form locking bars around the standing end.
- There is an approximate 4-inch tail (bight) after the double overhand safety knot is tied.
- The running end (bight) must be on the inside of the fixed loops.

heading: BOWLINE ON A BIGHT (TWO-LOOP BOWLINE)
text: The bowline on a bight is used to form two fixed loops in the middle of a rope. (See figure 8-21.)

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a bowline on a bight:
- STEP 1. Form a bight in the rope about twice as long as the finished loops will be.
- STEP 2. Form an overhand loop with both strands.
- STEP 3. Pass the bight up through the loop.
- STEP 4. Fold the bight, passing the entire knot through, until the bight is around the standing ends.
- STEP 5. Dress the knot down so that the bight is tight around the standing ends, and the loops are adjusted to the desired size.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- There are two fixed loops that will not slip.
- There are no twists in the knot.
- A double loop is held in place by a bight.

heading: GIRTH HITCH
text: The girth hitch is used to attach a cord or sling to an anchor or piece of equipment. (See figure 8-22.) The hitch is also used to attach a sling to a harness.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a girth hitch:
- STEP 1: Form a bight.
- STEP 2: Bring the running ends back through the bight.
- STEP 3: Cinch the knot tightly.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- Two wraps exist with a locking bar running across the wraps.
- The knot is dressed tightly.

heading: PRUSIK
text: The prusik is a friction hitch that can be loaded in either direction. When force is applied to this friction hitch, it is very difficult to move or loosen. It can be tied with the middle or end of a cord.

heading: Tying the Knot
text: The prusik can be tied with a cordelette to an installation rope. An installation rope is the primary load-bearing rope or strand in a rope system. A minimum of three turns should be used for this knot. The closer in diameter the cordelette is to the installation rope, the more turns may be required for the knot to function. Ideally, there should be a 3-mm difference in diameter between the cordelette and installation rope. Always check to see if the prusik grabs prior to operation.

heading: Middle-of-the-Rope Prusik
text:
The following steps are used to tie a middle-of-the-rope prusik (see figure 8-23):
- STEP 1. Double the cord, forming a bright, with the working ends even. Lay it over the installation rope so that the closed end of the bight is below the installation rope and the remaining part of the rope (working ends) is the closest. Spread the working end apart.
- STEP 2. Reach down through the 12-inch bight. Pull up both working ends and lay them over the installation rope. Repeat this process twice more, making sure that the working ends pass in the middle of the first two turns. Now there are six turns and a locking bar working across them on the installation rope.
- STEP 3. Dress the wraps and locking bar down to ensure they are tight and not twisted.

heading: End-of-the-Rope Prusik
text:
The following steps are used to tie an end-of-the-rope prusik (see figure 8-24, page 176):
- STEP 1. Take approximately 1 meter of cord and place it over the installation rope.
- STEP 2. Form a complete round turn in the rope.
- STEP 3. Cross over the standing part of the cord with the working end of the cord.
- STEP 4. Lay the working end under the installation rope.
- STEP 5. Form a complete round turn in the rope, working back toward the middle of the knot.
- STEP 6. There are six turns and a locking bar running across them on the installation rope. Dress the wraps and locking bar down. Ensure they are tight, parallel, and untwisted.
- STEP 7. Finish the knot with a bowline with the tail, ensure both strands have tension on it and running end of the prusik knot cannot be pulled through and undo the knot.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- Six complete turns with a locking bar.
- The knot is tight and dressed down with no ropes twisted or crossed.
- The end-of-the-rope prusik hitch should be closed out with a bowline to prevent slipping.

heading: AUTOBLOCK
text: The autoblock creates a friction hitch that is releasable even when force is applied. (See figure 8-25.) This knot is used as a hands-free backup for rappelling and lowering.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie an autoblock knot:
- STEP 1. Begin with a joined length of webbing or cord about 24-inches long. A presewn sling is also acceptable.
- STEP 2. Offset the joining knot, keeping it close to one end of the loop. If using sewn webbing, treat the sewn portion as the knot.
- STEP 3. Begin wrapping the clean portion of material around the rope. Create a minimum of three complete turns.
- STEP 4. Secure both bights into a locking carabiner that is attached to the harness and lock it.
- STEP 5. Ensure the autoblock grabs the rope by testing it prior to use. Smaller diameter ropes may require more than four wraps.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- Both bights of the joined material are secured into a locking carabiner.
- There is a minimum of three turns.
- The joining knot, tails, or sewn portion is not incorporated into any of the wraps or in the carabiner.

heading: KLEMHEIST
text: The klemheist is a friction hitch. Like the prusik, it is difficult to move or loosen while force is being applied. It is easier and quicker to tie than the prusik. It is also easier to loosen and move after applying force than the prusik. It cannot be loaded in both directions. (See figure 8-26, page 178.)

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a klemheist (see figure 8-26):
- STEP 1. Using a cordelette or webbing offsets the ends by 12 inches. Find the center of the rope and form a bight. Lay the bight over the installation rope.
- STEP 2. Wrap the tails of the cordelette around the installation rope back toward the direction of pull. Create at least four complete turns.
- STEP 3. With the remaining tails of the cordelette, pass them through the bight (see step 1).
- STEP 4. Dress the knot down tightly so that all wraps are touching.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- The bight is opposite the direction of pull.
- All wraps are tight and touching.

heading: BACHMANN HITCH
text: The Bachmann hitch is a friction hitch that is easily released and reset. (See figure 8-27.) The carabiner acts as a handle to help move the friction hitch along the rope.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a Bachmann hitch:
- STEP 1. Find the middle of a cordelette and insert it into a carabiner.
- STEP 2. Place the carabiner and cordelette next to the installation rope.
- STEP 3. With the two ropes parallel from the carabiner, make two or more wraps around the climbing rope and through the inside portion of the carabiner.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for a knot to be correct:
- The bight of the climbing rope is at the top of the carabiner.
- The two ropes run parallel without twisting or crossing.
- Two or more wraps are made around the long climbing rope and through the inside portion of the carabiner.

heading: CLOVE HITCH
text: The clove hitch is an anchor knot that can be used in the middle of the rope as well as at the end. (See figure 8-28, page 180 and figure 8-29, page 181.) This hitch is easily adjustable after it has been tied and it uses a little rope.

heading: Tying the Knot
text: There are two versions of the clove hitch: the middle-of-the-rope clove hitch and the end-of-the-rope clove hitch.

heading: Middle-of-the-Rope Clove Hitch
text:
The following steps are used to tie a middle-of-the-rope clove hitch (see figure 8-28, page 180):
- STEP 1. Hold the rope in both hands, palms down with hands together. Slide the left hand to the left approximately 10 inches.
- STEP 2. Form a loop away from and back toward the right.
- STEP 3. Slide the right hand approximately 10 inches to the right. Form a loop inward and back to the left hand.
- STEP 4. Place the left loop on top of the right loop. Place both loops over the anchor and pull both ends of the rope in opposite directions.

heading: End-of-the-Rope Clove Hitch
text:
The following steps are used to tie an end-of-the-rope clove hitch (see figure 8-29):
- STEP 1. Place approximately 30 inches of rope over the top of the anchor. Hold the standing end in the left hand. With the right hand, reach under the horizontal anchor, grasp the working end, and bring it inward.
- STEP 2. Place the working end of the rope over the standing end (to form a loop). Hold the loop in the left hand. Place the working end over the anchor to the left of the loop.
- STEP 3. With the right hand, reach down to the left-hand side of the loop under the anchor. Grasp the working end of the rope. Bring the working end up and outward.
- STEP 4. Dress down the knot.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- The knot has two round turns around the anchor with a diagonal locking bar.
- The locking bar is facing 90 degrees from the direction of pull.
- The ends exit l80 degrees from each other.
- The knot has more than a 4-inch tail remaining.

heading: MUNTER HITCH
text: The Munter hitch is used to form a mechanical belay. (See figure 8-30, page 182.) The Munter hitch produces friction, reducing the force required to hold a fall. It can be used to belay a climber going up or to lower a climber or load down.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a Munter hitch:
- STEP 1. Hold the rope in both hands, palms down about 12 inches apart.
- STEP 2. With the right hand, form a loop away from the body toward the left hand. Hold the loop with the left hand.
- STEP 3. With the right hand, place the rope that comes from the bottom of the loop over the top of the loop.
- STEP 4. Place the bight that has just been formed around the rope into a locking carabiner. Secure the locking carabiner.
- The carabiner is locked.

heading: Checkpoints
text: The following must be true for the knot to be correct: A bight passes through the carabiner with the close end around the standing or running part of the rope.

heading: SUPER MUNTER HITCH
text: The super Munter hitch is used to form a high-friction lower. (See figure 8-31.) The knot produces more friction with an additional wrap. Mountaineers use the super Munter hitch to lower very heavy loads.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a super Munter hitch:
- STEP 1. Hold the rope in both hands, palms down about 12 inches apart.
- STEP 2. With the right hand, form a loop away from the body toward the left hand. Hold the loop with the left hand.
- STEP 3. With the right hand, place the rope that comes from the bottom of the loop over the top of the loop.
- STEP 4. Place the bight that has just been formed around the rope into a locking carabiner.
- STEP 5. Take the brake strand or the strand not exiting the carabiner into the bight and pass it under the knot and carabiner. (A brake strand is the strand of a rope system that controls the rate at which a load is lowered or a rappeller descends.) Then bring it back up to form another bight. Take this bight and place it into the locking carabiner. Secure the carabiner.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- A bight passes through the carabiner, with the closed end around the standing or running part of the rope.
- An additional opposite bight is wrapped around the same strand as the first.
- The carabiner is locked.

heading: MUNTER MULE KNOT
text: The mule knot is used to create an easily releasable anchor knot in conjunction with a Munter hitch. (See figures 8-32 and 8-33, page 184.) This knot is used in systems where there is a need for releasability. The mule knot can be used to tie off a belay or lower to go hands free.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a Munter mule knot:
- STEP 1. Place a Munter hitch into a locking carabiner.
- STEP 2. With the brake strand of the Munter, create an overhand loop and place onto the load strand of the Munter hitch.
- STEP 3. Bring a bight through the overhand loop, capturing the load strand creating a slipknot.
- STEP 4. Dress the slipknot down against the Munter hitch.
- STEP 5. Pass the tails through the bight of the slipknot.
- STEP 6. Dress the bight to 4 to 6 inches.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- A bight passes through the carabiner, with the closed end around the standing or running part of the rope.
- An additional opposite bight is wrapped around the same strand as the first.
- The carabiner is locked.

heading: GARDA HITCH
text: The garda hitch (ratchet knot, alpine clutch) is a special-purpose knot, which allows rope to travel in one direction but not the other. The garda hitch is primarily used for hauling systems or rescue. (See figure 8-34.) The knot works in only one direction, and it cannot be reversed while under load.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a garda hitch knot:
- STEP 1. Place a bight of rope into the two nonlocking carabiners (which works best with two alike carabiners). D-shaped carabiners are the most effective.
- STEP 2. Take a loop of rope from the nonload side and place it down into the opposite carabiner so that the rope comes out between the two carabiners.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- When properly dressed, rope can only be pulled in one direction.
- The knot will not fail when placed under load.

heading: BIG HONKING KNOT
text: The big honking knot (BHK) is used to bring together strands of rope from multiple anchors to create a master point. (See figure 8-35, page 186.) It is often used in institutional top rope and rappel anchors. The BHK is a strong, secure knot that can handle repeated use, yet is still easy to untie.

heading: Tying the Knot
text:
The following steps are used to tie a BHK:
- STEP 1. Equalize all the strands from the anchor points, then fold back approximately 24 inches of the bight that is created.
- STEP 2. Tie a double overhand or figure-eight knot with all the strands.
- STEP 3. Check that all loops are fixed. The loop that exits behind the knot, toward the anchors, should be secured, either with a carabiner to one of the anchor legs or by passing the knot through the loop adding extra security.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- There are two fixed loops that exit away from the anchors.
- Four strands of rope should exit together from the back of the knot toward the anchors.
- Two of the strands in the back form an additional fixed loop.
- This fixed loop should be secured by a carabiner attached to a leg of the anchor or the knot should be passed through this loop to ensure it cannot be pulled back through the knot.

heading: FIELD EXPEDIENT HARNESS
text: The field expedient harness creates a seat harness out of tubular webbing used for climbing or rappelling. (See figure 8-36, page 188.) This improvised harness is more secure than the rappel seat and will not come loose while climbing. The field expedient harness can also be used in rescue to secure a patient not wearing a harness. Either 1- or 2-inch tubular webbing is acceptable for use.

heading: Constructing the Harness
text:
The following steps are used to tie a field expedient harness:
- STEP 1. Find the middle of a 25-foot section of tubular webbing and form a bight.
- STEP 2. Pass the bight between the legs from rear to front and pull it up to beltline level.
- STEP 3. Wrap the right and left tails of webbing around each respective leg from rear to front ensuring that the tails do not cross over one another.
- STEP 4. Pass the tails through the bight at belt level and wrap them back onto themselves.
- STEP 5. Wrap the remaining lengths of webbing around the body above the hips and continue to wrap in the opposite directions until enough is remaining to tie a square knot with safeties.
- STEP 6. Join the tails together just above the hip offset from front of the body on either side of the body using a square knot with overhand safeties.

heading: Checkpoints
text:
The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
- Webbing does not cross between the legs.
- Tails are passed through the diaper portion to create leg loops in the same direction.
- Minimum one full wrap around the body above the hips.
- Secured on one hip with a square knot. Safeties are only tied around the last strand around the waist.
- Square knot is far enough to the side that anything tied or clipped into the harness does not hit the square knot.

heading: CARRYING, AND THROWING
text: The service life of a rope depends on the frequency of use, applications (rappelling, climbing, rope installations), speed of descent, surface abrasion, terrain, climate, and quality of maintenance. Ropes may fail if misused, placed over sharp edges, or not properly inspected prior to use.

heading: PREPARING ROPES
text: The mountaineer must select the proper rope for the task to be accomplished according to type, diameter, length, and breaking strength. It is important to prepare all ropes before departing on a mission. Avoid rope preparation in the field.

heading: PACKAGING
text: New rope comes from the manufacturer in different configurations, boxed on a spool in various lengths, or coiled and bound in some manner. New ropes should be carefully unspooled or uncoiled to avoid kinks and prevent tangling.

heading: Coil
text: A coil is a secure configuration of rope that allows for easy transport without tangling.

heading: Precut
text: Precut ropes are usually packaged in a protective cover, such as plastic.

heading: SECURING THE ENDS OF ROPE
text: If still on a spool, the rope must be cut to the desired length. All ropes fray at the ends unless they are bound or seared. Both static and dynamic rope ends are secured in the same manner. The ends must be heated to the melting point to attach the inner core strands to the outer sheath. By fusing the two together, the sheath cannot slide backward or forward. Ensure that this is only done to the ends of the rope. If the rope is exposed to extreme temperatures, the sheath could be weakened, along with the inner core, reducing overall tensile strength. The ends may also be dipped in enamel or lacquer for further protection.

heading: CARE AND MAINTENANCE
text:
The rope is a climber's lifeline. The rope must be maintained and used properly. Climbers should use the following general guidelines when handling ropes:
- While in use, do not allow the rope to touch sharp edges. Rope is cut more easily when under tension. If the rope must be used over a sharp edge, pad the edge for protection and inspect often.
- Never allow one rope to continuously run over another. The friction causes the nylon to melt.
- Never leave a rope knotted or tightly stretched for longer than necessary. Doing so reduces the strength and life of the rope over time.
- UV radiation (sunlight) tends to deteriorate nylon over long periods. This becomes important if rope installations are left in place for months.
- Do not step on or drag ropes on the ground unnecessarily. Small particles of dirt grind between the inner strands slowly cutting them.
- All ropes should be washed periodically to remove dirt and grit and rinsed thoroughly. Army-issued rope washes are made from short pieces of modified pipe that connect to any faucet. Pinholes within the pipe force water to circulate around and scrub the rope as the Soldier slowly feeds it through the washer.
- Ropes should not be stored wet. Dry wet ropes by uncoiling and hanging them in large loops off the ground. Never dry a rope with high heat or in direct sunlight.
- When not in use, ropes should be loosely coiled and hung on wooden pegs rather than nails or other metal objects. Storage areas should be relatively cool with low-humidity levels to prevent mildew or rotting. Rope may also be loosely stacked and placed in a rope bag and stored on a shelf. Avoid storage in direct sunlight, as the UV radiation deteriorates the nylon over long periods.
- Inspect the rope before each use for frayed or cut spots, mildew or rot, or defects in construction (new rope).
- Do not mark ropes with paints or allow them to touch oils or petroleum products. Some of these weaken or deteriorate nylon.
- Never subject the rope to high heat or flame. Heat and flame significantly weaken rope.
- Never use a mountaineering rope for any purpose except mountaineering.
- Each rope should have a corresponding rope log DA Form 5752-R (Rope Log [Usage and History]), which is also a safety record. On the form, annotate use, terrain, weather, application, number of falls, dates, and so on. Annotate each time the rope is used on the form. DA Form 5752-R is authorized for local reproduction on 8 1/2- by 11-inch paper.

heading: INSPECTION
text:
Ropes should be inspected before and after each use, especially when working around loose rock or sharp edges.
- Although the core of the kernmantle rope cannot be seen, it is possible to damage the core without damaging the sheath. Check a kernmantle rope by carefully inspecting the sheath before and after use while the rope is being coiled. When coiling, be aware of how the rope feels as it runs through the hands. Immediately note and tie off any lumps or depressions felt.
- Damage to the core of a kernmantle rope usually consists of filaments or yarn breakage that results in a slight retraction. If enough strands rupture, a localized reduction in the diameter of the rope results in a depression that can be felt or even seen.
- Check any other suspected areas further by putting them under tension (the weight of one person, approximately 185 pounds standing on a prusik tensioning system is about maximum). This procedure emphasizes the lump or depression by separating the broken strands and enlarging the dip. If a noticeable difference in diameter is obvious, retire the rope immediately.
- Many dynamic kernmantle ropes are quite soft. They may retain an indentation occasionally after an impact or under normal use without any trauma to the core. When damage is suspected, patiently inspect the sheath for abnormalities. Damage to the sheath does not always mean damage to the core. Inspect carefully.

heading: COILING AND CARRYING ROPE
text: Use the butterfly or mountain coil to coil and carry the rope. Each is easy to accomplish and results in a minimal number of kinks, twists, and knots later during deployment.

heading: BUTTERFLY COIL
text: The butterfly coil is the quickest and easiest technique for coiling. (See figure 8-37.)

heading: Coiling
text: To start the butterfly coil, grasp both ends of the rope and begin back stacking, ensuring the ends of the rope are not buried at the bottom of the stack. Find the center of the rope and form a bight. With the bight in the left hand, grasp both ropes and slide the right hand out until there is approximately one arm-length of rope. Place the doubled rope over the head, draping it around the neck and over the shoulders. Ensure that it hangs no lower than the waist. Soldiers ensure the rest of the doubled rope is in front of them and continue making doubled bights and placing them over the head in the same manner as the first bight. Coil alternating from side to side (left to right, right to left) while maintaining equal-length bights. Continue coiling until approximately two arm-lengths of rope remain. Remove the coils from the neck and shoulders and hold the center in one hand. Wrap the two ends upwards around the coils with a minimum of three complete wraps, ensuring that the first wrap locks back on itself.

heading: Tie Off and Carrying
text: Take both strands from the tails of the rope, forming a double bight and pass it through the apex of the coils. Pull the loose ends through the doubled bight and dress it down. Ensure that the loose ends do not exceed 2 meters. In this configuration, the coiled rope is secure enough for hand carrying or carrying in a rucksack or for storage. To carry on the body, place the butterfly coil on the back, with one tail over each of the shoulders, bring back directly under the arms and wrap at least once around the body, ensuring to capture all the coils. Secure the ends with a square knot, which does not need overhand safeties. (See figure 8-37 for a farmer's tie off.)

heading: MOUNTAIN COIL
text: To start a mountain coil, grasp the rope about 1 meter from the end with one hand. Run the other hand along the rope until both arms are outstretched. Grasping the rope firmly, bring the hands together, forming a loop, which is laid in the hand closest to the end of the rope. This is repeated, forming uniform loops that run in a clockwise direction, until the rope is completely coiled. The rope may be given a one-quarter twist as each loop is formed to overcome any tendency for the rope to twist or form figure eights.

heading: MOUNTAIN COIL
text: To finish the mountain coil, form a bight about 30-cm long with the starting end of the rope and lay it along the top of the coil. Uncoil the last loop and, using this length of the rope, begin making wraps around the coil and the bight, wrapping toward the closed end of the bight. Make six to eight wraps to adequately secure the coil, and then route the end of the rope through the closed end of the bight. Pull the running end of the bight tight, securing the coil.

heading: MOUNTAIN COIL
text: The mountain coil may be carried in either the pack (by forming a figure eight), doubling it and placing it under the flap, or by placing it over the shoulder and under the opposite arm, slung across the chest. (Figure 8-38 shows how to coil a mountain coil.)

heading: COILING CORDS AND SLINGS
text: Length of cord, webbing, or rope less than 8 meters may be coiled so that they can be hung from the harness. Hold the ends of the cord or the joining knot in the left hand. Coil the doubled rope into 6- to 8-inch loops until an approximate 12-inch bight is left. Wrap that bight around the coil, ensuring that the first wrap locks on itself. Wrap until there is just enough bight left to feed through the bights formed at the top of the coil. Dress it down tightly. Now the piece of rope or webbing may be hung from a carabiner on the harness or attached to a gear sling and slung over the shoulder. The same can be done with slings.

heading: UNCOILING, BACK STACKING, AND STACKING
text: When the rope is needed for use, it must be uncoiled and back stacked on the ground properly to avoid kinks and snarls. Choose a location that is clear of sharp rocks, sticks, or other items that could damage the rope or cause snarls when deploying the rope. Also, avoid wet or muddy areas. When these locations are unavoidable, using a tarp, poncho, or rope bag to place under the rope when stacking can provide protection.

heading: UNCOILING, BACK STACKING, AND STACKING
text: Untie the tie off and lay the coil on the ground. Single back stack the rope to minimize kinks and snarls. (This is also useful when moving the rope a short distance and coiling is not desired.) Take one end of the rope in the left hand and run the right hand along the rope until both arms are outstretched. Next, lay the end of the rope in the left hand on the ground, ensuring that the standing end of the rope is laid off to the side and is not buried under the stack. With the left hand, regrasp the rope next to the right hand and continue laying the rope on the ground.

heading: UNCOILING, BACK STACKING, AND STACKING
text: The rope should be laid or stacked in a neat pile on the ground to prevent it from becoming tangled and knotted when throwing the rope, feeding it to a lead climber, and so on. This technique can also be started using the right hand.

heading: THROWING THE ROPE
text: Before throwing the rope, it should be back stacked to prevent it from tangling during deployment. The bottom end of the rope should be anchored to prevent complete loss of the rope over the edge when it is thrown. Several techniques can be used when deploying a rope.

heading: THROWING THE ROPE
text: If the cliff is steep enough, it may be unnecessary to throw the rope. Back stack the rope down the cliff face. The rope is less likely to be carried by the wind or to be caught in trees. It is more likely to be hung up on ledges and shrubs on the face than when thrown. The rope should be thrown at a low angle and blocky terrain.

heading: THROWING THE ROPE
text: To throw the rope, take the strand on the top of the stack and begin to create butterfly coils in the dominant hand. Create enough coils so that there is sufficient weight to carry the rest of the rope down when it is thrown. It is time consuming and almost never necessary to coil the entire length of rope to throw it. The rope is best thrown underhand and slightly up and out from the edge. Throwing the rope too high could cause it to be hung up in tree branches. At a training site where there may be people below, the thrower should confirm that no one is below and sound off with the following warning as they throw: ROPE.

heading: THROWING THE ROPE
text: When windy weather conditions prevail, adjustments must be made. In a strong crosswind, the rope should be thrown angled into the wind so that it lands on the desired target. The stronger the wind, the harder the rope must be thrown to compensate. If the wind is too strong, sometimes it is best to single back stack the rope in a pack. The first Soldier who descends the rope should guide it down the fall line. During the descent, the rope is stacked in such a way that it exits cleanly from the pack to avoid becoming tangled. Another technique is to coil the rope freely on the shoulders of the first Soldier, allowing it to easily uncoil as the Soldier descends.

heading: THROWING THE ROPE
text: This Soldier needs to incorporate a hands-free backup during the rappel to allow stopping and using both hands to manage the rope, if necessary. This page intentionally left blank.

heading: Anchor Selection and Construction
text: Understanding anchors is an important fundamental that must be understood early in the path to becoming a military mountaineer. An anchor is the point where manufactured equipment for mountaineering meets the surface of the earth. Great varieties of natural features are found in different operational environments that a Soldier could use to construct an anchor. Anchors are found in all rope systems and are built in many ways. This chapter gives Soldiers the tools to assess terrain for the suitability of anchor construction for a wide variety of rope systems. This chapter also exposes Soldiers to the principles of anchor construction that ensure they are building solid anchors in a wide variety of terrain for many different purposes. Anchor selection in mountainous terrain requires a certain degree of knowledge and substantial experience. Most mountaineering accidents occur at the anchor. Inexperienced Soldiers should stick to selecting anchor features that are obviously stronger than necessary and choose simple rigging techniques with which they are familiar.

heading: SECTION I - GENERAL PRINCIPLES: SINGLE AND MULTIPOINT
text: An anchor for military mountaineering is a fixed object to which a rope system is secured and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. It is a point in the operational environment, which a rope installation is attached, providing more than enough resistance to a directional pull. Rope systems can be used for moving casualties and equipment. Some, like rappels or fixed ropes, are used for aiding movement. Technical rope systems provide the tools for addressing many of the challenges posed by mountainous terrain. Anchor selection and evaluation together form the foundation of all systems.

heading: SECTION I - GENERAL PRINCIPLES: SINGLE AND MULTIPOINT
text: Considerations for selecting a natural feature to construct an anchor are its location and ability to resist any forces that are placed upon it. The anchor should be above any intended rope pathways. This reduces the pendulum effect on any loads attached to the anchor. Another important facet of anchor location is its proximity to the edge. In some situations, having the anchor a short distance away from the edge creates a platform to work on. In other situations, such as setting a top rope, it is best to have the anchor near the edge. This aspect of anchor building can be challenging as the strength of natural features, such as rocks, trees, roots, and boulders; can be difficult to judge. Soldiers must err on the side of caution and leave no doubt that an anchor is strong enough for its intended purpose. If there is any doubt about a single-point anchor's strength or security, then additional anchor components should be constructed and incorporated until sufficient strength and security are achieved to ensure that anchor failure cannot occur. The strength of an anchor should never be in question.

heading: SECTION I - GENERAL PRINCIPLES: SINGLE AND MULTIPOINT
text: Anchors in mountaineering should be loaded in a steady and slow manner. Avoid bouncing as much as possible as it could weaken the integrity of the natural object being used. Sometimes slack can generate in various types of rope systems and cause an anchor to be shock loaded. It is best to avoid any circumstances that may lead to this as shock loading results in very high forces on the anchor.

heading: SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS
text: Single-point anchors are the simplest in mountaineering and serve as the building blocks for more complicated anchors. If a single feature, object, or piece of equipment is to be used as an anchor, there must be no doubt that it is both strong enough and secure enough to hold if shock loading were to occur. The same goes for all rigging used in building the anchor. Correctly tied master points, locking carabiners, and double nonlocking carabiners opposite and opposed must be used for all points of connection. (See figure 9-1, page 196.)

heading: SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS
text: If using opposite and opposed carabiners in place of a locking carabiner, ensure they are properly configured. (See figure 9-1.)

heading: SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS
text: Single-point anchors are created by simply tying cordage or webbing around something of sufficient strength to form an adequate anchor.

heading: SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS
text: There are three basic methods of attaching webbing slings to single-point anchors: single loop (drape) with the webbing joined around the anchor, basket hitch (wrap), and the girth hitch. (See figure 9-2.)

heading: SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS
text: There are two basic methods to create single-point anchors using joined cordelette. They are the basket hitch and master point. (See figure 9-3, page 198, and figure 9-4, page 199.)

heading: SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS
text: A cordelette can also be doubled before tying a basket hitch. This keeps the attachment point closer to the anchor. Round turns can also be added around the anchor to hold the anchor in place. Certain specific situations require this (for example, a high redirect). (See figure 9-3, page 198.)

heading: SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS
text: A knot can be incorporated in the basket hitch to create a master point. A master point is the loop created from the knot that is incorporated into the anchor. It serves as an attachment point for carabiners for building rope systems or belays. This can be created by creating a fixed loop with a figure-eight or overhand knot.

heading: SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS
text: The master-point technique should be used if there is any chance the material could be cut on sharp rock edges when the cord is wrapped around a rock. The knot isolates the individual strands creating redundancy so if an individual strand were to break, the entire anchor would not fail.

heading: SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS
text: A master point is also useful for creating a clean and easily identifiable working point for use with multiple carabiners.

heading: MULTIPOINT ANCHORS
text: Multipoint anchors are more than one fixed object joined with technical rigging to form an anchor system capable of suspending the weight or arresting the fall of an attached load. They become necessary as suitable single-point anchors become scarce. This not only provides greater anchor strength but also adds redundancy or backup because of the multiple components. Multipoint anchors are used frequently in mountaineering. It requires a strong understanding of anchoring principles, creativity, and experience applying them in the field to ensure adequacy.

heading: ANGLE CONSIDERATIONS
text: When using only two anchor points, it is extremely important to recognize the angle that is created. Imagine holding two ends of a rope with a 5-gallon water can in the middle. It would be very difficult to hold the can up with the rope straight at 180 degrees . It would be much easier to support the weight of the water can if the two rope ends were almost touching in the middle. As the angle between anchor components increases, so does the force that is felt by each anchor. (See figure 9-5.)

heading: SELF-EQUALIZING ANCHORS
text: A self-equalizing anchor is a multipoint anchor comprised of adjustable strands from each anchor component to a shared attachment point that allows for maximum load sharing even when direction of pull changes during use. (See figure 9-6, page 202.) Self-equalizing anchors are rarely necessary in mountaineering as the direction of pull rarely changes, and there is the possibility of extension and shock loading if a component fails.

heading: PRE-EQUALIZED ANCHORS
text: A pre-equalized anchor is the preferred type of multipoint anchor used in mountaineering. The anchor distributes the weight of the load among each individual anchor component using fixed and independent strands. (See figure 9-7.) Multipoint anchors orient all strands together pointing in the direction that the anchor will be loaded. A pre-equalized anchor prevents extending and shock loading the anchor if an individual component fails. An anchor is pre-equalized by tying a master point using an appropriate loop knot in the webbing or sling.

heading: PRE-EQUALIZED ANCHORS
text:
The mnemonic EARNEST-H can be used as a guide to build optimal and efficient multipoint anchors. Multipoint anchors should be--
- E--equalized: Each component of the anchor shares the load evenly. Nonlocking carabiners are typically acceptable links between soft materials here.
- A--angle: The angles between the strands of individual components should not exceed 90 degrees , if possible. The goal is to minimize multiplying forces as shown in figure 9-7.
- R--redundant: The entire anchor system is not reliant on a single anchor component. Rigging of the cord is such that if a single strand breaks or is cut, the entire anchor would not fail. Redundancy is achieved by tying a master point.
- NE--no extension: If one leg of the anchor does fail, the anchor does not extend, causing shock load to the rest.
- S--solid: This is the big picture look at the anchor system. Ensure that there are no problems with how the individual segments work together, that the larger feature comprising the anchor is strong and secure, and that the whole thing is appropriate for the intended anchoring application. Anchor components should not all be placed in the same feature.
- T--timely: This is meant to remind mountaineers to remember efficiency when building anchors. The fastest and simplest anchor system to build that meets the above criteria is the best.
- H--high: This is not required, but if it can be achieved while meeting all the above criteria, then it is strongly recommended. Anchors with master points between waist and shoulder height make operating any attached system significantly easier and more efficient.

heading: SECTION II - TREES
text: Tree anchors should be considered for use first. They are usually strong and often simple to construct with minimal use of equipment. Trees are already in place and simply require a method of attaching the rope. However, they should be carefully studied and evaluated for stability and strength before use. Sometimes the rope is tied directly to the anchor, but under most circumstances, a cord or sling is attached to the tree and then the climbing rope is attached to the sling with a carabiner.

heading: CONSIDERATIONS
text:
The following are considerations for using trees as anchors for mountaineering rope systems:
- In rocky terrain, trees usually have a shallow root system. This can be evaluated by pushing on the tree to see how well it is rooted. If there is concern that a tree may be pulled over when loaded, another anchor should be selected. If this anchor is the only option, the rope should be anchored as low as possible to reduce leverage.
- When evaluating a tree for suitable strength, strive for a diameter at the base of the tree of at least 8 inches.
- In the summer months, it may be easy to determine if a tree is alive. The best indicator can be leaves. However, even trees that have fallen over may still grow leaves if they are still partially rooted. Ensure that a concentrated effort is made to evaluate the tree.
- In the winter, certain trees do not have leaves. This may make it difficult to establish if they are alive. Look at the tree trunk for signs of extensive rot, woodpecker holes, or fungus growing on the tree trunk. Trees that have no leaves in the winter can still be checked to see if they are alive. The tree will have buds at the ends of small twig branches that will turn into next year's leaves. Major deformities, cracks, or damage are also an indicator that the tree may not be a viable anchor.
- Use padding on soft, sap-producing trees to keep sap off ropes and slings.

heading: ROPE ANCHORS
text: The climbing or installation rope can be tied directly to the tree anchor using several different techniques. (See figure 9-8.) This requires less equipment but also sacrifices some rope length to tie the anchor. The rope can be tied to the anchor using an appropriate anchor knot, such as a bowline or triple bowline. Round turns can be used to help keep the rope in position on the anchor and reduce the likelihood of it slipping on the trunk.

heading: HIGH-STRENGTH TIE OFF (TENSIONLESS HITCH)
text: A high-strength tie off is a single-point anchoring method that retains maximum installation rope strength and releasability, using multiple-round turns around the anchor object to create friction, and securing the end back to itself ensuring no force is applied to any component knots or carabiners. It is used to anchor the rope on high-load installations used for bridging and traversing. (See figure 9-9, page 206.) The wraps of the rope around the anchor absorb the tension of the installation and keep the tension off the knot and carabiner. The anchor is usually tied with a minimum of three wraps, more, if necessary, to absorb the tension. A smooth anchor may require several wraps, whereas a rough barked tree might only require a few. The rope is wrapped from top to bottom without crossing strands so that it can be untied under tension, if desired. A fixed loop is placed into the end of the rope and attached loosely back onto the rope with a locking carabiner.

heading: MULTIPOINT TREE ANCHORS
text: When there are multiple tree anchors available that do not meet the criteria for a single-point anchor, then multiple trees should be used. Using multiple anchors incorporates redundancy in case one anchor fails. The same principles for multipoint anchors apply for trees and all other anchors. If using only two trees for anchors, then the angle created between the two trees should be less than 90 degrees as described in paragraph 9-14, page 200.

heading: BUSHES AND SHRUBS
text: Bush and shrub anchors are not recommended for use unless there are no other options, and a technical task cannot be avoided. An advanced-level mountaineer should be present to evaluate the rigging and strength of the anchor. They are constructed by equalizing many small bushes and shrubs together into a master point using cordelettes, slings, and anchor ropes. As with trees, the anchoring rope is placed as low as possible to reduce leverage on the anchor. All vegetation should be healthy and well rooted to the ground. It cannot be overstated that the strength and security of bush and shrub anchors cannot be easily assessed for strength.

heading: BOULDERS AND ROCK PROTRUSIONS
text: Boulders and rock protrusions make ideal anchors. (See figure 9-10.) Rock features should not be used as anchors if they can be moved by pushing or kicking it or sound hollow or detached when tapped. The surface a boulder rests upon should be inspected to ensure the boulder does not slide when force is applied to it. Rock protrusions should be a solid mass of rock. Crumbly or loose rock formations are not typically sufficient anchors. Talus and scree fields are an indicator that the rock in the area is not solid. All areas around the rock formation that could cut the rope or sling should be padded. It is also wise to consider the consequences if the rock were to dislodge.

heading: CHOCKSTONES
text: A chockstone is a rock that is wedged in a crack that narrows downward. (See figure 9-11, page 208.) Chockstones should be checked for strength, security, crumbling and should always be tested before use. All chockstones must be solid and strong enough to support the load. They must have maximum surface contact and taper with the surrounding rock to remain in position. Chockstones are often directional; they are secure when pulled in one direction but may pop out if pulled in another direction.

heading: TUNNELS, ARCHES, AND PINCH POINTS
text: Tunnels and arches are holes formed in solid rock. If viable, they provide one of the more secure natural anchor points as they can be pulled in any direction (See figure 9-12.) A natural anchor is a natural fixed object (such as a tree, rock formation, or ice formation) to which a rope system can be secured and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. A sling is threaded through the opening hole and secured with a joining knot or girth hitch. The load-bearing hole must be strong and free of sharp edges (pad, if necessary). A pinch-point anchor is used the same way as arches or tunnels; it is just formed by a pinch point between two large boulders, allowing a sling or cordelette to be tied around it. Boulders comprising a pinch point need to be large enough and secure enough to ensure they do not move when a force is applied. Sometimes a little digging in snow or earth provides a pinch-point anchor where no other options are available.

heading: ARTIFICIAL ROCK PROTECTION
text: Artificial rock protection is anything used to protect a climber or anchor a rope system and is not part of the natural environment. The evolution of artificial protection started with handmade pieces of metal called pitons. Now there are several companies that manufacture various lightweight artificial protection. There is fixed and removable protection. Fixed protections are bolts and pitons; they are left in the rock for future use and can be difficult to remove. Removable protection refers to spring-loaded camming devices (known as cams), chocks, and other specialty protection that is easily recoverable after use.

heading: ARTIFICIAL ROCK PROTECTION
text: Artificial protection is used to construct anchors in various ways. Anchors may be comprised of a combination of artificial protection and other objects, such as a tree or a boulder. The combinations are endless. However, when building anchors made with only artificial protection, multiple pieces are required. No single piece of artificial protection is considered adequate to comprise an anchor. A minimum of two components are needed to provide redundancy in the case of bad placement, poor rock quality, or any other factor causing a piece to fail.

heading: PITONS
text: Pitons have been in use for over 100 years. Although still available, pitons are not used as often as other types of artificial anchors due primarily to their impact on the environment. Most climbers prefer to use other artificial anchors rather than pitons because they do not scar the rock and are easier to remove. Pitons still have a place in military mountaineering since they are a relatively light, cheap, and expendable yet extremely strong and secure anchor option when placed properly. They are particularly useful during rocky alpine descents, when an ice axe with a hammer is already carried and natural rappel anchors are scarce.

heading: PITONS
text: One piton is not considered strong or secure enough to serve as a single belay or system anchor. When establishing an anchor using multiple pitons, they should be placed in different cracks or features. A single piton can also be combined with other viable natural anchoring methods, if available. Note. Properly placing pitons requires significant practice to master, which should be conducted in training scenarios involving backup systems to protect the trainee should a placement fail.

heading: ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
text:
Some advantages with using pitons are--
- Depending on type and placement, pitons can support multiple directions of pull.
- They are less complex than other types of artificial anchors.
- Pitons work well in thin cracks where other types of artificial anchors do not.

heading: ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
text:
Some disadvantages with using pitons are--
- During military operations, the distinct sound created when hammering pitons is a tactical disadvantage.
- Due to the expansion force of emplacing a piton, the rock could spread apart or break, causing an unsafe condition.
- Pitons are more difficult to remove than other types of artificial anchors.
- Pitons leave noticeable scars on the rock. They are prohibited in most established climbing areas.
- Pitons are easily dropped if not tied off when being used.

heading: PITON PLACEMENT
text: Properly positioning or placing pitons is critical. (See figure 9-13 for examples of piton placement.) Usually, a properly sized piton for a rock crack will fit one-half to two-thirds into the crack before being driven with the piton hammer. This helps ensure the depth of the crack is adequate for the size piton selected. As pitons are driven into the rock, the pitch or sound that is made will change with each hammer blow, becoming higher pitched as the piton is driven in.

heading: PITON PLACEMENT
text: Test the rock for soundness by tapping with the hammer. Driving pitons in soft or rotten rock is not recommended. When this type of rock must be used, clear the loose rock, dirt, and debris from the crack before driving the piton completely in.

heading: PITON PLACEMENT
text: While it is being driven, attach the piton to a sling with a carabiner (an old carabiner should be used, if available) so that if the piton is knocked out of the crack, it is not lost. The greater the resistance overcome while driving the piton, the stronger and more secure the anchor is. The quality of the rock around the crack a piton is placed into also greatly affects the strength and security of the anchor. The piton should not spread the rock, thereby loosening the placement.

heading: PITON PLACEMENT
text: Sometimes a piton cannot be driven completely into a crack because the piton is too long. Although this is not optimal, occasionally there are no other options. Instead of attaching to the piton hole, webbing should be attached to the shaft with a girth hitch as close to the rock face as possible to reduce leverage on the piton. (See figure 9-14, page 212.)

heading: REMOVING PITONS
text: Attach a carabiner and sling to the piton before removal to reduce the likelihood of dropping and losing it. Tap the piton firmly along the axis of the crack in which it is located. Alternate tapping from both sides while applying steady pressure. Pulling out on the attached carabiner eventually removes the piton. (See figure 9-15.)

heading: REUSING PITONS
text: Soft iron pitons that have been used, removed, and straightened may be reused, but they must be checked for strength. In training areas, pitons already in place should not be trusted since the weather loosens them in time. Also, they may have been driven poorly the first time. Before use, test them as described above and drive them again until certain of their soundness. Note. Fixed artificial anchors, such as pitons and bolts, are not widely accepted for use in all areas because of the scars they leave on the rock and the environment. They are often left in place and are unnatural fixtures in the natural environment. For training, consider local laws and courtesies for each area of operation.

heading: BOLTS
text: A bolt is a type of rock protection or anchoring component comprised of an expansion bolt or glue-in shaft attached to a hanger to which a carabiner can be attached. Bolts are often used in fixed-rope installations and in aid climbing where cracks are not available. Bolts provide one of the most secure means of establishing protection.

heading: BOLTS
text: Some bolts have rings attached for easy retrievable rappelling, clip-in points for top rope climbing, chains to aid in establishing tope rope climbing anchors, or other special-purpose attachment points.

heading: BOLTS
text:
There are two primary types of bolts: expansion bolts and glue-in bolts. Both involve drilling a hole into a rock face, cleaning out dust and debris, and inserting a bolt. The difference is in how the bolt is secured in the hole:
- Expansion bolts use a sleeve that expands as it is tightened. The sleeve expands against the walls of the hole to prevent it from coming out. (See figure 9-16.)
- Glue-in bolts are held in place by a high-strength adhesive. Glue-in bolts are used in softer, porous rock, such as sandstone. Delicate rock, like sandstone, may not be strong enough to support expansion bolts. Its porous structure allows the glue to expand deep into the rock around the original hole. (See figure 9-17, page 216.)

heading: ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
text:
Some advantages of using bolts in anchor construction are--
- Extremely strong and secure when installed properly.
- Very easy to use for climbing protection when already installed.
- Very easy to use in multipoint-anchor construction when already installed.

heading: ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
text:
Some disadvantages of using bolts in anchor construction are--
- Extremely time consuming to install relative to other artificial anchoring devices.
- Require the mountaineer to use both hands and hang during installation.
- Require special, relatively heavy tools (for example, drills, hammers, wrenches) to install.
- Noisy to install.

heading: INSTALLATION AND USE
text: There are enough differences in bolts available on the market that mountaineers should refer to manufacturers' instructions for installing bolts. Installing bolts permanently alters the rock. The climbing community has strong ethics regarding the placement of bolts. Ethics and regulations vary regionally, but in all areas, it is unacceptable to add bolts to existing climbs. Any bolting should be done with the consensus of the climbing community.

heading: INSTALLATION AND USE
text: When using existing bolts as climbing protection or as part of an anchor system, mountaineers should inspect them for anything indicating compromise. The first thing that should be inspected is the rock on which it will be placed. Bolts are only as strong and secure as the quality of the rock. The hanger should not be rusty or loose. Loose hangers can indicate the bolt being insecure, or the hole has not been drilled deep enough to secure the hanger to the rock's face. If the nut holding a hanger can be tightened to a point, then it is viable. If it keeps spinning, the bolt should not be used or at the very least backed up with additional protection.

heading: INSTALLATION AND USE
text: Many chock picks (sometimes referred to as nut-tools) have a hex cut out in them that can be used like a wrench to tighten loose bolts. A chock pick is used in lead climbing to aid a follow-on climber in removing protection. (See figure 9-18.)

heading: CHOCKS
text: The principles for using devices commonly called chocks, nuts, or stoppers are the same as with chockstones above. They are designed to work in smaller cracks, easier to place, and more secure. (See figure 9-19, page 218.) The direction of pull must be considered carefully when using chocks.

heading: ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
text:
Using chocks in anchor construction has the following advantages:
- Tactically quiet installation and recovery.
- Usually easy to retrieve and, unless severely damaged, are reusable.
- Light to carry.
- Minimal rock scarring as opposed to pitons.
- Sometimes can be placed where pitons cannot (expanding rock flakes where pitons would further weaken the rock).

heading: ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
text:
Using chock in anchor construction has the following disadvantages:
- May not fit in thin cracks, which may accept pitons.
- Often provide only one direction of pull.
- Practice and experience are necessary to become proficient in proper placement and removal.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: The principles of placing chocks are to find a crack with a constriction at some point, place a chock of appropriate size above and behind the constriction, and set the chock by gently jerking down. Maximum surface contact with a tight fit is critical. Chocks are usually good for a single direction of pull.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: Avoid cracks that have crumbly (soft) or deteriorating rock, if possible. Some cracks may have loose rock, grass, and dirt, which should be removed before placing the chock. Look for a constriction point in the crack, and then select a chock to fit it.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: When selecting a chock, choose one that has as much surface area as possible in contact with the rock. A chock resting on one small crystal or point of rock is likely to be unsafe. A chock that sticks partly out of the crack is avoided.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: All chocks used for lead climber protection should include a soft material extension, such as a runner, to prevent the rope from wiggling the chock out of placement.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: Chocks must be lightly tugged on to set them so that they do not fall out of placement. Weighting the placement helps to keep the protection in position. A carabiner often provides enough weight.

heading: CAMMING DEVICES
text: Camming devices are designed for building anchors in parallel-sided cracks where chocks are ineffective. There are several different types, but they all work by changing from a downward force to an outward force when loaded. This force creates enough friction that the device cannot move, even when no constriction in the crack is present. Camming devices increase force on surrounding rock as downward force is applied. Due to this, care should be taken to inspect the security of the rock on which they are placed.

heading: CAMMING DEVICES
text: Camming devices become even more secure when placed above a constriction. If the lobes slip during loading, they cannot exit the crack.

heading: CAMMING DEVICES
text: Cams are the most used camming devices in mountaineering. They have advantages and disadvantages and require extensive practice and experience to place and use properly.

heading: SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES
text: Cams are the most versatile and widely used artificial rock anchoring devices available to mountaineers. Although there are several types of cams, the modern design consists of two sets of lobes that oppose each other and rotate from one or two axles, connected to a trigger mechanism on a single, flexible stem that runs perpendicular to the axle. Attached to the axle is a presewn connection sling. They are designed to work in parallel-sided cracks where a chock would just slide down.

heading: SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES
text: Cams come in a wide variety of sizes to fit cracks from 0.5 inches to over 21 inches. Each unit has an expansion range that enables it to function properly within a certain width of cracks. It may be necessary to carry many sizes depending upon the route, mission, and intended use. Most come with color-coded slings to help the user select the correct size for use.

heading: SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES
text: Three quality camming devices equalized together are required to establish an adequate anchor. An exception is two large camming devices perfectly placed in solid rock with constrictions below them. A single camming device is usually placed for intermediate lead-climbing protection. Suboptimal placements or rock features require additional pieces to achieve an acceptable anchor.

heading: ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
text:
The advantages of using cams in anchor construction are listed below:
- They are much faster to place and remove, for creating anchors or as points of protection while lead climbing.
- They require only one hand to place, so the mountaineer can hold on to the rock with the other.
- They are easy to insert and remove when placed properly.
- They can be more forgiving than other anchor devices if the direction of pull changes.
- They provide many possibilities for rigging multipoint anchors.
- They do not damage the surrounding rock.

heading: ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
text:
The disadvantages of using cams in anchor construction are listed below:
- They can wiggle or walk out of proper placement, resulting in a compromised anchor, or in a stuck camming device that is difficult or impossible to remove.
- They are much more expensive compared to other types of anchors.
- They can be heavy and bulky to carry.
- They have the potential to generate enough outward mechanical force to damage the surrounding rock and compromise the anchor when loaded.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: To place cams, find a uniform, parallel spot in the crack where the rock is clean and solid. Retract the lobes by pulling back on the trigger. Gently insert the camming device and release the trigger so the lobes expand to fit the crack. The spring mechanism works to hold the camming device in place. Ideally, the lobes should be open between 10 percent and 80 percent of full expansion. (See figure 9-20 and figure 9-21, page 222.)

heading: PLACEMENT
text: Avoid overcamming, which can make the unit difficult or impossible to remove, or undercamming, which results in too little surface area contact and reduced stability. The unit should also be placed deep enough to not break the edge of the crack but not so deep that the trigger mechanism cannot be reached.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: Orient the stem to point in the direction from which the camming device is loaded.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: Inspect the final placement to ensure the angle of the lobes in relation to each other is even and within the acceptable range.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: An extension using a runner may be added between the camming device and climbing rope to reduce likelihood it walks out of position during lead climbing.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: Single cam placements can be used for fall protection while lead climbing. Multiple cam placements can be equalized together with cordage or webbing to create load-bearing anchors.

heading: PLACEMENT
text: To remove cams, simply pull the trigger mechanism and gently remove the device.

heading: SECTION IV - ICE ANCHORS
text: Fall protection and anchors can be constructed in alpine or waterfall ice using specialized ice screws. Occasionally, natural ice features can be found allowing anchor construction without them.

heading: TYPES OF ICE ANCHORS
text: Ice anchors consist of ice pillars, ice screws, and V-threads. Except for the case of large ice pillars, ice anchors should incorporate two or more anchor points to be strong and secure enough.

heading: ICE PILLARS, ICE SCREWS, AND V-THREADS
text: Ice pillars often form in steep alpine terrain. It is sometimes possible to pass a length of cordage or webbing around the whole mass of ice and create a single-point anchor in the same fashion as a rock protrusion or tree. (See figure 9-22.) Ice pillars should be totally frozen to the ground, comprised of dense, crack-free ice, and greater than 1 foot in diameter to use as a single-point anchor. Smaller pillars may be used as part of multi-point anchors.

heading: ICE PILLARS, ICE SCREWS, AND V-THREADS
text: Occasionally, ice pillars can be created in ice features, such as sufficiently thick ice curtains where there is a hollow space behind, and a hole can be broken through a thin section with a mountain ax. Then an anchor can be established as above. Care must be taken not to damage the selected ice mass when creating a hole.

heading: ICE SCREWS
text: The ice screw is the most common type of ice protection. An ice screw is a threaded tubular screw with teeth on the end. Some screws have longer hangers or handles, which allow them to be easily twisted into position by hand. Ice screws come in various lengths for use in various ice thicknesses. Newer ice screws come manufactured with a twist knob on the hanger for easier placement.

heading: ICE SCREWS
text: The security of an ice screw is determined by the quality of the ice in which it is placed. The thicker and denser the ice is, the stronger it is. Thinner ice, aerated ice, or ice with air pockets is weak; mountaineers should avoid this sort of ice. Deep, thick ice is generally bluish in color, while ice that has air pockets is often white in color. It takes significant experience to judge the strength of ice, but even a novice can learn much about ice quality by the resistance felt when placing the ice screw. Air pockets are felt as a reduction in resistance. The more resistance, the denser the ice. The longer the core grows as it is screwed in, typically the better the ice. (See figure 9-23.) Evaluate the integrity of the ice structure. If possible, avoid fracture lines, the apex of ice bulges, and ice blocks that are not attached to a main flow.

heading: ICE SCREWS
text: One ice screw in quality ice is sufficient to protect a lead climber. Two or more ice screws must be placed in quality ice to create a secure anchor. (See figure 9-24.) The same principles apply for creating multipoint anchors for ice screws. If the ice quality is suboptimal, then additional screws should be incorporated.

heading: Advantages and Disadvantages
text:
The advantages of using ice screws in anchor construction are that they--
- Can be placed almost anywhere in an ice flow.
- Can be placed with one hand.
- Fastest protection to place in ice.

heading: Advantages and Disadvantages
text:
The disadvantages of using ice screws in anchor construction are that they--
- Are bulky and difficult to carry in large numbers.
- Require difficult and tedious maintenance to keep sharp because of the double angle and curvature of the teeth.
- If not removed and cleared correctly, ice can freeze in the core of the screw, rendering it useless.

heading: Placement
text: Ensure all rotten ice is cleared away from the surface.

heading: Placement
text: Hold the hanger end of the screw, and press teeth against the surface at an approximately 90 degrees angle to the ice with a twisting motion. An acceptable range is +/-20 degrees . (See figure 9-25, page 226.) Typically, several twists are necessary to get it started. The screw is started when it does not fall out of the ice. This is more easily done at about waist level for leverage, especially if the footing is poor.

heading: Placement
text: Once started, fold out the screw's knob or handle, and twist in a circular motion clockwise until the hanger is tight to the ice. Fold knob or handle down and out of the way. Avoid overturning the screw once it has become tight. If the screw is tight and the hanger is not pointed downward, back the screw out enough to achieve a downward hanger. The screw should be tight and secure; the threads in contact with solid ice are what absorb any force placed on the screw.

heading: Placement
text: Clip a carabiner to the hanger, then incorporate into a multipoint anchor or clip rope when lead climbing.

heading: Placement
text: Remove the ice by folding out the knob or handle and spinning counterclockwise. Clear any ice out of the tube so that it does not freeze.

heading: Placement
text: Melting of the ice around a screw must be considered. The effective time or strength of an ice screw placement are limited. The screw will heat from solar radiation, or the ice may crack or soften. Solar radiation can be nearly eliminated by covering the screw with ice chips once it has been emplaced. If repeated use is necessary for one installation, such as top roping, the screws should be inspected frequently and relocated when necessary. When an ice screw is removed, the ice that has accumulated in the core of the screw must be cleared immediately.

heading: V-THREADS
text: An ice anchor can be improvised using one long screw. This is particularly useful when the climber is short on ice screws or does not want to leave ice screws behind while rappelling. V-threads are common in fixed rope construction in snow and ice. Vertical or horizontal V-thread anchors can be created depending on the nature of the ice flow. Multiple V-thread anchors may be created and joined to create a secure ice anchor when ice quality is suboptimal. (See figure 9-26.)

heading: Advantages and Disadvantages
text:
The advantages of using V-threads in anchor construction are that--
- They can be placed almost anywhere in an ice flow.
- They require very little to build many of them.
- Their gear placed in the ice is expendable.

heading: Advantages and Disadvantages
text:
The disadvantages of using V-threads in anchor construction are--
- Compared to other ice anchors, it takes a long time to construct, and two are necessary for a strong and secure anchor.
- They require a fair amount of experience to use appropriately.

heading: Placement
text: Place a long (19+ cm) ice screw into quality ice at a 60 degrees angle to the ice face, and then remove it, creating a borehole the length of the screw.

heading: Placement
