text: Use the length of this ice screw to measure how far away from the first hole (either vertically or horizontally) a second hole should be bored.

heading: Placement
text: Bore another 60 degrees angle hole in the opposite direction as the first so that it intersects the first at the back of the hole, creating a roughly triangular column of ice.

heading: Placement
text: Pass a piece of cordage or webbing through the tunnel created and tie it off with an appropriate knot to complete the anchor. Usually a V-thread tool is used to fish the cordage or webbing out of the hole.

heading: Placement
text: V-thread tools can be made from a wire coat hanger by cutting the length of wire, bending one end into a small hook and the other into a handle (See figure 9-27, page 228.)

heading: SECTION V - EARTH ANCHORS
text: Using improvised earth anchors becomes necessary when naturally existing anchors, such as trees, are unavailable. These anchors are created using materials that are readily available. The strength of these anchors depends on the material used, the depth, and the density of the earth in which they are placed. The art of constructing and placing good earth anchors requires a great deal of practice and experience. It is especially important to load earth anchors in a slow and steady manner. It is also important to ensure the direction of the pull is low and does not pull up on any component of the earth anchor.

heading: DEADMAN ANCHOR
text: A deadman is an effective means of building an anchor in earth or snow when there are no other natural anchors available. A deadman is constructed by digging a trench perpendicular to the direction of pull and placing a lengthy solid object with a sling or cordelette attached into it. A thinner slot is cut into the ground in the direction of pull and bisecting the trench to form a T-shape. The attached cordelette or webbing is then routed through this slot in the direction of pull.

heading: DEADMAN ANCHOR
text: The object is then buried. A rope or rope system can then be attached to it. The strength of a deadman anchor is determined by the density of soil it is placed into. The security of it is determined by the depth of the trench. Objects such as lengthy rocks, sticks, poles, and mountain axes can be buried.

heading: PICKET HOLDFAST
text: A picket holdfast can be constructed in the absence of suitable existing anchors. It requires three suitable pickets that can be made from sturdy sticks at least 3 inches in diameter and 3-feet long. The pickets can also be improvised from sturdy metal stakes or poles, if available. It is best to sharpen one end of each wooden stick or picket, so they are easily driven into the ground. (See figure 9-28.)

heading: PICKET HOLDFAST
text: Next, drive the pickets in line with the load a safe distance from the edge. Drive the pickets approximately 2-feet apart from each other at a 45 degrees angle leaning away from the edge. The pickets should be driven into the ground at least half their total length.

heading: PICKET HOLDFAST
text: Attach the rear picket at its base with a cord. Then attach the other end at the top of the middle picket. Using a clove hitch here will make it easy to adjust so there is equal tension on the pickets.

heading: PICKET HOLDFAST
text: Repeat this process from the middle picket to the front picket, then attach a cord to the front picket at its base and create an attachment point for the anchor.

heading: SECTION VI - SNOW ANCHORS
text: Snow anchor effectiveness is determined by the density of the snow into which they are built. Two or more snow anchor points can be equalized into a multipoint anchor if strength and security are questionable.

heading: PICKETS AND ICE AXES
text: Pickets and ice axes may be used as snow anchors. The picket should be driven into the snow at 10 degrees to 15 degrees off perpendicular from the lower surface. If the picket cannot be driven in all the way to the top hole, the carabiner should be placed in the hole closest to the snow surface to reduce leverage. The picket may also be tied off with a short loop of webbing or rope girth hitched low on the picket. (See figure 9-29, page 230.)

heading: PICKETS AND ICE AXES
text: When the snowpack is loose or it is suspected that a single picket cannot act as a sufficient anchor, then use multiple pickets if available. (See figure 9-30.) If the snow picket goes into the snow with ease, consider placing it in the deadman orientation to maximize strength and surface contact. If the snow picket requires pounding to place in vertically, the placement is most likely solid. The same general principles apply to constructing this multipoint anchor as any other. Ensure that each picket shares the load equally. They can be placed in succession similarly to the picket holdfast described in section V in this chapter or in a reverse V-shape shown in figure 9-31, page 232. If the snow is extremely loose, it may be better to build a deadman anchor that is dug in quite deeply where there is firmer snow.

heading: PICKETS AND ICE AXES
text: In softer snow conditions, both snow pickets and mountain axes can be used effectively in constructing a deadman anchor in the same fashion that they are constructed in earth (described in paragraphs 9-93 through 9-99, page 228). Longer objects, such as skis, can be used for increased strength. (See figure 9-31, page 232.) Snow density determines strength, and depth of the deadman determines security. Deadman anchors are the most reliable compared to all other techniques described. (See figure 9-31, page 232.) This is the most simple and reliable improvised snow anchor that can be used in a variety of snow conditions.

heading: BOLLARD ANCHOR
text: This is an artificial anchor shaped generally like a horseshoe. (See figure 9-32.) It is formed from either ice or snow and constructed by either cutting with an ice axe or stamping with the boots. When constructed of snow, the width should not be less than 10 feet. In ice, this width may be narrowed to 2 feet, depending on the strength of the ice. The length of the bollard should be at least twice the width. The trench around the horseshoe should be stamped as deeply as possible in the snow and should be cut not less than 6 inches into the ice after all rotten ice is removed. The backside of the anchor must always be undercut to prevent the rope from sliding off and over the anchor.

heading: BOLLARD ANCHOR
text: This type of anchor may be used for fixed ropes or rappels. It must be inspected frequently to ensure that the rope is not cutting through the snow or ice more than one-third of the length of the anchor. If it is, a new anchor must be constructed in a different location.

heading: BOLLARD ANCHOR
text: A horseshoe anchor constructed in snow is always precarious; its strength depends upon the prevailing texture of the snow. For dry or wind-packed snow, the reliability of the anchor should always be suspected. The backside of the bollard can be reinforced with ice axes, pickets, or other equipment for added strength. A snow-T trench is an example of a horseshoe anchor. (See figure 9-31.) This page intentionally left blank.

heading: Rope Systems for Climbing
text: There is an inherent risk to moving in the mountains. Much of the terrain is high consequence, where a misjudged foothold, a loose rock, a slip, trip, or fall can kill. However, troops fighting in the mountains are often exposed to greater risk by not being able to move through the terrain. Examples exist throughout history. Modern examples include the assaults on Riva Ridge and Monte la Difensa in Italy, both examples of failed conventional assaults, where defensive positions in the heights were taken by assaults through more difficult terrain. More recently, the Indians retaking hilltops in the Kargil Conflict display all the same principles. Successful offensive operations in the mountains require troops who can move in difficult terrain and under poor conditions. The alternative is costly, often unsuccessful attacks where the defenders hold significant tactical advantage. To manage the risk involved with movement through these types of terrain, Soldiers must be trained in a variety of rope systems for climbing.

heading: SECTION I - RISK MITIGATION
text: Fighting in the mountains requires exposure to mountain hazards. The mountain environment is defined by its hazards and difficulties. Often, the control measures used to address one hazard increase the exposure to another. Installing or using ropes to protect against a fall increases movement time and increases the exposure to compromise by enemy forces.

heading: MANAGING RISK
text: Managing risk in the mountains is a dynamic process, where the most appropriate measures for managing risk change with the terrain and situation.

heading: MANAGING RISK
text: Control measures target either the consequence or the likelihood of an incident. Protective equipment, such as a helmet to protect against rockfall, only reduces the consequence. The likelihood of being hit by rockfall is addressed by avoiding areas of loose rock and routing Soldiers so that they do not travel above one another.

heading: REDUCING THE LIKELIHOOD OF A FALL
text: The mountaineer has several technical tools for managing fall hazards. However, while the consequence of a fall can be reduced, it cannot be eliminated. Even a short fall while rock climbing can cause severe injury. To manage the risk, target factors that will reduce the likelihood of a fall.

heading: JUDGEMENT
text: The safety of a mountaineer comes from the ability to read the terrain. Judge the rock, snow, or ice, and see where it can be climbed and where it cannot. This includes identifying features and weaknesses that can be linked together. Judgement is developed through time spent climbing in a controlled environment and through experience and mentorship.

heading: TECHNIQUE
text: Soldiers must possess the physical ability to make the moves, use footholds, and maintain balance as each move is made. As with judgement, climbing technique is the product of extensive training.

heading: LOAD
text: Increased Soldier load rapidly increases the difficulty of climbing, even in easy terrain. Operations in the mountains are subject to the mindset that occupying high terrain requires more equipment for sustaining life than at lower elevations. However, to maintain maneuverability, the Soldier's load must be reduced. Soldiers conducting offensive operations, reconnaissance patrols, or any maneuver in high-consequence terrain need to travel light.

heading: FOOTWEAR
text: Proper footwear will enhance the military mountaineer's ability to move safely and efficiently through the rugged terrain found in the mountains. (See chapter 4 for footwear considerations.)

heading: ROPE
text: Ropes are used to reduce the consequence of a fall. Ropes can be fixed in place to manage or reduce the consequences of a fall (see chapter 11) or can be used to provide belays (see section III in this chapter).

heading: SECTION II - CONSIDERATIONS FOR MOVING UNROPED
text: Moving unroped is the fastest and most efficient method of moving through terrain. It requires little equipment and is quiet. Team members can move together, making communication quiet and easy. In instances where the greatest hazard is not falling, but rock or icefall, impending severe weather threat, enemy observation, or failing to meet an operational timeline, moving unroped may be the safest way to move. (See figure 10-1.) Moving unroped in terrain above 3rd-class should only be done after thorough risk analysis has been conducted and speed has been identified as a critical control measure for managing overall operational risk.

heading: SECTION II - CONSIDERATIONS FOR MOVING UNROPED
text: Moving unroped should only be done in 4th-class terrain or lower. It should never be considered in 5th-class terrain.

heading: SECTION II - CONSIDERATIONS FOR MOVING UNROPED
text:
Moving unroped exposes Soldiers to very high consequences in the event of a fall and could have catastrophic results including death. A rescue or body recovery in this terrain would likely become its own operation. Moving unroped should not be the default choice. The risk of a fall must be balanced against the other hazards. If the choice is made, there are measures to manage the risk.
- Target likelihood--maximize the use of every control measure to reduce the likelihood of a fall. Everyone in the team should have good movement skills. Loads should be reduced to the essentials. The team should be wearing appropriate footwear for climbing.
- Conservative route selection--the difficulty of the route must be within the comfort zone of the entire group. It is necessary to have the ability to adjust to a more conservative movement strategy, which requires harnesses to be worn and rope accessible.
- Route planning--use all available tools to build route plans. Often, climbing unroped goes badly not because a route is too difficult, but because a climber ends up off route in more difficult terrain.
- Pace--climb at a slow, deliberate pace. An easy pace allows full focus on the movement.
- Attention--keep attention focused on the climbing. Every foothold and handhold are critical. Stop often and assess the terrain ahead. Do not commit to features to which a Soldier cannot back off.
- Communication--a nontechnical risk management tool is coaching. Communicating a hazard focuses awareness on the hazard. During a movement, check in with group members and reassess their comfort with the risks at rest halts and decision points.
- Descent plan and tools--down climbing is more difficult than climbing up. Always have a multilayered descent plan and a rope and equipment to get down.
- For most units, there is limited terrain where climbing unroped may be appropriate. Average combat loads are heavy and issued combat boots are poorly suited for climbing. Limited steps of 3rd-class terrain, without exposure, are the upper limit for most units, and even then, should be assessed and managed carefully. Without individual mobility training and teams selected for their movement proficiency, there is a high risk of someone falling.

notices.text:
- Never climb unroped in 5th-class terrain.
- Climbing unroped in 4th-class terrain requires high skill, extensive experience, and superior confidence. Unroped climbing is only an option when the need to move quickly due to exposure to enemy or environmental hazards exceeds the risk of an unroped fall.
- Unroped climbing is a high-risk activity that requires a deliberate risk mitigation process and commander approval.

heading: SECTION III - BELAYED CLIMBING
text: A belay is a system of using a rope as a backup in steep terrain to arrest a Soldier's fall should one occur. This section will discuss an overview of various strategies for using ropes and belays.

heading: TYPES OF BELAYED CLIMBING
text: When terrain is too dangerous to move unroped, a team will transition to belayed climbing. Belayed climbing is usually done in a party of two, with each climber tied into one end of the rope. One team member is always anchored and providing a belay for the other.

heading: TOP ROPE CLIMBING
text: Military mountaineers are first introduced to top rope climbing. Top rope climbing is where the rope is run through an anchor at the top of a climb and kept relatively snug to avoid longer falls. It is a training tool used to teach climbing technique. (See section IV for more information on top rope climbing.)

heading: LEAD CLIMBING
text: As military mountaineers progress, they are later introduced to lead climbing. Lead climbing is climbing a route while attached to the end of a rope to place devices in rock, ice, or snow for fall protection with a belayer located below. When lead climbing, one climber leads climbs, placing protection and clipping the rope through it as they go. The belayer (sometimes referred to as the second) belays and is prepared to catch a fall. Lead climbers climb to another secure stance, build a solid anchor, and then belay second climbers as they climb to the new stance. Each length of climbing is called a pitch, which is a section of a climb that comprises the distance between two belay stations, which can be up to a standard rope length (60 meters) on easy ice and snow. In more broken rock, it may be just 10 to 15 meters, to minimize rope drag and aid communication.

heading: LEAD CLIMBING
text: Lead climbing provides security for both members of the party. Leaders accept more risk because they are climbing above their protection. Any fall will be well past the last piece of protection they placed before the rope begins to come tight, so it is still imperative that leaders have good movement skills. The second has a top rope unless the route traverses. The overall security of the team is good. The team always has a solid attachment, and the belays can be placed in sheltered stances, with solid anchors. (See section V for more information on lead climbing.)

heading: LEAD CLIMBING
text: Most climbers will protect themselves with belays in 5th-class terrain. In 3rd- or 4th-class terrain, in darkness or bad weather, belayed climbing is the most conservative strategy for protecting the team and provides the greatest margin of safety.

heading: AID CLIMBING
text: If the climbing is too difficult for the leader, aid climbing is a climbing technique in which standing on or pulling oneself up via devices attached to fixed or placed protection is used to make upward progress. (See figure 10-2.) Aid climbing is when climbers use anchors and protection to support their weight as they climb. In a recreational setting, climbers on big walls may do extensive aid climbing, with webbing ladders called etriers (or aiders) that can be clipped to pieces of rock protection and climbed, and daisy chains or webbing tethers, to hang from. Aid climbing can also be as simple as pulling on pieces of protection to get through difficult sections of what would otherwise be a free climb.

heading: AID CLIMBING
text: Aid climbing is slow. It may take hours to climb one pitch. Aid climbing requires significantly more rock protection. An aid rack may have three times the equipment used by leaders to protect themselves. Advanced military mountaineers should be familiar with aid climbing but expect to improvise the tools to make it happen.

heading: Simul-climbing (Running Belay)
text: Simul-climbing is a belay technique involving two Soldiers climbing simultaneously while attached to the ends of a rope which runs through the fall protection. It is a variation of belayed climbing, where leaders continue to climb rather than stopping to belay the second. Second climbers climb simultaneously, removing protection as they go. Leaders continue to climb while trying to keep a few pieces of protection between the two climbers at all times. If one falls, they may pull their teammate off their stance, but they will be caught eventually, counterbalanced through the protection with the other climber. Simul-climbing is faster than belayed climbing and useful for covering easy ground quickly. (See figure 10-3, page 240.) Simul-climbing provides more security than soloing. Climbers may find it necessary to shorten ropes between 20 and 30 meters to help with communication and prevent rope drag.

heading: Simul-climbing (Running Belay)
text: When both climbers are moving together, both share the consequence of a fall. Climbers should only use simul-climbing where a fall is unlikely and with partners of similar ability. If rockfall or icefall is a concern, it is not appropriate because the second is exposed to anything dislodged by the leader. Simul-climbing is best suited for easy alpine ridges where rocks fall off the feature. Simul-climbing is an appropriate technique for easy climbing, 3rd class through easy 5th class, with well-matched partners.

heading: Simul-climbing (Running Belay)
text: Simul-climbing is a technique used when the environmental or tactical situation presents a greater threat than the fall hazard. Simul-climbing sacrifices some level of fall protection to gain speed of movement.

heading: Short Roping
text: Short roping is a technique that may have some use in training military mountaineers. (See figure 10-4, page 242.) Short roping is used by more experienced mountaineers for protecting less experienced Soldiers in easy but exposed terrain. The climbing rope is shortened to just a few meters, and the leader holds the rope close to the other's harness and the two move together. Short roping cannot arrest a fall. It manages risk by putting the senior mountaineer close to the other climber, where the senior mountaineer can coach and model. If someone slips, leaders pull the rope connected to their harness to prevent the slip from becoming a fall. The only anchor is the senior mountaineer's stance. Short roping is appropriate only in terrain where leaders are confident climbing unroped and do not need their hands to climb.

notices.text:
- Only highly experienced advanced or master military mountaineers are qualified to simul-climb. They should only simul-climb in terrain that is well below their ability level, when speed is needed due to enemy contact, or when environmental hazards outweigh the risk of a long-roped fall.
- Simul-climbing is a high-risk activity that requires a deliberate risk mitigation process and commander approval.

heading: Short Roping
text: Short roping has limited application for military mountaineers. Short roping requires practice and the leader's full attention. In an operational environment, the military mountaineer's focus must be forward, looking for upcoming hazards or enemy contact. All Soldiers operating in the mountains, especially those working in small teams, should have the mobility skills to move in easy terrain.

notices.text:
- Only highly experienced master military mountaineers are qualified to short rope. They should only use short rope as part of a formal risk management process that identifies short roping as the appropriate risk mitigation method for the circumstances of the movement.
- Short roping is a high-risk activity that requires a deliberate risk mitigation process and commander approval.

heading: Short Pitching
text: Experienced leaders often combine short pitching with short roping as they manage less experienced Soldiers in 4th-class terrain. It is used when leaders need to use their hands to climb and cannot provide security with a short rope. Leaders place others in a safe position, and then scramble up the more technical section to a stance. From above, they can anchor or brace themselves to provide a belay as they climb. Often, because 4th-class terrain is more stepped, with plenty of ledges and stances, the leader can use simpler belay techniques and anchors than when rock climbing in 5th-class terrain and use a much shorter rope.

heading: Short Pitching
text: Most of the military mountaineer's time is spent avoiding the steepest and most difficult terrain. Operationally, they are more likely to use terrain where short pitching and simul-climbing would be most efficient. The techniques used in short pitching are faster than belayed climbing in longer pitches. A shorter rope helps with communication and fast transitions.

heading: Short Pitching
text: Short pitching requires training and practice in techniques to become safe and efficient. These techniques may not be as commonly practiced as other belay techniques, but they still have a place in alpine terrain, with good stances, and in positions where the second will not be stuck, hanging from the belay.

heading: Short Pitching
text: Hasty belays may be necessary during short pitching where anchoring options that are more substantial are not available. (See figure 10-5.) These involve leaders using their own body, positioned in a good stance, as the anchor or partial anchor. Ideally, the leader is also attached to a back-up anchor of some type, even if it does not meet the usual standards for a climbing anchor. This technique should only be used by experienced advanced military mountaineers when operationally necessary or when no other secure anchoring or belaying technique is possible.

heading: Shortening the Rope
text: When climbing in variable terrain, most pitches are short. This type of terrain is usually associated with 4th-class terrain. A full-length climbing rope is often too long and slows every transition with extra rope management. Teams may choose to carry shorter ropes if the terrain can be descended easily without long rappels, or they may choose to shorten their full-length climbing rope. Ropes are typically shortened for simul-climbing, short roping, and short pitching.

heading: Kiwi Coil
text: The Kiwi coil is the most common method of shortening a rope for climbing. (See figure 10-6, page 244.) After a climber ties into the end of the rope, the rope is coiled in a circular fashion, and then put over the shoulder of the climber. To secure this coil, a bight is run through the belay loop and around the coils. The bight is then tied off to the strand going to the other climber with an overhand on a bight, and a carabiner secures the bight to the harness. After the rope is shortened, team members can begin movement and adjust the length between them as necessary. Since the climber is tied into the end and the rope was shortened towards the other climber, it is easy to adjust the distance between climbers. This distance between climbers is usually dictated by the terrain. To lead a longer pitch, the coils can be removed from around the body. To stay closer to one another, the rope can be shortened.

heading: OPERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS
text: The various strategies and techniques described above for moving while roped will compromise speed and security. In a training environment, safety and conservative decision making must be the primary focus. As military mountaineers progress in their training, they may be exposed to alpine terrain above tree line. Weather and environmental hazards can pose a greater threat than falling. Each strategy for protecting the movement of the team is a compromise that should match the difficulty of terrain and the consequence of a fall. It should not expose the team to greater risk from another hazard. For combat operations, military mountaineers may need to compromise on protection and belays even further. Speed, stealth, and the ability to react are critical if enemy contact is expected.

heading: SECTION IV - TOP ROPE CLIMBING
text: A top rope is a belay in which both rope ends are on the ground and the rope runs up to the top of the cliff (or climb) and passes through a pre-established anchor point. This enables one Soldier to climb while the other Soldier belays. The belayer keeps the rope tight to prevent the climber from falling more than a short distance. This system also enables the belayer to lower the climber back down to the ground after completing the climb. (See figure 10-7 for an example of top rope climbing.)

heading: SECTION IV - TOP ROPE CLIMBING
text: A top rope is a training tool. It allows Soldiers to learn the fundamentals of tying in and belaying and to practice individual climbing techniques without the consequences of a long leader fall or unroped fall. It allows one instructor to coach and supervise both the climber and the belayer. It also facilitates learning the climbing technique because all participants can observe one another.

heading: EQUIPMENT CONSIDERATIONS
text: The UIAA develops safety and testing standards for mountaineering equipment. Equipment used for any mountaineering training should meet these standards as outlined in chapter 8 and appendix C.

heading: HELMETS
text: Helmets will protect a Soldier from rockfall and debris. They also offer some protection from impacts in a swinging fall. Climbing helmets are lightweight and certified to standards set by the UIAA.

heading: HELMETS
text: Most units do not have access to climbing helmets. The combat helmet, while not rated or designed for impact protection from rockfall or in climbing falls, is already issued to most Soldiers and provides adequate protection.

heading: HARNESS
text: There are many types of climbing harnesses. Harnesses must be made and tested to UIAA standards, and users must ensure that wear and use conforms to manufacturer recommendations. The high-angle mountaineering kit (HAMK) is issued to units where most Soldiers have no formal mountaineering training. The harness that was selected for the HAMK (see figure 10-8), is a harness with a single, reinforced tie-in portion. It is a simpler harness than most recreational climbing harnesses. It is one-size fits all and easy to put on and inspect. It has one gear loop on the left side, which can be used to rack equipment. When worn, it should be tight around the waist, with the leg loops snug enough to take some of the force while falling or sitting into the harness.

heading: HARNESS
text: If harnesses are not available, tubular webbing can be used to make field expedient harnesses, although this is not preferred. Soldiers must ensure their seats are tied correctly, and military mountaineers acting as safeties must carefully inspect several more points. This introduces several more points for human error.

heading: HARNESS
text: The rappel seat (Swiss seat) should not be used as a climbing harness as it is not designed for this purpose. In addition to being uncomfortable, it quickly loosens with repeated loading and unloading.

heading: ROPE
text: Dynamic ropes are used for all climbing training. Dynamic ropes stretch and reduce the peak impact force felt by a climber in a fall. Falls while top roping should not generate as much force as a lead fall; however, if slack develops in the belay, such as from a stuck rope or slow belayer, there is potential for generating significant force.

heading: ROPE
text: Top rope training puts significant wear and tear on ropes. New climbers fall often, and because a rope may be used on the same climb for the entire day, there may be significant wear in the same sections of rope. Heavy-duty climbing ropes in the 10-mm range are recommended for top rope training. The 10.2-mm dynamic rope included in the ACTKs provides good durability.

heading: PREPARATION
text: Advanced and master military mountaineers should plan and supervise mountaineering training that involves roped climbing and rappelling. They advise the commander on training requirements, priorities, and equipment needs, as well as plan, organize, and conduct training.

heading: SITE RECONNAISSANCE
text: Visit the training area before the scheduled training date and conduct a rehearsal or walkthrough with key personnel. This will help proof the plan, identify hazards, and develop controls. It is also an opportunity to save time with set up by identifying anchors and cleaning the area of loose rock or other hazards ahead of time.

heading: TIME MANAGEMENT
text: Ensure the training plan provides ample time to cover movement, set up, demonstrations, and training time. Extra time for contingencies is often needed.

heading: COMMUNICATION
text: All key personnel should have reliable communication with each other to communicate changes to hazards or conditions or to coordinate the response to emergencies.

heading: PARTICIPANT-TO-INSTRUCTOR RATIO
text: Ensure an adequate number of trained personnel are available to effectively supervise the given number of participants. In cases where there are only one or two trainers working with a much larger group, it may be necessary to limit the number of Soldiers being trained at one time.

heading: ORGANIZATION OR PLACEMENT OF KEY PERSONNEL
text: Critical points must be identified, and key personnel must be placed or distributed to facilitate supervision of the training site.

heading: EMERGENCY AND MEDICAL EVACUATION PLANS
text: Emergency and MEDEVAC plans must include special equipment and must consider the nature of the terrain in the training area. These plans must be rehearsed to ensure the viability of the plan.

heading: TRAINING SITE CONSIDERATION
text: The following are important considerations when managing a top rope training site.

heading: EASE OF ACCESS
text: The top of the cliff must be accessible to safely establish the anchors and hang ropes. Otherwise, a climb may have to be led prior to rigging. The bottom of the cliff must be easily accessible for the group and have adequate space to safely move around and store equipment.

heading: LENGTH OF CLIMBS
text: The length of the climbs must be less than half the length of the available ropes. Longer climbs can be used by joining two ropes together but is more complex and should be avoided, if possible, when working with beginners.

heading: DIFFICULTY
text: Ensure the difficulty of climbing is appropriate for the Soldiers. A common mistake is to use climbs that are too difficult for Soldiers to learn the basic movement skills and establish confidence. It is best to have a variety of difficulty levels available.

heading: DISTANCE BETWEEN CLIMBS
text: Climbs should be far enough apart so that climbers are not falling on or swinging into other climbers; however, they should not be so far apart that supervision and control are hindered. With climbs in close proximity, the instructor can often maintain adequate supervision of more than one climb.

heading: TRAINING SITE ANCHORS
text: Anchors at training sites are built stronger and more redundant than others used in climbing. A top roping anchor is used for long durations of time and is often out of the user's sight. It either is loaded frequently, with climbers falling or as each climber is lowered back down to the ground. Extra care should be taken to avoid sharp edges and add padding where necessary.

heading: LOCATION OF ANCHORS
text: Anchors should be located directly above the climb. If the anchor is not above the climb, during a fall climbers will pendulum, swinging across the face until they are in line with the anchor. This is more pronounced the closer to the top the climber gets.

heading: CONSTRUCTION OF ANCHORS
text: Anchors must be strong and redundant. Developed climbing areas often have bolted anchors at the top of climbs. A top roping anchor can be built with these with a cord as for other applications. (See figure 10-9.) Locking carabiners may be substituted for non-locking carabiners to ensure that the anchor is secure, even if it is checked only a few times during the training day. If anchors are unavailable at the cliff edge or are not in line with the top of the climb, static rope can be used to extend anchors out over the edge of the cliff and create a master point that is in line. Anchor ropes should be at least 9.5 mm in diameter.

heading: INSPECTIONS
text: Inspection is one of the most critical components of any technical mountain training event. Many accidents can be attributed to lack of inspection or instructor error during the inspection process. Level 2 or higher military mountaineers should inspect all rigging. The site should be organized in such a way that participants are unable to climb or proceed towards edges or dangerous terrain without first being inspected. Trainers must have a clear, logical sequence to follow when conducting inspections, whether it is anchor points, harnesses, tie-ins, rappel hook ups, or other. These should be conducted hands-on, not viewed from a distance.

heading: TOP ROPE BELAY
text: Top rope training develops two main skills. One is the individual mobility skill of the climber. The other is belaying. Belaying is the most important for safe training.

heading: POSITIONING THE BELAYER
text: The best position to catch a fall is directly below the anchor. The belayer will be pulled straight up and not off-balance. However, belayers should be offset enough so that the climber will not fall on them. They should also be positioned so that the rope will not interfere with climbers as they climb the route or entangle the climber in the event of a fall. The belayer should be protected from hazards, such as falling rock or ice. They should be placed into a protected feature under a roof or bulge or offset out of the path of any falling objects.

heading: ANCHORING THE BELAYER
text:
Anchoring belayers can keep them from being pulled off their stance during a fall. It is not always necessary, but the decision not to anchor should be deliberate. It is recommended that the belayer is anchored when--
- Belayers are inexperienced and may lose control of the belay if they are pulled up.
- The climber severely outweighs the belayer.
- It is necessary to keep them from being pulled into hazards and obstructions.

heading: BACK-UP BELAYER
text: Using back-up belayers can achieve several things. Back-up belayers improve the overall security of the climbers, since it decreases the likelihood that a Soldier could be dropped to the ground. Back-up belayers help to convey the importance of the belay when learning is first taking place and keeps additional Soldiers occupied and focused when unit trainers are working with large numbers of participants. To provide a back-up belay, one Soldier stands just behind the primary belayer, on the brake-hand side, and keeps additional control of the rope while making sure not to interfere with the primary belayer's movements.

heading: BELAYING WITH A TUBE-STYLE DEVICE
text: A belay device acts as a brake on the climbing rope by applying friction to it. The device, plus the belayer's braking hand, keeps tension on the rope in the event of a fall and helps protect the climber at the other end. It is an essential device for climbing safety.

heading: BELAYING WITH A TUBE-STYLE DEVICE
text:
Tube-style devices are the most used belay devices. (See figure 10-10.) They are lightweight, simple, and do not twist the rope. The brake position with a tube-style device is down, with the brake hand below the device, creating two sharp bends in the rope that provide the necessary friction. Attention must be paid to the belay technique, as there is very little friction outside of the brake position.
- Place a locking carabiner into the tie-in portion of the harness or into the belay loop. Thread a bight of the climbing rope through the tube slot of the device opposite the side of the keeper loop. Attach both the bight of rope and the keeper loop to the carabiner and lock the gate.
- To take in the rope, grasp the brake strand a few inches from the device and with the thumb pointed towards the device. Reach out and place the guide hand on the load strand with the thumb pointed up. Pull down with the guide hand and up with the brake hand simultaneously until the brake strand is approximately 1 foot away from the waist. Return the brake strand immediately to the brake position (below the device). Move the guide hand down to the brake strand just underneath the brake hand and slide the brake hand back to within a few inches from the device. Reach back up to the load strand with the guide hand and repeat.
- Never let go of the brake strand. The climber's life depends on it.
- To lower the climber, remove all slack from the system. Hold the brake strand in the brake position with both hands, and feed rope slowly back through the device until the climber is safely on the ground. (See figure 10-11, page 252.)

heading: BELAYING WITH A MUNTER HITCH
text:
The Munter hitch is rarely used for top roping, but for units that are not fielded mountaineering kits, it provides an adequate belay. It has the advantage of requiring no extra equipment and maintaining a sufficient level of friction to stop a fall with the brake strand in a variety of positions. Its main disadvantage is that it twists and kinks the rope.
- Place a locking carabiner into the tie-in portion of the harness. Tie a Munter hitch in the climbing rope and clip it into the carabiner for either a right-hand or a left-hand brake. Lock the carabiner.
- To take in rope, grasp the brake strand with the brake hand a few inches away from the Munter hitch and with the thumb pointed up. Pull down with the guide hand and up with the brake hand simultaneously until the brake hand is just below the guide hand. With the guide hand, grasp both ropes just above the brake hand, and then slide the brake hand back down to its original place, a few inches from the Munter hitch. Reach back up the rope with the guide hand, and repeat.
- During a fall, the bight of the Munter hitch will pass from the brake side of the carabiner to the guide-hand side. The hitch creates enough friction for the belayer to easily hold the climber's body weight. The brake position for the Munter hitch is with the brake strand and the load strand parallel.
- Never let go of the brake strand.
- To lower the climber back down, place both hands on the brake strand and feed the rope slowly back through the Munter hitch until the climber is safely on the ground. (See figure 10-12.) Note. Do not put the brake hand too close to the Munter hitch. Fingers caught in the Munter hitch could cause a mountaineer to lose control of the brake, dropping the climber.

heading: CLIMBING COMMANDS
text: Using standardized verbal climbing commands is a necessary safety protocol to ensure both members are ready before any actions are taken. Commands while top roping also teach proper communication before introducing lead climbing, where communication may occur over a much longer distance. Clear communication minimizes the chance of human error and helps to ensure safe operation of the belay. All commands must be preceded by the other Soldier's first or last name, like a radio transmission, to gain the other Soldier's attention. This is especially important at training sites where there are multiple top rope climbs set up nearby to avoid confusion.

heading: CLIMBING COMMANDS
text:
Units and schoolhouses should develop their own SOPs to determine appropriate commands. Consider the following when choosing these terms:
- Avoid using terms that sound alike or may be confused with another word (for example, GO, SLOW, and WHOAH may sound like NO and vice versa).
- Avoid using words that are not definitive (for example, GOOD is a vague term that does not define any specific action).

heading: CLIMBING COMMANDS
text: Table 10-1, page 254 lists common terms that are widely used. To manage risk and avoid confusion, consider these commands as the bare minimum associated for top rope climbing. Units or schoolhouses may add additional commands if they feel they are necessary to help further mitigate risk.

heading: Belayer Climber Command Description
text: THAT'S ME This command is said when the climber feels tension from the rope as the belayer takes all the slack out of the system. This command is intended to let belayers know that they have tension to the climber and the rope is not caught somewhere. BELAY ON This command is given when all slack between the climber and belayer has been taken out of the rope, and the belayer has control of the break strand with at least one hand. SLACK The climber may use this command to release some tension in the rope. This may be necessary in situations where the rope may be caught on a flake of rock and the climber can safely adjust it. TAKE This command is used to tell the belayer to take in more rope. It is also used when there is unwanted slack in the system, climbers have reached the top of the climb and are preparing to be lowered down, or if they feel they may fall and would like additional tension. ROCK or ICE ROCK or ICE This command is used to describe any falling object. Anyone can use this command, when necessary. I'VE GOT YOU The command is given when the climber reaches the top or needs to be lowered for any reason. The belayer will say TAKE, place two hands on the brake strand, and then give the command. ON YOU Once climbers sit back into their harnesses and are ready to be lowered, they will give the belayer this command. The belayer should never begin to lower the climber until this command is given. BELAY OFF Once climbers are safely on the ground and have good footing, they will give this command to let the belayer know they can take them off belay.

heading: SECTION V - LEAD CLIMBING
text: Lead climbing is where a roped team has one climber take the lead while the other climber follows. While ascending the route, the lead climber periodically connects the rope to protection for safety in the event of a fall. This protection can consist of permanent bolts to which the climber clips quick draws, or removable protection, such as nuts and cams. One of the climbers below the lead climber acts as a belayer. The belayer gives out rope while the lead climber ascends and stops the rope when the lead climber falls or wants to rest.

heading: SECTION V - LEAD CLIMBING
text: In military mountaineering, the primary mission of a roped climbing team is to fix a route with some type of rope installation to assist movement of less trained personnel in the unit. This duty falls upon the most experienced climbers in the unit, usually working in two- or three-man groups or teams. Even if the climbing is for another purpose, roped climbing should be performed whenever the terrain becomes difficult and exposed.

heading: SECTION V - LEAD CLIMBING
text: Units or schoolhouses should develop their own SOPs for lead climbing commands and establish alternative means of tactically communicating actions while lead climbing. Examples of climbing commands are described in table 10-1 in the top rope section.

heading: EQUIPMENT CONSIDERATIONS
text: The ACTK contains the equipment necessary for lead climbing operations and includes mountaineering harnesses, chocks, and cams in a wide variety of sizes, locking and nonlocking carabiners, dynamic climbing rope, webbing and accessory cord, ascenders, and belay devices. The specific use of this equipment is described in chapters 8 and 9.

heading: EQUIPMENT CONSIDERATIONS
text: The snow and ice mobility kit (SIMK) is designed to outfit a platoon with safety and mobility equipment for operations in snow- and ice-covered mountainous terrain. This kit will be required if moving through this type of terrain and the specific use of this equipment is described in chapters 6 and 15.

heading: HELMETS
text: As outlined in chapter 6, lighter weight or climbing-specific helmets offer several advantages and are recommended for lead climbers.

heading: HARNESS
text:
The ACTK contains three basic mountaineering harnesses. These harnesses are a bare minimum, and lead climbing in any type of field expedient harness is not recommended. Lead climbing requires much more gear than general mountaineering tasks, so harnesses with additional features can increase efficiency and functionality. (See figure 10-13.) Typical features of harnesses well-suited for lead climbing are--
- Adjustable leg loops with buckles.
- Four or more gear loops designed to hold extra gear.
- Thick and durable padding increases comfort when spending a long time in the harness.
- Extra lumbar padding helps to stabilize the lower back and waist.

heading: ROPE
text: Lead climbing can be protected by different rope systems. The UIAA develops safety and testing standards for mountaineering equipment. It sets standards for three different types of climbing rope: single ropes, half ropes, and twin ropes.

heading: Single Ropes
text: Single ropes are the most common type of climbing rope. Diameters can range from 8.9 to 11.1 mm.

heading: Half Ropes
text: Half ropes are a set of two ropes that are clipped separately into points of protection. This reduces friction and rope drag during long wandering routes and serves as a second rope for longer rappels. The disadvantage to half ropes is the increased complexity required for both the climber and belayer to manage these ropes separately. The diameters for half ropes can range from 8 to 9 mm. Half ropes are used for a party of two in wandering alpine terrain, on rock, or on ice.

heading: Twin Ropes
text: Twin ropes are also a set of two ropes, but both strands are clipped into each point of protection and managed as one rope. Diameters for twin ropes range from 7 to 8 mm. Twin ropes are primarily used on routes needing two ropes for rappels. Note. Some ropes may hold more than one, or all, of these certifications, which can add to confusion during rope selection. Weight, versatility, and durability should be the primary considerations. In most cases, lightweight, single ropes offer the best balance of these factors.

heading: PROTECTION
text: The amount of protection the lead climber brings depends upon the character of the climber and the skill of the lead climber. In easy alpine terrain, the rack may be just a few pieces of rock gear to protect exposed steps and make simple anchors. Protecting sustained, multipitch rock may require a rack of doubles, two sets of the entire size range of cams.

heading: PROTECTION
text: The presence of pre-established anchors or bolts found in some commonly used training areas are some of the biggest variables in protection. Climbing a route that has bolts placed for protection, known as sport climbing, provides security and allows the climber to carry less equipment. Sport climbing is useful for training purposes only. Sport climbing provides a safe way to introduce climbers to lead climbing and allows more experienced climbers to work on climbing terrain that is more difficult without having to place traditional protection.

heading: PROTECTION
text: In winter and alpine environments, ice screws must be incorporated.

heading: ROCK SHOES
text: Rock shoes are specialized pieces of equipment that are only necessary when moving through difficult technical terrain. The practical application of this equipment is limited operationally but can greatly enhance climbing training and should be utilized when building Soldiers' skillset in rock climbing. These specialized shoes provide more friction, support, and precise footwork, allowing the Soldier to move more effectively through the terrain. (See figure 10-14.) It is a common misconception that climbing is about upper-body strength. Climbing requires a lot of upper-body strength, but the legs typically propel the climber up the wall. The reason Soldiers fall while learning how to rock climb is typically some failure of their foot placement. While lead climbing, especially when learning, rock shoes are invaluable in managing risk by increasing the security of foot placements and reducing the likelihood of a fall.

heading: BELAYING A LEAD CLIMBER
text: Belayers must first identify a place to stand when belaying that is free from rockfall or other objective hazards they can trip over or be pushed into. Belayers must also achieve an adequate stance or brace their body positions to help absorb the energy from a lead fall. They should consider attaching themselves to an anchor near the ground to help prevent being pulled off their stance and losing control of the belay. (See figure 10-15.) The climbing rope should then be back stacked, and both climber and belayer will tie into the appropriate ends of the rope.

heading: BELAYING A LEAD CLIMBER
text: The best position to catch a fall is directly below the first piece of protection. Belayers will be pulled straight up and not lose their balance. However, they should be offset enough so that the climber will not fall directly on them. The belayer should be positioned so that the rope does not interfere with the climber as they climb the route, and they do not become entangled in it in the event of a fall.

heading: BELAYING A LEAD CLIMBER
text: As the leader climbs, the rope is fed out ensuring that climbers have full freedom to move, and they are not hindered by the rope. Ensure that there is always a slight sag in the rope, but no more. Anticipate the climber's movements and be prepared to feed rope out quickly when protection is being clipped. If belayers cannot see the climber, they must feel the climber through the rope. Unless the climber says otherwise, the belayer can slowly give slack on the rope as the climber proceeds on the route. The belayer should keep just enough slack in the rope so the climber does not have to pull it through the belay. If climbers want a tighter rope, they can call for it. If belayers notice too much slack developing in the rope, they should take in the excess rope quickly. It is the belayers' responsibility to manage the rope, whether by sight or touch, until the climber tells them otherwise.

heading: BELAYING A LEAD CLIMBER
text: To catch a fall, immediately drop the guide hand down next to the brake hand and lock the rope off in the brake position. Bend the knees slightly to help absorb the impact.

heading: LEAD CLIMBER
text: Lead climbers have a lot to consider while climbing. A lead climber is the first climber to negotiate a route, for whom a top belay is not possible, and who assumes the most risk of injury in a fall. They should spend sufficient time reviewing the various techniques available for protecting themselves and their followers before selecting one, as well as preparing their equipment for efficient use before beginning a climb.

heading: RACKING
text: The protection the lead climber brings with them is referred to as the rack. The term racking is simply the process a climber goes through to prepare the equipment for climbing. Racking should be organized so the right gear can be found and accessed quickly. Equipment should be spread out between a gear sling over the shoulder and the gear loops on the harness. The specific location and order of placement of the protection falls to personal preference, but there should be a logical sequence to the process.

heading: CLIMBING
text: The procedures for conducting a lead climb with a group of two are relatively simple. The most experienced individual is the lead climber or leader. Leaders are responsible for selecting the route. They must ensure that the route is well within their climbing ability and that of the second climber ("second"). The lead climber carries most of the climbing equipment to place protection along the route and set up the next belay. The leader must also ensure that the second has the necessary equipment, such as a chock pick, to remove any protection that the leader may place.

heading: CLIMBING
text: The leader is responsible for emplacing protection frequently enough and in such a manner that if either the leader or the second should fall, their fall is neither long enough nor hard enough to result in injury. The leader must also ensure that the rope is routed so that it can run freely through the protection placements, thus minimizing friction, or rope drag.

heading: CLIMBING
text: The other member of the climbing team, the second, is responsible for belaying the leader, removing the belay anchor, and retrieving the protection placed by the leader between belay positions (also known as cleaning the pitch).

heading: CLIMBING
text: The leader continues the route until either a designated belay location is reached, or the near end of the rope is reached. At this position, the leader sets an anchor, connects to the anchor, and says OFF BELAY. The belayer remains attached to the anchor until the command BELAY ON is given.

heading: CLIMBING
text: Leading a difficult pitch is the most hazardous task in roped climbing. Lead climbers may be exposed to potentially long, hard falls. They must exercise keen judgment in selecting routes, placing protection, and routing climbing rope through the protection. Every effort should be made to keep the climbing line as direct as possible to the next belay to allow the rope to run smoothly through the protection with minimal friction. Protection should be placed whenever the leader feels it necessary to prevent hazardous situations and before moving past a difficult section.

heading: PLACING PROTECTION
text: Generally, protection is placed from one stable position to the next. If the climbing is difficult, protection should be placed more frequently. If the climbing becomes easier, protection can be placed farther apart, saving hardware for difficult sections. On some routes, an extended diagonal or horizontal movement, known as a traverse, is required. As leaders begin this type of move, they must consider the second's safety as well as their own. The potential fall of the second will result in a pendulum swing if protection is not adequate to prevent this. The danger comes from any objects in the swinging path of the second.

heading: REDUCING ROPE DRAG; USING RUNNERS
text: No matter how direct the route, the climber often encounters problems with rope drag through the protection positions. Rope drag is caused when there are exaggerated changes in direction of the rope between carabiners attached to protection that creates excessive friction. Minimal rope drag is an inconvenience; severe rope drag may pull the climber off balance, inducing a fall. When belaying the second, rope drag can be mistaken for the climber, causing the belayer to not take in the necessary slack. This can potentially result in a serious fall. To prevent this, the placements should be extended by using runners, when necessary, so the rope creates a smooth, almost straight line as it passes through the carabiners. (See figure 10-16.) Do this by attaching an appropriate-length runner to the protection to extend the rope connection in the necessary direction. The runner is attached to the protection while the rope is clipped into a carabiner at the opposite end of the runner. Extending placements with runners allows the climber to vary the route slightly while the rope continues to run in a relatively straight line.

heading: REDUCING ROPE DRAG; USING RUNNERS
text: Not only is rope drag a hindrance, but it can also cause undue movement of protection as the rope tightens between any out of line placements. Rope drag through chock placements can be dangerous. As the climber moves above the placements, an outward or upward pull from rope drag may cause correctly set chocks to pop out, even when used correctly. Passive protections, like chocks, are especially prone to wiggling loose as the rope pulls on the cable attachment. All wired chocks used for leader protection should be extended to reduce the chance of the rope pulling them out. (See figure 10-17, page 262.)

heading: CLIPPING TECHNIQUE
text: Clip the climbing rope into a point of protection by reaching down and grabbing the rope between the thumb and index finger. Use the middle finger to stabilize the carabiner at the protection or runner, and use the thumb and index finger to clip the rope in. Alternately, the rope can be held between the middle and index finger and clipped in as shown in figure 10-18. Ensure the gate of the carabiner faces out (not towards the rock), and the rope is clipped in the direction of travel to prevent the rope from potentially becoming unclipped in a fall. Recreational climbers typically do all their clipping while hanging onto rock holds as much as they can; however, as a Soldier not worried about preserving the free climbing style, simply grab the point of protection and hang onto it while clipping the rope and runner into it. This may provide better temporary hold or provide a much-needed rest.

heading: BELAYING A SECOND CLIMBER
text: Typically, one climber takes the lead while belayed from below, moves up the route to the next ledge or desired spot, and then sets up a new anchor and belay. This distance between these belays is known as a pitch. The length of a pitch is limited to the length of available rope and convenient, suitable to belay positions.

heading: BELAYING A SECOND CLIMBER
text: In most cases, the leader attaches to the anchor with either separate sling material or by using the climbing rope with a clove hitch and locking carabiner. Using a clove hitch in the climbing rope itself has the distinct advantage of allowing more room and material to fine tune the distance between the anchor and the cliff edge to enable better communication with the climber below. The leader then uses the command of OFF BELAY. Once the belayer has removed the belay, enabling the rope to run freely, the belayer would use the command BELAY OFF. The leader then pulls in all the remaining rope until it is tight with the second. Once an appropriate belay is set up, the leader uses the command BELAY ON letting the second know that it is safe to climb.

heading: BELAYING A SECOND CLIMBER
text: Many techniques can be used to belay the second, depending upon the terrain, difficulty of the climbing, availability of anchors, and likelihood or consequences of a fall. The second is essentially on a top rope, with a snug rope being maintained throughout the climb.

heading: INDIRECT BELAYS
text: An indirect belay occurs when a leader is anchored and belays the second off the harness with either a Munter hitch or tube-style belay device. While this does work, it has several drawbacks. It can oftentimes be quite awkward in the event of a fall that pulls the belayer down towards the ground or if there is a climber who is struggling and hanging excessively on the rope. The belayer is forced to hold the rope in the brake position with much or all the climber's weight pulling in a downward direction on the harness. Additionally, should belayers need to tie off the climber and escape the belay for any reason, several steps would be required to free themselves from the system. For these reasons, this technique is only preferred when using an anchor that is suspected to be weak. With a weak or bad anchor, belayers' bodies, in this case, act as the primary anchor with the other simply backing them up. Once again, a good, braced position is necessary. The preferred technique otherwise is to always use direct belays.

heading: DIRECT BELAYS
text: Belaying directly off the anchor allows any forces to be transmitted solely to the anchor so that the belayer is not pulled in any direction and cannot become trapped in the system should problems arise. Direct belays are also generally more comfortable and give the belayer freedom to move while maintaining control of the brake rope. This can be done either using a Munter hitch or using a plaquette-style belay device in guide mode. In either case, the first step is for the climber to attach to the anchor and shout, OFF BELAY. Pull the remainder of the rope up until the second shouts, THAT'S ME. Then use one of the following belay methods: the Munter hitch or the autolocking tubular device in guide mode.

heading: Belaying with the Munter Hitch
text: Using a Munter hitch as a belay is quick, easy to tie, and can be used to easily lower the second back down, if necessary. It is an alternative in case a Soldier does not have a belay device. Attach a locking carabiner to the anchor master point, pull the slack out of the rope to the climber below, and tie a Munter hitch with the climbing rope. (See figure 10-19.)

heading: Belaying with the Munter Hitch
text: Place the guide hand on the load strand and the brake hand on the brake strand a few inches away from the Munter hitch, ensuring both thumbs are pointing towards the anchor. To take in rope, hold firmly and slide both hands towards each other until they meet. With the guide hand, grab both strands of rope just beneath the brake hand, then slide the brake hand back up to within a few inches of the Munter hitch. Slide the guide hand back down and repeat. Care should be taken to ensure that the brake hand does not get so close to the Munter hitch that a thumb or finger could be sucked in and pinched during a fall.

heading: Autolocking Tubular-Style Device
text: The tube-style belay or rappel devices issued in the Army mountain kits can be used in guide or autolocking mode. To use this device in autolocking mode, a locking carabiner is clipped through the metal loop and attached to an anchor. A bight of rope is then fed into the device, with the climber's strand on top, and a second "braking" locking carabiner is clipped through the device's carry wire and the bight of rope. One locking carabiner is used to attach the device itself to the anchor, and a second is used as a braking carabiner after the rope is fed through the device. The shape and orientation of the device allows rope to pass smoothly through it in one direction, but lock off in the opposite direction, being pinched around the stock of the braking carabiner. (See figure 10-20, page 266.)

heading: Autolocking Tubular-Style Device
text: To use the device, attach it to the anchor with a locking carabiner in the appropriate spot. Then feed a bight of rope into the device, paying close attention to the diagram on its side. Clip an additional locking carabiner around both the rope and the keeper, ensuring again that the brake strand is between the Soldier's body and the load rope. Pull down on the load rope to make sure it is rigged correctly and locks off in the correct direction before shouting ON BELAY. To take in rope with a device in guide mode, use the same technique described above for the Munter hitch.

heading: Autolocking Tubular-Style Device
text: One advantage of these devices over the Munter hitch is that they do not require holding power on the part of the belayer because they lock off automatically, oftentimes allowing the belayer to multitask at the anchor. They can also be used when using half or twin ropes or when belaying two seconds simultaneously on two separate ropes. They are particularly useful in these situations or if the climbing is difficult and the second is expected to be hanging a lot. A disadvantage is that since it only allows rope to pass through in one direction, giving "slack" or lowering a climber back down requires additional training. Note. Never use a device in standard tube-style mode to belay directly off the anchor.

heading: ROPE MANAGEMENT WHILE BELAYING
text: Pay careful attention to ensure that rope taken in when belaying the second is stacked or coiled neatly to make the belay transition easy and to ensure that it does not fall down the cliff and become tangled or caught.

heading: On Ledges
text: On small or large ledges, it is usually possible to stack the rope in a neat pile as it is pulled through the belay. This allows for an easy transition and for smooth rope feeding.

heading: At Hanging Stances
text: At hanging belay stances, it may be necessary to stack the rope back and forth over the tie-in strand as the Soldier pulls rope through the belay. If this is done, the rope should be looped back and forth in large bights (not so long as to becoming caught on things below). If the second becomes the new leader for the next pitch, these bights should start big and gradually become smaller. This allows the rope to feed out without becoming tangled during the next lead. If the original leader leads the next pitch, the rope may have to be restacked over the second's tie-in strand when they reach the anchor. Another option is to stack the rope back and forth over a leg or foot. However, feet tend to get shifty when belaying during a long lead, which can lead to dropping the rope where it could possibly become stuck or jammed below.

heading: ROPE TUG COMMANDS
text: Sometimes yelling cannot be heard when the climber and belayer are far apart. This is especially true in windy conditions or if the climber is around a corner, above an overhang, or at the back of a ledge. It may be necessary to use a series of tugs on the rope in place of the standard voice commands. To avoid any possible confusion with interpreting multiple rope tug commands, use only one. Rope tug commands may also have a tactical application where noise discipline is particularly important. Units or climbing teams should develop their own SOPs for rope tug commands. These commands should always be discussed and confirmed prior to a climb.

heading: TRAINING CONSIDERATIONS FOR LEAD CLIMBING
text: Due to the high consequences involved, advanced and master military mountaineers must plan and supervise mountaineering training that involves lead climbing. They advise the commander on training requirements, priorities, and equipment needs, as well as plan, organize, and conduct training. Lead climbing training is particularly demanding of trainers and supervisors. For inexperienced climbers, a 2:1 ratio is often required. Supervision of climbing training must be thorough and deliberate. A large part of this supervision is inspecting every component of the rope system. The ability to balance the rigid process of supervision and inspection with the soft skills of mentorship and coaching can help maximize the safety and value of the training.

heading: TRAINING CONSIDERATIONS FOR LEAD CLIMBING
text: Assess the mental readiness of the climber. The fear of heights is real and is not something that can be ignored. A Soldier becoming panicked while lead climbing can create hazardous situations and may dissuade the Soldier from continuing further climbing training.

heading: TRAINING CONSIDERATIONS FOR LEAD CLIMBING
text: Consider climber skill when selecting routes for training. Climbs should be challenging but achievable with a couple of tries. Routes for new climbers should not exceed intermediate difficulty (see appendix A for more on climbing classification). A common mistake is to place Soldiers on climbs that are too difficult, steep, or strenuous, where they cannot first focus on the processes. Established bolted climbs are often an excellent place to begin lead climbing training. Traditionally protected routes can be attempted after proficiency has been achieved with these. For initial training, the length of climbs is ideally less than half the length of the available ropes to allow quick transitions to rappel and maximize repetitions. These shorter lengths also make it easier for the supervising trainer to ascend next to the climber when necessary.

heading: TRAINING CONSIDERATIONS FOR LEAD CLIMBING
text: Soldiers should already be proficient at placing protection, clipping ropes into protection, belaying leaders, belaying follow-on climbers, and constructing multipoint anchors. These skills can often be practiced on the ground in advance.

heading: TRAINING CONSIDERATIONS FOR LEAD CLIMBING
text: Mock lead training is a useful tool to prepare Soldiers for lead climbing. Mock leading occurs when a Soldier climbs a route on top rope while also leading up with another rope. This allows the Soldier to focus on placing protection, clipping, and managing the rope on lead with the security of having a top rope as backup in case of a fall.

heading: SECTION VI - ALPINE BELAY TECHNIQUES
text: In broken alpine terrain, with secure stances, and no chance of second climbers falling and hanging from a belay, hasty techniques may provide adequate protection for the team. Safety should never be compromised for the sake of speed. Use of standard belay techniques should be used if there is any question as to security.

heading: BODY BELAYS
text: Body belays can sometimes be used on short sections of less steep terrain where a fall is unlikely and there is a good, braced belay stance of which to take advantage. To create a body belay, simply run the rope around the body at the waist to create friction, with the chest facing the direction of pull. The load rope is at one hip and the brake strand is in the opposite side hand. To take in rope, pull in on the load rope with the guide hand and out with the brake hand. Grab both ropes above the brake hand with the guide hand and slide the brake hand back towards the body. To brake, pull the brake hand up and across the chest. The body belay can be used in either the sitting or standing position; however, the sitting position offers a lower center of gravity and is preferred. It can also be used with an anchor or without. The advantage of the body belay is its speed and simplicity for belaying short sections where a climber is moving quickly. However, there are disadvantages as well. Because the force of a fall is dissipated as friction against belayers' bodies, serious rope burns can occur to the body and hands, possibly causing them to lose control of the belay. It also generates less braking force and causes more slippage than other techniques, causing the climber to fall farther. For this reason, it is only used on low-angle easy terrain. The belayer must have a good, braced position and must keep the rope tight. (See figure 10-21.)

heading: SHOULDER BELAY
text: A shoulder belay is a way to add a level of friction to the rope as the belayer pulls it tight with a climber below. The shoulder belay shares many of the advantages and disadvantages listed above for the body belay. The level of friction created with this method is relatively low and should only be used on short steps where there is no risk of the climber hanging from the belay in a fall. A classic example of terrain where the shoulder belay is appropriate is a short, steep step where the belayer can stand directly above the climber below. The rope is routed under the arm, over the opposite shoulder, and down to the opposite hand and is kept tight with the climber below. The belayer's body creates friction on the rope and acts as the anchor at the same time. A shoulder belay is fast to create, but it is only suitable on rare occasions. (See figure 10-22, page 270.)

heading: SHOULDER BELAY
text: A terrain belay can be used when there is a feature that the rope can go around and create enough friction to arrest a fall or lower a load. The natural feature must be solid and not have sharp edges. Terrain belays are an effective means of belaying a climbing partner, but they require good judgement. When using a boulder or horn of rock, the belayer must ensure the rope will not slide off the rock in the event of a fall and that the rock is wedged securely. Trees are another good example of a natural object that can be used as a terrain belay. (See chapter 9 for more information on tree selection.) (See figure 10-23.)

heading: SECTION VII - CLIMBING IN A TEAM OF THREE
text: Level 2 mountaineers are trained to work as a team of two. There are numerous examples of when it may be beneficial to work and move as a team of three. Moving as a team of three has added complexity and much more challenging rope management at each belay. To progress into managing two ropes, a climber must first become proficient in managing one.

heading: SECTION VII - CLIMBING IN A TEAM OF THREE
text: It is good for military mountaineers to have options for roped travel through terrain with changing hazards. The mountaineer must constantly assess terrain and hazards and fluidly adapt the technique to mitigate those hazards as best as possible. Time is always against mountaineers, and efficient transitions from one roped movement style to the next are important. A mountaineer should not default to using one style of movement for all types of terrain and should know how to properly apply different roped movement techniques to different terrain.

heading: CATERPILLAR
text: Caterpillar technique is usually the first technique learned for managing a party of three. The lead climber and second climber tie into the ends of one rope. The second also ties into another rope with the third climber. The leader leads as usual, clipping protection, and then builds an anchor and belays the second. Rather than cleaning the protection, the second climbers remove their rope and clip the second rope into the protection. Once the second climber is anchored, the leader then belays the third climber.

heading: CATERPILLAR
text: Climbing while using the caterpillar technique is often slower than other techniques. It can take the party twice as long to cover a pitch in some situations but is the simplest method of managing a party of three. It builds on the skills already used for two-party climbing, with only slightly more complex rope and station management. This technique also reduces the workload on the following climbers.

heading: END ROPING
text: In easy terrain, two climbers can tie into the end of the same rope. One ties into the end of the rope, the second attaches with a cow's tail and a bight of rope long enough that they can move up and down independent of the climber below. (See figure 10-24, page 272.) It is tied with an overhand on a bight loop with a 30-cm bight. This bight should be far enough from the other climber that the two do not interfere with each other as they climb, usually about 4 meters. The second attaches to the cow's tail with a clove hitch around two opposite and opposed locking carabiners. This is almost as fast as climbing in a party of two. Rope management is simple for the leader and no different from climbing in a party of two. The two followers can be clove hitched into the anchor on the rope between them, securing them both. The followers can also coach and assist each other with the climbing.

heading: END ROPING
text: This is only appropriate in easy terrain, where there is little risk of a fall. It is used primarily in 4th-class terrain. Note. When attaching to a rope to climb, the preferred method is to be tied directly into the rope. Locking carabiners can unlock and open if they are not being monitored, and while climbing, they may end up in a position where they can be cross loaded. When clipping into a rope to climb, it should be with two lockers, opposite and opposed, and with a knot that secures around the carabiners to keep them oriented correctly.

heading: PARALLEL
text: For parallel technique, the lead climber ties into both ropes and the two followers tie into the other ends. The leader leads on one strand, clipping it into the protection. The second rope can either be clipped into the protection as well, clipped into just specific pieces as directional, or routed on a separate line, depending on the terrain and the hazards. (See figure 10-25.) At the anchor, the leader sets up to belay the two followers.

heading: PARALLEL
text: Belay devices with a guide mode (plaquette or autolocking) can be used to belay two climbers, on two ropes, simultaneously. For rock climbing, with little rockfall hazard, both followers often climb together, offset enough so that they do not fall onto each other. Where loose rock is a concern or when ice climbing, this must be managed differently, often one climber climbing at a time, either for the whole pitch, or bounding from sheltered stance to sheltered stance. (See figure 10-26.)

heading: PARALLEL
text: Rope management is more difficult with two ropes and two climbers moving simultaneously. Organization at the belays requires additional thought, ensuring that the followers are anchored in a manner that the ropes are not twisted, and both strands feed up from them.

heading: PARALLEL
text: The parallel technique is used frequently. In steep terrain, it is often the fastest way to move as a party of three. However, to avoid complications, it requires mastery of the basics and practice.

heading: FIXED STRANDS
text: It is also possible for leaders to fix the strand of rope they led onto the anchor at the top. This frees up leaders from any belaying responsibilities and allows them the ability to provide security, if necessary. This concept of the leader fixing strands of rope after leading a pitch provides many options for moving Soldiers through terrain.
