These sorts of systems are used to control the speed of descent for personnel or equipment using rope. They are an integral part of both highand low-angle rescue. (See chapter 15.) Lowering a victim or a load is always preferred over hauling if the terrain and situation allows. No two situations are identical. Each new situation will dictate which lowering techniques and systems are appropriate. Understanding basic lowering concepts is key to achieving a safe and efficient solution to the problem.

heading: LOWERING CONCEPTS
text: There are many devices and techniques available depending on the weight of the load. The bottom line for any lowering system is that enough friction must be created to safely control the descent of the load. Different terrain demands different methods of creating friction. When the terrain is steep and broken, selecting a device or technique that provides varying levels of friction is preferred.

heading: LOWERING CONCEPTS
text: All lowering systems should be closed by securing the free end of the rope (the end not attached to the load). This prevents lowering the load off the end of the rope if the distance of the lower versus the length of rope is misjudged.

heading: LOWERING CONCEPTS
text: When lowering Soldiers, a hands-free backup for the system should be used. (See figure 11-15, page 300.) This can be achieved in multiple ways. Hands-free backups provide additional measures of protection against human error and allow the Soldier or team operating the lowering system flexibility while controlling the brake strand.

heading: TECHNIQUES AND DEVICES FOR CREATING FRICTION
text: There are numerous ways to create friction for lowering. The least technical solution to safely lower the load is the goal. Three basic methods are the terrain feature, Munter hitch, and redirected belay device.

heading: TERRAIN FEATURE
text: This method involves simply wrapping the rope attached to the load around a natural object, such as a tree or boulder. (See figure 12-13, page 316.) The number of wraps depends on the amount of friction desired. This technique is used for gentle, low-angle terrain, when speed is needed, or when equipment is in short supply. It also provides variable friction but may often require more than one Soldier on the brake strand to operate safely.

heading: MUNTER HITCH
text: The Munter hitch provides enough friction for a one-person load. The Munter hitch can be easily converted to a super Munter if more friction is desired. (See figure 12-14.) Note. Take care not to open the gate of a fully loaded carabiner. This could cause potential failure of the carabiner.

heading: MUNTER HITCH
text: The super Munter provides an enormous amount of friction; it is used for lowering only. In most circumstances, the super Munter provides more friction than needed. Therefore, its use is limited to when a single Soldier is lowering a heavy load.

heading: REDIRECTED BELAY DEVICE
text: A redirected belay device provides enough friction for up to two people and causes fewer twists in the rope than a Munter hitch. (See figure 12-15, page 318.)

heading: TECHNIQUES FOR CREATING HANDS-FREE BACKUP
text: Hands-free backups are an important component of lowering systems. They provide a critical element of safety when Soldiers are being lowered. There are two main options for creating hands-free backups: a friction hitch on the load strand or friction hitch on the brake strand.

heading: TECHNIQUES FOR CREATING HANDS-FREE BACKUP
text: Friction hitches on the load strand are used when the Soldier operating the lowering system does not have a harness on. (See figure 12-16.) This can be achieved by tying a prusik with the middle of a cordelette to the lowering rope, then clipping a fixed loop tied with the tails to the master point of the anchor. If the backup must be releasable, a releasable knot such as a Munter mule can be used instead of a fixed loop. Deciding which technique to use is based off the terrain and the situation. Soldiers must be careful to keep the prusik close to the Munter hitch during the lower so that it does not grab the lowering rope and stop the operation unintentionally. They must also ensure that the wraps of the prusik do not become loose. This could prevent the prusik from automatically gripping the rope if control of the lower is lost. This requires careful operation from a single rescuer or the assistance of a second Soldier to mind the prusik.

heading: TECHNIQUES FOR CREATING HANDS-FREE BACKUP
text: Friction hitches on the brake strand require the Soldier operating the lowering system to be wearing a harness. (See figure 12-17, page 320, and figure 12-18, page 321.) The preferred technique is an autoblock in a carabiner attached to the belay loop of the harness. This technique allows for Soldier flexibility in knot passes and load transfers for operation when moving away from the anchor toward the edge for better visibility and communication. Friction hitch backups on the brake strand are simpler to manage and preferred when a harness is available.

heading: Knot Pass Special Note
text:
- A wide array of situations require a knot pass. It is not feasible to cover them in-depth in this training circular.
- The conduct of a safe knot pass with a lowering system under tension can be complicated and technical. It should be conducted or overseen by a level 2 mountaineer.
- Seek qualified instruction to gain proficiency in the skills mentioned below.

heading: Knot Pass Special Note
text: Situations arise when a knot must be passed through the lowering system. This can occur when there is a damaged section of the rope that has been isolated with a knot or when ropes have been joined to lower longer distances. If passing a knot is necessary, it is usually conducted or overseen by a level 2 mountaineer. It is preferable to construct the lowering system to facilitate passing the knot prior to beginning the lower. (See figure 12-19.)

heading: Knot Pass Special Note
text: The simplest way to pass the knot occurs when the terrain and situation facilitate safely unweighting the lowering system temporarily. This is generally in low-angle terrain where most of the load is resting on the ground. This unweighting enables creates enough slack to place a new friction hitch or device behind the knot, and then remove original friction hitch or device from in front of the knot, so that lowering can continue.

heading: Knot Pass Special Note
text: If the terrain and weight of the load do not allow the lowering system to be safely unweighted, a weighted load transfer is required to pass the knot. These techniques are best learned with formal hands-on training and should only be conducted by level 2 and 3 mountaineers.

heading: Knot Pass Special Note
text: The construction and operation of lowering systems requires training, experience, and judgement. Soldiers and leaders must understand what they are doing and why they are doing it. Strive to use the right amount of friction for the terrain, situation, and load.

heading: Mountain Stream Crossing
text: In 480 BC, Persian King Xerxes constructed a pontoon bridge that spanned a mile and a quarter across the Hellespont. After a previous failure to take Greece, the king weighed the options of either finding alternate routes to the north that added months to his expedition or pinpoint potential water crossing locations for his army. Xerxes insisted on the fastest and most direct route across the Aegean inlet for his 300,000 men. While negotiating the linear obstacle involved massive resources and engineering, it would save precious time for his army to reach their objective.

heading: SECTION I - MOUNTAIN STREAM FUNDAMENTALS
text: A mountain stream crossing is essentially an approach to negotiating a potentially swift and cold waterway that Soldiers may encounter in the mountains. Learning to cross small streams forms a foundation of skills for personnel to manage larger streams and rivers, where consequences could be far more hazardous.

heading: SECTION I - MOUNTAIN STREAM FUNDAMENTALS
text: In an operation involving the crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to protect remaining personnel. This operation should be conducted economically and with minimal loss of momentum.

heading: SECTION I - MOUNTAIN STREAM FUNDAMENTALS
text: There are limits on the safe use of the techniques discussed in this chapter. Not all mountain rivers or streams will be fordable with these techniques. If a water obstacle is too wide, swift, or deep, an alternate route should be used. It may require using aircraft transport if engineer support is unavailable. Reconnaissance of questionable crossing sites is essential. This chapter covers the techniques for crossing mountain streams that have a depth generally not exceeding waist level.

heading: SECTION I - MOUNTAIN STREAM FUNDAMENTALS
text: Stream crossings should not be taken lightly. The force of flowing water may be extremely great and is most often underestimated. All rivers and streams are obstacles to movement. They should be treated as danger areas and avoided whenever possible. When rivers or streams must be crossed, there are many techniques that the small-unit leader may choose from, depending upon the type of stream, its width, speed of the current, and depth of the water. This activity should be rehearsed prior to execution in the operational environment.

heading: RECONNAISSANCE
text: Performing a site survey of potential crossing locations (map, photo, or aerial) may not always reveal that a water obstacle exists. In a swamp, for example, unfordable sloughs may not show on the map, and they may be concealed from aerial observation by a canopy of vegetation.

heading: RECONNAISSANCE
text: Site selection is extremely important once Soldiers determine that they must make a crossing. Elevated positions offer an optimal vantage point from which to analyze a large area of possibilities. This is sometimes better than a hundred close views from a riverbank. Select the site selection before the main body arrives and examine the site around a similar time of day that the crossing will be conducted.

heading: RECONNAISSANCE
text: A suitable crossing site should have specific characteristics. A river crossing site should limit exposure to observation, facilitate the installation team crossing (if necessary) or swimming with ropes, and minimize drowning hazards. Care must be taken to avoid an installation team crossing upstream of rapids, waterfalls, or fallen trees in the river. For dry features, such as gorges or ravines, the site should facilitate the installation team's descent and ascent crossing while minimizing any falling hazards that exist. While dry crossings are preferred to wet crossings for speed and safety factors, they can become locations for an enemy to place landmines and improvised explosive devices.

heading: RECONNAISSANCE
text: The time of day is an important factor. Recent precipitation or increased temperatures could cause water levels to rise as glaciers or snow-covered peaks begin to melt. Early morning crossings are preferred, as the cooler night temperatures usually reduce the melt from snow and ice. A morning crossing also allows clothing items to dry throughout the day. Whether a crossing is made in daylight or in darkness depends on the need for concealment, proficiency of troops, nature of the terrain, characteristics of the water obstacle, enemy disposition and capabilities (such as minefields on far banks), and the need for speed.

heading: RECONNAISSANCE
text: A crossing point should be chosen where the river widens. The sudden width of the channel normally yields a shallow depth. Avoid sharp turns in the river or a narrowing choke point in the river or stream since the water is likely to be deep and have a strong current on the outside of the bend for curves.

heading: RECONNAISSANCE
text: Many mountain streams, especially those fed by glacier runoff, contain sections with numerous braided channels. While often shallower than a main river, this changing landscape offers little in the way of cover and concealment of exposed personnel. Shoals, or partially submerged sandbars, can act like quicksand depending on the riverbed composition.

heading: RECONNAISSANCE
text: Riverbanks should be low enough to accommodate for easy entry and exit from the water. Banks that are tall and steep may require employing installations such as hasty rappels (see figure 11-11, page 293) or simple fixed ropes (see figure 11-2, page 278).

heading: RECONNAISSANCE
text: Logjams and other large obstructions present their own hazards. Floating debris, while often hung up in shallow spots, can potentially hit personnel in the water. Water flowing around logjams creates riverbed erosion and swift waters. If crossing upstream of logjams, ensure that Soldiers are far enough away to react and do not become entangled in branches beneath the water surface.

heading: RECONNAISSANCE
text: When possible, cross with ample overwatch in place for support and with an approach that offers minimal detection by enemy forces.

heading: PREPARATION OF TROOPS AND EQUIPMENT
text:
Special considerations should be taken for personnel and the items they carry for the mission. Water can weigh personnel down, as can the uniform posture when dealing with submerged equipment. Most of the preparation should happen long before entering the water, with only special considerations executed in a short halt prior. Preparation should include--
- Water-sensitive items. Wrap radios, binoculars, documents, maps, and any extra clothing in waterproof bags (trash bags also work well), if available. These bags also provide additional flotation, should Soldiers find themselves in deeper water than expected. Pack these dry clothing items on top, along with other necessary items (such as munitions, sensitive items, and machine gun tripods) quickly before getting into the water.
- Uniform. If the tactical situation permits, a crossing can be made with minimal clothing. Once on the far side, Soldiers can change into dry clothing. Normally, a complete uniform is worn. Unblouse boots and untuck shirts. Ensure all pockets are buttoned or closed. If water has a point of entry, ensure that it has an easy way to exit. Trapped water can weigh down personnel who may need to swim at a moment's notice. Socks and boot insoles can be removed and stowed. Once on the far bank, boots can be drained, and wet socks replaced.
- Load-carrying equipment and body armor. Unbuckle fighting load carrier or other modular equipment and be prepared to remove, if necessary. It is difficult to remove a buckled harness in the water during an emergency.
- Helmets can be removed and stowed, but if Soldiers fall in water with debris, the helmet protects their head from impacts.
- The rucksack should be worn well up on the shoulders and snug, so it does not flop around and cause imbalance. The waist and chest straps must be unbuckled so Soldiers can rid themselves of the rucksack if they are swept off their feet and must resort to swimming. Securing everything inside the pack will help if it needs to be discarded. It is easier to find one large pack than several smaller items.
- Weapons should be secured to the pack or slung over the shoulder.

heading: SECTION II - CROSSING TECHNIQUES
text: Several techniques and methods exist to successfully negotiate water obstacles. Variables that can influence the most optimal crossing style are water depth and speed, confidence around water and swimming proficiency, riverbed surface, daylight or night crossing, and resources available. When available, a dry crossing is always preferred.

heading: SECTION II - CROSSING TECHNIQUES
text: In this section, we will discuss three different variations that work well for mountain stream crossings: the individual crossing, team crossing, and belayed crossing.

heading: INDIVIDUAL CROSSINGS
text: Whenever possible, and when the degree of experience permits, streams should be forded individually for a speedier crossing. (See figure 13-1.) The average Soldier should be able to cross most streams with mild to moderate currents and water depths of not much more than knee-deep using proper techniques. An advantage to the individual crossing is that there is nothing to recover once Soldiers have performed the crossing. A disadvantage is the time of exposure for the individual and time invested for the element to negotiate the water obstacle.

heading: INDIVIDUAL CROSSINGS
text: The water depth at a suitable crossing site should be about knee height or below, and the water's speed should be mild to moderate. The velocity of the water and the presence of debris are used to determine the effect, if any, on the ford's condition. Currents are categorized as--? Swift (more than 1.5 meters [5 feet] per second). ? Moderate (1 to 1.5 meters [3 to 5 feet] per second). ? Slow (less than 1 meter [3 feet] per second).

heading: INDIVIDUAL CROSSINGS
text: Individuals should look upstream for obstacles, and pick up a good athletic stance, angling their body slightly perpendicular to the current. Adjust to a more parallel stance and lean upstream if the current is stronger.

heading: INDIVIDUAL CROSSINGS
text: Pick a location slightly downstream to the Soldier's position. Traveling at 90 degrees causes Soldiers to fight the current rather than work with the flow of water as much as possible. Always lead off with the downstream foot and take small steps while keeping the feet close to the ground. Avoid moving one foot before securing the other foot, and do not cross legs. This will decrease the likelihood of moving water throwing the Soldier off balance. Additionally, it will allow the Soldier to explore the riverbed for obstacles such as holes, rocks, shoals, or debris for optimal management. If a sizeable rock is found, Soldiers should always step on the upstream side of it. Water cresting the top and sides of rocks picks up speed, digging around and on the downstream side. The integrity of these rocks is unknown and could roll downstream at any time.

heading: INDIVIDUAL CROSSINGS
text: For added stability, using a third contact point is encouraged. A long stick or staff, ice axe, or tree limb could be used. By placing the end of the third point as upstream as possible, Soldiers can create a tripod, while exercising a body position described above to create a streamlined signature. The third point can be useful as a probe, searching for obstacles and depth.

heading: TEAM CROSSINGS
text: When the water level begins to reach thigh deep, or anytime the current is too swift for personnel to safely perform an individual crossing, a team crossing may be used. With each of these methods, have a leader call each step. One advantage to the team crossing is reduced exposure time for higher concentration of personnel, and there is no equipment to recover once Soldiers have performed the crossing. Disadvantages for all team crossings include a lack of interval for free movement and negotiation of riverbed makeup. Additionally, the close concentration of personnel makes them an easy target for direct or indirect enemy fires. The speed at which Soldiers can move fire teams and squads is that of a singular unit.

heading: CHAIN CROSSING
text: Two or more individuals cross arms with each other and lock their hands in front of themselves. (See figure 13-2.) The line formed faces the far bank. The largest individual should be on the upstream side of the line to break the current for the group, leaning upstream, into the current. The line formed will then move across the stream using the same principles as for individual crossings but with the added support of each other. The team still moves at a slight downstream angle, stepping off with the downstream foot in the lead. If the formation begins to degrade, avoid trying to excessively hang onto personnel who have lost control. In that scenario, the alternative of swimming is the safest.

heading: CHAIN CROSSING (CONGA VARIATION)
text: All personnel in the team face into the current, with their hands grasping clothing or gear just behind the shoulders of the person on their upstream side. The largest individual should be on the upstream side of the line to break the current for the group, leaning upstream, into the current. The line formed will then move across the stream using the same principles as for individual crossings but with the added support of each other. The team still moves at a slight downstream angle, stepping off with the downstream foot in the lead. If the formation begins to degrade, avoid trying to excessively hang onto personnel who have lost control. In that scenario, the alternative of swimming is the safest. (See figure 13-3.)

heading: WEDGE OR DIAMOND TEAM CROSSING
text: Three or more individuals form a wedge, with the largest individual upstream to break the current for the group. Cross arms behind the back or rucksack and grasp the upstream individual, developing structured support. Subsequent personnel widen the wedge with smaller personnel or casualties filling the middle portion. Maintain an interval that supports free movement without tripping on other personnel. The wedge formed has the added support of each other. Move across the stream using most of the same principles as for individual crossings but all facing upstream. The team still moves at a slight downstream angle, stepping off with the downstream foot in the lead stepping together as one unit. If the formation begins to degrade, avoid trying to excessively hang onto personnel who have lost control. The alternative of swimming is the safest in that scenario.

heading: BELAYED CROSSINGS
text: Certain conditions may require using a rope system to aid in crossing or even keep Soldiers from being exposed to water. When the depth begins to approach knee to waist level and the current is strong enough to potentially knock a Soldier off balance, then using a handline (one rope bridge with belay line) could be appropriate. This is the safest form of crossing simply because Soldiers have direct influence from either riverbank.

heading: BELAYED CROSSINGS
text: Crossing on a handline will still require everyone to enter the water. In a case where water and air temperature significantly increase the risk of hypothermia, artificial height or other considerations may need to be implemented. Joining two or more ropes will only be possible for a handline. The maximum distance a one-rope bridge is capable of spanning is about one-half to two-thirds the length of the rope in use.

heading: BELAYED CROSSINGS
text: An advantage of using a belayed crossing is the safety aspect. If individual control is lost, personnel can be pulled to the unloading bank by those belaying. Disadvantages of this technique are the time required for preparation, the number of available anchors, and the time dedicated to recovering the crossing site.

heading: ESTABLISHING THE FAR ANCHOR
text: Whether a handline or rope bridge (see chapter 16) is to be installed, someone must cross the stream with one end of the rope and anchor it on the far side. The most capable and strongest swimmer in the party should perform this duty. Swimmers should be belayed across for their own safety. The belay position should be placed as far above the crossing as possible. If the current is too strong for individuals, they will pendulum back to the near bank. Rescuers should be poised on the near bank at points where individuals will pendulum back, should they fail to reach the far bank. The initial crossing site should be free of obstacles that would snag the rope and prevent the pendulum from going back to the bank for an easy recovery.

heading: ESTABLISHING THE FAR ANCHOR
text: Individuals may attach the belay rope to their seat harness or a swami belt with a carabiner. They should never tie directly into the rope when being belayed for a stream crossing. If swimmers are swept away and become tangled, they must be able to release themselves quickly from the rope and swim to shore as best they can. Individuals may also choose to tie a fixed loop into the end of the belay rope and hang on to it, where they can immediately release it in an emergency.

heading: ESTABLISHING THE FAR ANCHOR
text: Anytime a crossing site must be used where swimmers may encounter problems getting to the far bank, they should wear a life vest or other personal flotation device (PFD). If swimmers must release the rope at any time, they will have to rely on their own water survival skills and swimming ability to get to shore. A PFD greatly increases personal safety. A PFD may also be used by the last individuals across, as they will release the rope from the anchor and be belayed across as the first individual.

heading: INSTALLATION OF A HANDLINE
text: If it is possible to use a rope high enough above the water to enable Soldiers to perform a dry crossing, then a rope bridge should be installed as such. If this is impossible, and the rope must be installed to assist in a wet crossing, then it should be installed as a handline. (See figure 13-4.)

heading: INSTALLATION OF A HANDLINE
text: The far anchor should be downstream from the near anchor so that the rope will run at an angle downstream from the near anchor, about 30 degrees to 45 degrees , rather than straight across the stream. Here again, it is easier to move with the current as opposed to directly across or against it.

heading: INSTALLATION OF A HANDLINE
text: The rope may be anchored immediately on the far bank, pulled tight, and anchored on the near bank. If a tighter rope is required, the handline may be installed with a transport tightening system. (See chapter 16.)

heading: INSTALLATION OF A HANDLINE
text: A second climbing rope is used as a belay. (See figure 13-5, page 330.) One end of the belay rope will be on the near bank and the other end on the far bank. It should be sent across with the strong swimmer. An appropriate knot is tied into the middle of the belay rope to form two fixed loops. Each loop is approximately 6-inches long. One loop is connected to the handline with a carabiner and individuals crossing connect one loop to themselves. The loops are short enough so individuals are always within arm's reach of the handline should they slip and let go. Individuals are belayed from both the near and far banks. If a mishap should occur, the individual can be retrieved from either shore, whichever appears easiest. The belay on the opposite shore can be released, allowing the individual to pendulum to the bank. It is important not to anchor or tie the belay rope to the belayer so that it may be released quickly if necessary.

heading: MOVEMENT
text: Crossing will always be performed on the downstream side of the handline, shuffling the feet with the downstream foot in the lead. Under most circumstances, the handline should be crossed by one person at a time. This keeps rope stretch and load on the anchors to a minimum. Hands should remain on the handline, on either side of the belay line tie-in point. Individuals should look upstream for obstacles, and pick up a good athletic stance, keeping their body slightly perpendicular to the current. Take small steps while keeping the feet close to the ground to avoid any unwanted influence forced onto the body by rushing water. Either rucksacks can be carried on the back the same way as for individual crossings, or they can be attached to the handline and pulled along behind the individual. If a large amount of equipment must be moved across the stream, especially heavier weapons, such as mortars, recoilless rifles, and so on, then a site should be selected to install a rope bridge. (See chapter 16.)

heading: MOVEMENT
text: Disadvantages to the belayed crossing include the large amount of time dedicated to site preparation, individual crossings, positioning of security teams, and lack of natural anchors on the riverbanks. Additionally, only one person is belayed at a single time, with personnel on each bank dedicated to the belay, leaving fewer personnel for security at any given time.

heading: SWIMMING
text:
Soldiers may find themselves alone and have no choice but to swim across, or they may find themselves suddenly plunged into a swift river or rapids. Soldiers should consider the following actions if Soldiers are in a situation that forces them to swim during a crossing:
- Immediately strip away gear or clothing that restricts free movement and increases their signature.
- Instead of fighting the current, work with the flow of water to get to a dry location downstream. It is often easier to negotiate hazards and see where Soldiers are going if they face downstream and fan the hands alongside the body to add buoyancy. They should use their hands to also fend off submerged rocks and position their feet as a shock absorber to shove off unseen or hidden obstacles.
- Keep the head above water to identify obstacles or debris that Soldiers may impact. Take the opportunity to breathe between breaks if waves begin to rise over Soldiers' heads.
- Avoid backwater eddies, bubbly water, water churning upwards, and converging currents. All these hazards have the potential to create unpredictable buoyancy and possibly undertow.
- If the shore is too difficult to reach, seek out the closest and safest spot, such as a sandbar, to get out of the water as quickly as possible. Hypothermia will set in quickly in colder waters.

heading: SECTION III - ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS AND HAZARDS
text: River and stream crossings present one of the most hazardous situations faced by military mountaineers. Substantial experience is necessary to properly evaluate and mitigate swift water hazards.

heading: SAFETY GUIDELINES FOR RIVER AND STREAM CROSSINGS
text:
The following safety procedures are minimum guidelines that should be followed when conducting a river or stream crossing:
- All weak swimmers should be identified before a crossing so that stronger swimmers may assist in crossing.
- Not every river or stream can be crossed safely. If it is possible, cross at a different time or place, use a different technique, or choose another route.
- The technique used is directly dependent upon water depth, speed of the current, stream bottom configuration, width of the stream, and individual experience.
- The safest methods of crossing in the water are always with the use of a handline or rope bridge.
- If the installation of a handline or rope bridge becomes too difficult at a given crossing site, then that site should be considered too hazardous and another site selected.
- A lookout should be posted 50 to 100 meters upstream to watch for any obstacles that may be carried downstream and interfere with the crossing.
- When conducting individual crossings (those without a handline or rope bridge), spotters or security should be posted downstream with poles or ropes prepared to throw, for assistance or rescue. Medical personnel should be prepared for cases of hypothermia.
- When the unit knows a rope installation is required for crossing, at least two life vests or other PFDs should be on hand. These PFDs provide additional safety for the strong swimmer who must establish the far anchor and the last individual across who retrieves the system.

heading: WATER SURFACE CLUES
text:
Observing and analyzing the top of the water can give military mountaineers an indication of what to expect beneath the surface. Water is not often clear enough to see all the hazards that could make the crossing difficult or have adverse effects on personnel attempting to cross. The following are common clues that can provide ideas of what lies beneath the surface.
- Riffles or ripples--if they are lined up, there are likely one or several rocks that form a line. In shallower water, it could mean a stable, rocky riverbed.
- Holes, souse holes, or keepers--depressions that can form from water moving around an obstacle. The rise and drop on the surface can be visibly seen. Avoid stepping here as these rises and drops could suction Soldiers' feet and debris can fall.
- Convergences and their depth--can increase the force the water has on someone attempting to cross.
- Eddy or back eddy--swirling of water and the reverse current created when water flows over or around an object or terrain. The consistency of a current is very unpredictable. This page intentionally left blank.

heading: Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue
text: Ten percent of the Earth's land mass is covered by glaciers. Glaciers are rivers of ice flowing under the influence of gravity, constantly restructuring the mountains around them. They often provide the best route in otherwise impassable terrain but can contain crevasses and other hazards that can cause injury, death, or compromise a unit's mission. Soldiers operating in glaciated terrain must understand these hazards, be well versed in the fundamentals of glacier travel, and be proficient with crevasse rescue techniques.

heading: SECTION I - GLACIER FUNDAMENTALS
text: Glaciers can be large enough to cover an entire continent. They may move only inches or hundreds of feet a year. Movement is caused by gravity, slippage over the bedrock, or by the internal flow in the ice. It is important for route planning and risk management to understand glacial features and understand how they form and move. Dismounted movement across glaciers is hazardous; however, glaciers often provide the easiest passage through more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces.

heading: GLACIERS
text: Glaciers form over time by the weight of accumulating snow compressing older layers of snow into ice. As snow accumulates, gravity takes over and the ice begins to move downhill. The weight of millions of pounds of ice makes a small film of water that acts as a lubricant, enabling it to slide.

heading: GLACIERS
text: The upper part of the glacier where the annual snow accumulation exceeds the melt is called the accumulation zone. Further down the glacier, the area where melt exceeds accumulation is an area called the ablation zone. The imaginary line between the two zones is known as the firn line.

heading: CLASSIFICATION
text: There are two classifications of glaciers: alpine glaciers and ice caps. Alpine glaciers form in high mountain bowls. Ice caps can cover thousands of square miles, such as those that cover Greenland and Antarctica.

heading: TYPES OF ALPINE GLACIERS
text:
The following are four types of glaciers:
- Valley glacier--resides and flows in a valley.
- Cirque glacier--forms and resides in a bowl. These do not advance beyond the bowl.
- Hanging glacier--these are a result of valley or cirque glaciers flowing and deteriorating. As the movement continues, portions separate and are sometimes left hanging on mountains, ridgelines, or cliffs.
- Piedmont glacier--formed by one or more valley glaciers, spreads out into a large area.

heading: GLACIER OBSTACLES
text: Units intending to use glaciers for travel routes must be familiar with their hazards and characteristics to ensure safe and efficient movement on them. Failure to identify and prepare for obstacles, which can come in the form of vertical terrain, can slow or prevent movement. Failure to identify and prepare for hazards can result in significant injury or loss of life.

heading: GLACIER OBSTACLES
text:
Glaciers contain many different features that can impede travel. (See figure 14-1.) They are--
- Bergschrund--the bergschrund is a giant crevasse found at the upper limit of glacier movement. It is formed where the moving glacier breaks away from the ice cap or snowfield above. The bergschrund can be high and overhanging and can create an obstacle to movement when moving from the valley floor onto the mountainsides.
- Crevasses--crevasses are cracks in the glacier caused by irregularities in the bedrock under the glacier as it moves and flows. Crevasses often form where the angle of the slope increases greatly, causing tension to split open the snow and ice. They also commonly form wherever the glacier makes a turn. They can be transverse, longitudinal, or lateral, depending on their orientation to the direction of the glacier's movement. Crevasses can be 200-feet deep but are normally 40- to 100-feet deep. Crevasses often hinder travel across glaciers. Snow often conceals crevasses, causing possible major falling hazards to Soldiers. Bypassing them can increase travel time and distance. Snow bridges that form over them can give way without warning. During the summer, the ice is less covered with snow and most crevasses are exposed. They can still be hazardous at night or in reduced visibility.
- Moat--the moat is a gap formed where the snow and ice are melted by the warmer rock along the edge of a glacier. The edge of a moat is often undercut. Depending on its size, the moat may be an obstacle to moving on or off the glacier.
- Icefalls--icefalls result from the flow of the glacier down a steep ridge. The ridge forces the ice up into a jumbled mass as the glacier flows over the rock. These present formidable obstacles and should be avoided.
- Serac--seracs are ice walls and towers that form in icefalls or on the lower edge of hanging glaciers. They are unstable and can fall unexpectedly. Travel below seracs or hanging glaciers should be avoided when possible.
- Nunatak--a nunatak is an island of bedrock that protrudes up through the glacier, creating an obstacle to glacial movement. It creates pressure in the ice that can form crevasses, seracs, and icefalls.
- Water hazards--streams that run on the surface and then disappear into a hole are called moulins. Moulins form when meltwater from the glacier finds a crevasse and moves to the ground below the ice. A fall into a moulin can carry a Soldier into the glacier and result in almost certain drowning. The glacial streams above this point must also be treated with respect. They are cold, can be deep, and the slick walls of their channels make them difficult to escape. In the summer, glacial thaw water can form troughs. This water can freeze at night, forming glacial swamps.
- Steep slopes--glaciers often include steep slopes that can create falling hazards, especially in firm snow conditions.
- Moraines--moraines are piles of rock and other debris that have either fallen onto the glacier or been pried loose by it as it moves along. There are four basic types:
- Lateral moraine--this is the rock debris along the valley wall.
- Medial moraine--formed when two glaciers come together, and the lateral moraines are forced out into the middle of the glacier.
- Terminal moraine--the rock debris at the toe of the glacier, which is being dredged up and pushed down the valley. A glacial stream often flows out from under the terminal moraine.
- Ground moraine--the rocks and debris under the glacier that can be exposed if the glacier stops and then begins to move again.
- Generally, the outside of a moraine wall is stable, but the side facing the glacier can be steep and loose and should be avoided. A moraine may be the only path, but it can be awkward and tiring due to the unstable rocks.

heading: SECTION II - FUNDAMENTALS OF GLACIAL TRAVEL
text: Glaciers are often good avenues of approach to the interior of a mountain range. Travel can be slow, and dangerous but easier than traveling on steep, loose, or exposed ridgelines. Glaciers are typically large open danger areas and should be treated as such during tactical operations. Units traveling on glaciers are subject to observation from all the surrounding high ground. A capable detachment may be required to provide an overwatch for the force traveling below.

heading: EQUIPMENT
text: A variety of specialized mountain equipment may be necessary for Soldiers traveling on glaciers. The following items are not a comprehensive list.

heading: ROPES
text: The use of ropes allows Soldiers to move in small rope teams and have some protection from crevasse falls. The type, length, and diameter of ropes selected for this purpose may vary depending upon how steep and heavily crevassed the glacier is. It is also determined by the number of Soldiers per rope team, and whether there are mutually supporting teams. Smaller diameter, lighter weight ropes are generally preferred.

heading: HARNESSES
text: Harnesses enable the individual connection to the rope team.

heading: ICE AXE AND CRAMPONS
text: Ice axes and crampons may be necessary for movement over snow or ice on a glacier but also provide the ability for a Soldier on a rope team to self-arrest to control, stop, and hold the fall of another climber. Ice axes may also be used for snow anchor construction for crevasse rescue.

heading: SKIS AND SNOWSHOES
text: In deep snow conditions, skis or snowshoes make movement more efficient. They also distribute weight over a greater area when crossing crevasses, which can reduce the likelihood of breaking through a hidden snow bridge. Snowshoes may be more practical than skis for roped glacier travel unless all members of a rope team are skilled skiers.

heading: PRUSIKS, SLINGS, AND CORDELETTES
text: Short prusik loops, slings, and cordelettes can be used for ascending a rope after a crevasse fall. They are used for belaying rope team members and creating anchors, load transfers, and hauling systems in crevasse rescue. Slings can be used to improvise a chest harness, if necessary, and can be useful to rig the rucksack for removal in the event of a fall. Each Soldier should carry a cordelette, a sling, and a short prusik.

heading: SNOW ANCHORS
text: Snow or ice anchors, such as pickets and ice screws, are often carried for use in crevasse rescue. In some snow conditions, ice axes, skis, and other items may be used to create an anchor.

heading: WANDS
text: Wands are sticks used as markers and can be utilized in many ways. They can be used to mark the location of known crevasses on frequently used routes or used in pairs forming an X to indicate danger. They can be used while setting up bivouac sites to mark the boundaries of safe areas. They are sometimes useful for whiteout navigation in heavily crevassed terrain. Wands can be made using 4-foot bamboo garden stakes with tape or flagging.

heading: OTHER GLACIAL GEAR
text:
The following items are typically carried and necessary for connecting to rope, connecting to prusiks, securing rucksacks or sleds, and facilitating crevasse rescue.
- 2 to 3 locking carabiners.
- 2 or more nonlocking carabiners.
- Belay or rappel device.
- Rescue pulley (optional).

heading: USE OF THE ROPE
text: A central question when considering travel over glaciers is whether to use a rope for fall protection. The hazard of hidden crevasses on a glacier varies considerably. In some circumstances, it may be preferable to travel unroped on crevassed glaciers; however, this is not typical. Deciding whether to rope together as a team depends upon the season, mode of travel, snow conditions, and the conditions of the glacier itself.

heading: USE OF THE ROPE
text: Traveling unroped is faster. It makes communication and dissemination of information easier; it can be done with untrained Soldiers. It eliminates the transition times required for tying in and preparing for roped travel. It also allows for movement in tactical formations and a better security posture.

heading: USE OF THE ROPE
text:
During the summer season, with clear skies and good visibility, crevasse risk on a glacier below the ablation zone is often negligible because crevasses can easily be seen as avoided due to lack of snow cover. In early season, or in low visibility, this same glacier could be quite dangerous. The decision of whether to rope up should not be taken lightly and should be made by only experienced mountaineers. Below is an example of various risk levels and guidance:
- Zero risk--bare glacier ice, free of snow and with few crevasses. There is no concern for hidden crevasses because all crevasses are visible. In periods of limited visibility, rope up. In good visibility, travel unroped. If there is a danger of a sliding fall that could lead to a crevasse fall, use the belayed climbing techniques covered in chapter 10.
- Low risk--hard, dense snow conditions in summer, or early morning frozen conditions after a cold night. Concern for hidden crevasses is low and snow bridges are strong. In limited visibility, rope up. In good visibility, travel unroped with caution and be alert for changing conditions. Have harnesses on and equipment available to make the transition to roped travel easier.
- Moderate risk--soft summer snow conditions. Breaking through a snow bridge or into a hidden crevasse is possible. Rope up.
- High risk--soft or weak snow on a glacier with many crevasses. Crevasses are hidden and snow bridges are weak. Breaking through snow bridges and falling into hidden crevasses is likely. Avoid travel, if possible. If travel is required, rope up and use cautious route finding.

heading: DETERMINING FALL HAZARD VERSUS CREVASSE HAZARD
text: In glaciated terrain, there can be both a risk of falling on steep ground as well as a risk of falling into crevasses. These risks are not managed in the same way. Crevasse hazard is best managed with good route finding and by keeping 8 to 10 meters of rope between Soldiers. Rope teams can usually stop crevasse falls because these occur on low-angled terrain without falling hazard. On flat terrain or soft snow, the arresting Soldiers are not typically at risk of sliding into the crevasse and are often able to stop the fall by slumping in the snow, rather than a full team self-arrest.

heading: DETERMINING FALL HAZARD VERSUS CREVASSE HAZARD
text: Falls on steep firm snow or an icy slope have almost no chance of being stopped by a rope team. Steep fall hazard is better managed by belaying Soldiers individually as described in chapter 10 or simul-climbing with protection placed for the team. It can be tempting to travel on steep slopes using crevasse fall protection techniques, but this is an illusion of safety. A fall can pull the entire rope team from the slope, often with fatal consequences.

heading: DETERMINING FALL HAZARD VERSUS CREVASSE HAZARD
text: Since these risks can change often from crevasse hazard to falling hazard and vice versa, changing strategies is important. The following paragraphs discuss using the rope for crevasse fall protection only.

heading: DETERMINING ROPE TEAM SIZE
text:
When using the rope, team size can be a difficult decision, and several factors must be considered. Smaller rope teams are faster and can move more efficiently than larger teams. Larger teams can easily arrest a fall and have more immediate resources to haul someone out of a crevasse. Training levels and overall unit size are also factors in determining team size. The following list describes advantages and disadvantages of various rope teams:
- Two-person teams--travel is faster and more efficient. However, in the event of crevasse fall, one Soldier must hold the fall. When not traveling with other rope teams nearby, that Soldier must also construct an anchor while holding the fallen Soldier, transfer the weight, and then conduct a rescue. For this reason, only use two-person teams when both team members are highly experienced. Requires approximately 60 meters of rope.
- Three-person teams--generally preferred for most glacier travel. Maintains a relatively low team size, while having two Soldiers to hold a fall and potentially haul the Soldier out. It is possible to have one untrained or minimally trained Soldier on this team when placed in the middle. End climbers must both have good route finding and crevasse detections skills and must be proficient with all crevasse rescue strategies. Requires 45 to 50 meters of rope.
- Four-person teams--travel is slower and less efficient, but the large team is more likely to hold a fall. May be preferred versus multiple two-person teams when there is more than one untrained or inexperienced Soldier. Requires 30 to 40 meters of rope.
- Teams of five or more--travel is slow and cumbersome. Obstacles slow the group even more with each additional Soldier. The entire team must slow down or wait as each member negotiates it. Rope management and communication between members become more difficult. Teams of five or more are not recommended but may be necessary in situations where there are many Soldiers without sufficient experience. Multiple ropes or sections of ropes may be necessary to ensure adequate spacing between Soldiers on rope teams of more than five.
- Mutually supporting teams--mutually supporting teams, such as two teams of three, (rather than one team of six), or a team of two and a team of three, (rather than one team of five), should be used when experience levels make it possible. Multiple teams allow one team to simply hold the fall and supporting teams to use their own rope and resources to conduct a crevasse rescue. This strategy can also decrease the amount of excess rescue rope that individual teams must carry.

heading: DETERMINING SPACING BETWEEN SOLDIERS
text:
It is best to have no more rope between Soldiers than necessary. Longer rope distance slows progress and makes it more difficult to communicate and coordinate movements. Smaller teams need slightly more spacing than larger teams. This distance needs to span crevasses so that only one Soldier is at risk at a time when crossing. Some general guidelines are given but spacing may need to be increased for exceptionally large crevasses.
- Two-person teams--10 to 12 meters.
- Three-person teams--8 to 10 meters.
- Four-person teams--7 to 9 meters.

heading: Two-Person Teams
text: In the event of a crevasse fall, each member of a two-person rope team must have enough spare rope available to reach fallen Soldiers and back to haul them out. (See figure 14-2.) This usually involves 60 meters or more of rope to have adequate spacing between Soldiers. With Soldiers spaced approximately 12-meters apart, they would each have 24 meters of spare rope to be used for rescue. A figure eight on a bight can be tied at 6 meters on each side of the rope's middle mark. These can be used as attachment points for team members and are each clipped into the harness with a locking carabiner and a nonlocking carabiner opposite and opposed. The remaining rope can be coiled and worn over the shoulder or placed into the rucksack. Soldiers must also tie several stopper knots on the rope connecting them. These additional knots aid in arresting a fall by catching in the lip of the crevasse and can often greatly reduce tension on the arresting climber, making it easier to construct an anchor. These are mandatory for two-person teams and can be either alpine butterfly knots or overhands on a bight. Since each knot takes up about 1 meter of rope, this length must be factored in as well.

heading: Three-Person Teams
text: For three-person teams, the rope is broken up into quarters. (See figure 14-3.) Each end Soldier carries enough extra rope to reach the middle Soldier. So, with 10 meters of spacing between people, each end Soldier will be carrying an additional 10 meters or more of rope each. Stopper knots are unnecessary in threeperson teams because there is generally sufficient holding power. A figure eight on a bight is tied and attached to the middle person's harness with a locking carabiner and nonlocking carabiner opposite and opposed. Each end Soldier measures approximately 10 meters out from the middle and attaches the same way with a figure eight on a bight. Remaining rope can be coiled and worn over the shoulder or stuffed in the rucksack.

heading: Four-Person Teams
text: Four-person teams can simply divide the rope into thirds and use the entire length. The end Soldiers tie into the ends of the rope and the middle Soldiers clip in as described for two- and three-person teams. If a longer rope is used and shorter spacing between Soldiers is desired, end climbers can coil and stow rope as described above.

heading: OTHER PREPARATIONS
text: Mountaineers often pre-place one or more prusiks on the rope. (See figure 14-4, page 340.) These can be used as part of a system to ascend a rope for self-rescue in a crevasse fall or for load transfer when rescuing another Soldier. Having at least one is useful for keeping slack out of the rope when grouping in one location to communicate or conduct other tasks. The prusik can be attached to the harness with a separate locking carabiner or the same locking carabiner used for the attachment to the rope.

heading: OTHER PREPARATIONS
text: A 120-cm sling (48 inches), or two 60-cm slings (24 inches) attached together, can be improvised quickly to construct a chest harness. To do this, pass the loop through both arms and behind the back, forming an X in the back, then connect the two bights in the front with a carabiner. This is only to be used after a crevasse fall to remain upright and make self-rescue easier. Chest harnesses are worn when a crevasse fall is likely.

heading: OTHER PREPARATIONS
text: Mountaineers can prepare the rucksack with a sling and carabiner so that in the event of a crevasse fall the Soldier can remove the rucksack immediately and clip to the rope to dangle below.

heading: OTHER PREPARATIONS
text: Snow anchors, wands, or other equipment should be distributed among the team.

heading: ROPE MANAGEMENT
text: The rope should be kept extended on a glacier. It should not have unnecessary slack or be taut. Excess slack will cause a Soldier to fall deeper into a crevasse, placing more force on other members of the team and increasing the difficulty of arresting the fall. The falling climber is more likely to hit something or become stuck or wedged.

heading: ROPE MANAGEMENT
text: A rope with the correct amount of tension lies on the snow with a gentle curve, out of the way of the feet. It can be helpful to hold the rope to the front when traveling downhill and to the rear when traveling uphill. Pace should be adjusted to maintain correct tension in the rope by feel, especially during stops and starts. The Soldier in the lead should set a pace that others can easily follow.

heading: ROPE MANAGEMENT
text: During sharp turns, the rope tends to go slack as the lead Soldier makes a change in the direction of travel, but then it becomes taut as the next Soldier approaches the turn. During turns, team members should adjust pace and keep appropriate tension. New tracks may need to be made outside the leader's footprints to do this.

heading: ROPE MANAGEMENT
text: As a rope team reaches a rest area or bivouac location, the rope must remain extended until the area has been probed for crevasses. Once it has been deemed safe, the lead member may belay team members into the area by pulling rope through the prusik, with ice axe in hand, ready to self-arrest. Soldiers in the rear may also belay themselves into the location in the same manner. When leaving the location, the same process happens in reverse. (See figure 14-5.)

heading: ROUTE FINDING AND CREVASSE DETECTIONS
text: Crevasse falls are extremely dangerous, even when traveling roped up with experienced Soldiers. Even when all Soldiers manage the rope well and the fall is stopped immediately, severe injuries can result. Ice axes, crampons, and collapsing snow bridges can cause injuries. Detection and avoidance are the primary skills needed to eliminate the need for crevasse rescue. On heavily crevassed glaciers, it is advisable to use an advanced party to scout and mark the safest route in advance of the main body. This can save hours of wandering, slow progress, and running into dead ends. Once relatively safe routes are established, it can reduce the skill and experience level required of the main body.

heading: INFORMATION GATHERING
text: Big picture views of the terrain can be very helpful. A maze of crevasses can be analyzed more easily from above than from within. It is a good idea to take digital photos whenever high ground provides a vantage point. Because glaciers move so slowly, crevasse patterns remain constant from year to year, making even old photographs useful for study. Intelligence products or online mapping resources (see appendix B) that contain satellite imagery can provide overhead views. These may contain imagery taken during the summer or late season and show the general trends and locations of dense crevasses that may be only partially filled in or have suspect snow bridges when traveling during winter and early season.

heading: TIMING
text: On snow covered and heavily crevassed glaciers, snow bridges are firmer at night or early in the morning. If stable, they can often provide more direct lines of travel. Warmer daytime temperatures can soften these snow bridges, increasing the likelihood of crevasse fall. This may require finding a longer alternative route.

heading: TIMING
text: Be cautious after snowstorms. Fresh snow can fill in and blend in what might otherwise be detectable crevasses.

heading: TIMING
text:
Seasonal timing is equally important. Although unit leaders may not have much say in the time of year they are required to travel on glaciers, a basic understanding of how seasonal changes affect surface conditions is important. Below are descriptions of typical conditions in the midlatitudes:
- Autumn--in late season conditions, most crevasses are clearly visible and snow bridges have melted out to their maximum extent. Travel is generally safest, as there is little risk of unexpected crevasse fall, but route finding can be difficult and require long detours and lengthy movement times around crevasse fields. In steeper terrain, firm conditions can make falling hazard a higher concern.
- Winter--early winter is especially hazardous. Unconsolidated snow hides crevasses but often does not effectively bridge them. Crevasses are more difficult to detect, and unexpected falls are more likely. In late winter, deeper snow conditions may provide more effective snow bridges. Increased snow loads may cause bridges to sag, making detection easier. Skis or snowshoes are often required.
- Spring--snowfall has reached its maximum depth, making glacier travel safest. Snow bridges are at their strongest and the snowpack strengthens from warmer weather. Skis or snowshoes are often required, but lines of travel are typically much more direct.
- Summer--early morning travel on firm snow surfaces makes travel easier, but snow bridges are beginning to weaken. As crevasses open, finding direct routes becomes challenging again. Seracs and icefalls also become more hazardous.

heading: TIMING
text: In some geographical regions further from the poles, these trends can be nearly opposite with surface conditions revolving strictly around dry and rainy seasons.

heading: ZONES OF TENSION AND COMPRESSION
text: Crevasses are formed by tension. Tension is created as glacier ice stretches over rolls in the terrain and where it stretches due to different rates of flow within the glacier. These crevasses form perpendicular to the direction of the stretch. Recognizing where this tension is likely to occur can help with predicting their likely locations when snow fills in or conceals them. Crevasses are more likely at the top of a roll, where the terrain gets steeper and drops away below it. They are also common near the edges of valley glaciers, where additional drag and friction occurs against the valley walls, and the center of the glacier is moving faster. These "marginal" crevasses point toward the center of the glacier at an angle. For this same reason, the centers of glaciers generally have fewer crevasses and are preferred travel routes.

heading: ZONES OF TENSION AND COMPRESSION
text: Compression zones occur where the underlying bedrock flattens out and where glacial ice slows down or piles up. Here, crevasses become narrow and eventually disappear. Glacial ice can also pile up in bowls and flat benches in the terrain and where glaciers flow together. These areas of compression can be relatively crevasse-free. Observing these zones and working to link them together are keys to good route finding.

heading: SURFACE CLUES
text:
Clues to locating crevasses below the surface of the snow can be subtle and difficult to recognize, but it is important for determining an appropriate crossing technique. It can also be just as important to recognize similar clues that do not indicate crevasses and to not waste time and effort on long detours.
- Sagging--snow covering larger crevasses gradually deforms and sags under its own weight. Early in the process, this may be barely noticeable, but later the outlines of the crevasse become more defined. Sometimes a slight change in sheen or texture can be observed. Other times, a slight change in color, from dust or windblown snow settling in a subtle depression, can be visible. These should be approached with caution. Snow is, however, an inherently uneven surface, so not every dip, groove, or color change represents a crevasse. In low visibility or flat light, these can be impossible to recognize.
- Nearby crevasses--since crevasses are often found in groups and tend to form parallel to one another, look for other crevasses, patterns, or depressions nearby that have similar orientation.
- Parallel cracks--in the case of larger crevasses, parallel thin cracks can sometimes form at the edges of a giant snow bridge. Although these can have the appearance of two narrow crevasses, they can be the boundaries of a single, giant snow bridge.

heading: PROBING
text: Snow probing in areas that look suspicious can be done using an ice axe. It can identify crevasses, determine its true lip, and investigate the extent, length, and width of a crevasse. To probe, the shaft of the axe is thrust into the snow a couple feet ahead of where one moves, looking for a noticeable reduction in resistance. If there is a sudden drop in resistance, there is likely a crevasse, but it can also be a soft snow layer. Probing requires experience to accurately interpret. The short length of an ice axe makes this difficult. Avalanche probes and ski poles with the basket removed are better choices, if available. Probing is also required for determining safe bivouac locations.

heading: CROSSING TECHNIQUES
text: There are a variety of options and techniques for crossing crevasses, and leaders must understand and be capable of incorporating any combination of them to adapt to the terrain. Rope teams should travel perpendicular to the direction of crevasses to reduce the risk of exposing more than one Soldier at a time. (See figure 14-6, page 344.)

heading: End Running
text: There is no guarantee as to the dependability of snow bridges. Sometimes it is preferable to cross at one end of a crevasse where its width narrows, rather than take a chance with a snow bridge. (See figure 14-7.) With large crevasses, this could lead to traveling a quarter of a mile or more to gain 30 feet of forward progress. In winter or spring, seasonal snow may still cover the narrow ends of a crevasse. What looks like the end of the crevasse might not be its actual end. This assessment can require some judgement. Make a wide swing, probe carefully, and cross at a right angle to the crevasse.

heading: Using a Snow Bridge
text: When end running is not practical, use snow bridges to cross. (See figure 14-8.) Always attempt to get a look at the crevasse from the side before committing to it, and probe when approaching the lip. The remaining Soldier in the team provides a moving belay by controlling the slack and remaining ready to self-arrest. Once the leader is across, the rest of the team must follow exactly in the leader's footsteps. At this point, the leader controls slack and remains prepared for self-arrest. Prusiks can be used here to manage slack in the rope during this process as well. If there is doubt as to one's ability to stop a fall, a fixed belay must be constructed with a snow or ice anchor.

heading: Jumping
text: Only conduct jumping when the gap is short. Running leaps requiring big push offs from suspect crevasse lips and falls can result in serious injury. Jumping should not be attempted unless there are no other options. Enough slack must be provided for the jumper to clear the crevasse without question. Be wary of catching a crampon and use common sense.

heading: Climbing into the Crevasse
text: Occasionally, it may be practical to climb down into a shallow crevasse and climb back out the other side. Standard belay techniques (see chapter 10) should be used. Be especially aware of bottoms that appear solid but are not.

heading: Echelon Formation
text: When it is impractical to travel perpendicular to existing crevasses and Soldiers must travel parallel, the echelon formation can be used. (See figure 14-9.) This keeps team members still to the rear but offset slightly to the side. This provides an alternative to following the leader's tracks in a single-file line. This should only be used on heavily crevassed sections where all crevasses are visible and there is very little risk of falling into a hidden one.

heading: SECTION III - CREVASSE RESCUE TECHNIQUES
text: Solid crevasse rescue skills are essential for elements traveling in glaciated terrain. While this may be impractical in circumstances involving large numbers of personnel, the ability to react appropriately to crevasse fall cannot be overlooked.

heading: CREVASSE FALL CONSIDERATIONS
text: Mutually supporting rope teams should have a minimum of one Soldier per team who is trained in crevasse rescue. This will ensure that rescue capability can always be provided, even when the more experienced member of another rope team is the one to fall in. Two trained Soldiers are necessary in rope teams traveling independently, away from supporting teams.

heading: CREVASSE FALL CONSIDERATIONS
text: Crevasse falls are rarely dramatic and sudden falls that rip team members off their feet and result in someone dangling down inside an abyss. In fact, most crevasse falls involve breaking through a snow bridge but falling no further than waste deep, and with minimal force exerted on team members. Despite this, Soldiers must be trained to deal with more severe falls and be able to adapt and adjust to a variety of circumstances. Options for crevasse rescue involve an abundance of variables. They depend largely upon the breakdown of rope teams, the number of Soldiers per rope, conditions of the glacier, and specific equipment carried. A comprehensive and detailed description of crevasse rescue techniques is well beyond the scope of this publication. Instead, the steps and decision process typically used for a three-person rope team are described below.

heading: STEPS TO TAKE FOR CREVASSE FALL
text: The following steps should be considered in the event of a crevasse fall with a three-person rope team.

heading: STOP THE FALL
text: Stop the fall immediately. Some falls may be barely noticeable, while others may require dropping into the self-arrest position in the opposite direction. Stopping falls on firm surfaces can be more difficult than soft ones. Once the fall is arrested, both rescuers should kick crampon points into the snow to establish a strong, stable position to prevent the victim from slipping any further. Communication can often be made with the victim at this point. In circumstances where Soldiers have only fallen a few feet or are stuck in the snow bridge, they may be able to climb out unassisted. If a Soldier is not able to quickly self-recover, then the following steps must be taken. (See figure 14-10, page 348.)

heading: CONSTRUCT AN ANCHOR AND TRANSFER THE LOAD
text: When another rope team is available, then they can construct an anchor and help the team transfer the load of the fallen Soldier onto it. (See figure 14-11.) Otherwise, the Soldier on the opposite end is usually the one to complete this step. End Soldiers slowly get out of the self-arrest, making sure that middle Soldiers can still hold the weight. End Soldiers establish an anchor (see chapter 9 for snow and ice anchors) below the middle climber and towards the crevasse. They attach a prusik to the loaded rope and clip it to the anchor with a locking carabiner. If there is limited distance between the middle climber and the crevasse lip, the anchor can be constructed above the middle climber. In this case, the slack rope itself, between the middle and end climber can be used to attach directly to the anchor.

heading: CONSTRUCT AN ANCHOR AND TRANSFER THE LOAD
text: Next, the end Soldiers get back into the self-arrest position to back up middle Soldiers as they transfer the weight of fallen Soldiers onto this prusik. Once pressure is relieved from middle Soldiers, it is common for them to continue backing up this anchor while the end climber improves it or constructs additional components. This anchor must be unquestionably strong, as it may be used to haul the Soldier out. The prusik should also be backed up with a suitable knot clipped to the anchor.

heading: COMMUNICATE WITH THE FALLEN CLIMBER AND MAKE A PLAN
text: To make a clear assessment and develop a plan, it is best to approach the edge of the crevasse where the fallen Soldier can be seen and heard. This can be done by one of the team members using a safety prusik attached to the unweighted portion of the rope. Exercise caution approaching the edge. Determination of what to do next will depend on how far down the climbers are, whether they sustained injuries, extent of any injuries, and characteristics of the terrain in and around the crevasse. The loaded rope can often become entrenched into the lip of the crevasse, complicating rescue options. This may be a good time to pad underneath the rope to prevent this from becoming worse with an ice axe shaft, foam pad, or rucksack slid underneath the rope as close to the edge as can be reached. This can take some work, and items used for padding should be anchored so that it cannot fall into the crevasse. Various options for rescue are described below.

heading: Self-Rescue
text: Self-rescue can be achieved by the fallen climber ascending the rope itself using a prusik ascent (see paragraphs 11-39 through 11-49, pages 282 through 284) or other techniques discussed in chapter 11 and is also shown in figure 14-10, page 348. When possible, this is often the easiest and fastest option. The prusik ascent prevents the fallen Soldier from becoming cold waiting for rescuers. Getting the weight of the rucksack off the body and onto the rope is also particularly helpful for staying upright. Assistance from team members may be required to surmount the crevasse lip. The method does not work if the fallen Soldier sustained significant injuries.

heading: Belay
text: Belays may be a fast, easy option when crampons and ice axes can be used to climb out of the hole, especially if or when the rope is too entrenched in the crevasse lip to prusik out. The remaining free end of the rope can be passed down to the fallen climber to tie into the harness with, while a team member above creates a belay at the anchor. Again, if the fallen Soldier is injured, this method may not be possible.

heading: Haul
text: If none of the above options are viable, a more complex solution of hauling the fallen climber out will be needed.

heading: HAULING
text: Hauling techniques used for MA described in chapter 12 may be used for hauling; however, there are circumstances specific to working with crevasses that must be considered.

heading: Direct Haul
text: This refers to hauling systems constructed on the fallen climber's weighted strand of rope. A common example is the 3:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-4, page 307.) This is constructed by untying the backup knot behind the prusik and using this remaining rope to construct the system. A disadvantage to the direct haul is that it does not work if the rope is entrenched in the crevasse lip. This method is also impractical if there are knots tied in the weighted rope to help hold the crevasse fall. (See figure 14-12.)

heading: Drop Loop
text: Drop loops refer to hauling systems that use a bight of rope sent down and attach to the fallen climber's harness, independent of the climber's weighted strand. (See figure 14-13.) An example is the 2:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-3, page 307.) This is often the preferred method because the crevasse lip can be padded prior to hauling and because the victim can often assist by pulling on the strand opposite the haul strand. Drop-loop hauls do require victims to clip the bight of rope into the harness, so in the case of an unconscious victim, this step may need to be done by first rappelling to them then re-ascending. Drop-loop systems can be performed using the remainder of the rope or by a separate rope team utilizing a different rope altogether. Progress must still be captured during the haul for safety. This may be done by pulling rope through the prusik on the original tensioned rope.

heading: SECTION IV - TRAINING
text: Even when mutually supporting rope teams are used, good route finding, and crevasse detection skills are critical. Every rope team must have at least one Soldier with solid crevasse rescue skills. Commanders cannot just hope for seasonally low-risk conditions, nor can they rely solely on advanced parties or recon teams to consistently find routes that are passable without the need for ropes. A lack of expertise can leave units with a large capability gap.

heading: SECTION IV - TRAINING
text: Training and experience in glacier travel are most productive when conducted on glaciers. Most glaciated terrain in the lower 48 states is in the Pacific Northwest. The high cost of travel and time commitments to access them make training plans difficult for units to execute. Most of those glaciers involve acquiring climbing permits. It can take the better part of a training day for the approach on foot to these higher elevations; any training would typically involve a bivouac. This makes it inconvenient even for units located at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington. Ambitious commanders, however, might utilize these or other glaciated terrain in Alaska, Europe, or elsewhere, to create training events that combine glacier experience with other aspects of mountain warfare.

heading: SECTION IV - TRAINING
text: In the absence of glaciated terrain, units can still conduct simulated training exercises focusing on the basic strategies for roping up and preparing individual and team equipment. Crevasse rescue skills can be rehearsed using short sections of steep terrain. This should be conducted in locations without serious falling hazard, and back-up ropes or belays should be considered while techniques are being learned. Having a few unit members with advanced level training will improve the quality and outcomes of this training.

heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation
text: A unit's capability to conduct mountain rescue and evacuation is a critical part of mountain operations. Swift and efficient rescue can mean the difference between success and failure of a mission or even the survival of a casualty. In mountainous terrain, even relatively minor injuries may require evacuation. The type of injury, distance to be moved, terrain, training level of the team, and litter capabilities determine the evacuation technique chosen. Air evacuation is preferred. However, the weather, tactical situation, or operational ceiling of the aircraft may make this impossible. Therefore, it is imperative that all personnel are trained in mountain evacuation techniques and are self-sufficient. Casualties should be triaged before evacuation. The most experienced medical personnel available perform triage (physician, physician's assistant, or medic).

heading: SECTION I - RESCUE OPERATIONS
text: Every commander should have a MEDEVAC plan before undertaking an operation. This plan should have dedicated assets (primary, alternate, contingency, and emergency) in place so as not to rely on a single evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes and gusting winds reduce the ability of fixed-wing or rotary-wing aircraft to assist in operations. Therefore, relying solely on aircraft or specialized equipment is a poor substitute for careful planning.

heading: SECTION I - RESCUE OPERATIONS
text: The two types of rescue operations encountered by units operating in mountainous environments are deliberate and improvised.

heading: DELIBERATE
text: Deliberate rescue is when the mission objective itself is a rescue operation, thus allowing time for focused planning and the use of specialized rescue specific equipment.

heading: IMPROVISED
text: Improvised rescue situations are encountered when a casualty is sustained during normal operations and conducting a rescue was not the intended objective. Even improvised rescue operations should be practiced and rehearsed to minimize the negative effects on mission capability. All operations should have a CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. These plans must be understood by all who may be involved in a potential rescue.

heading: PLANNING
text:
The rescue tasks must be identified by obtaining the following information:
- Number of casualties by precedence (urgent, priority, routine, convenience).
- Number of casualties by type (litter or ambulatory) and the nature of their injuries.
- Terrain features and with respect to the location of the casualties.
- Tactical situation.
- Any assets available to aid in security, rescue, treatment, and evacuation.
- If treatment can be provided at the scene or if the casualty requires movement to a safer location.
- Additional personnel or equipment required for the rescue operation.
- Any circumstances that may require specialized skills.
- Weather conditions.
- Difficulty of the terrain.
- Time available.

heading: PLANNING
text: Route selection when planning mountain CASEVAC often depends upon technical capabilities. In some cases, trained personnel and equipment available for low- or high-angle rescue may allow for safer, less physically demanding operations. A lack of these resources and capabilities may require traveling longer distances around steeper terrain, greatly increasing the burden on rescuers.

heading: CONSIDERATIONS
text: Time considerations can cause a leader to compromise planning stages or treatment (beyond first aid). Make a realistic estimate of time available as quickly as possible to determine the action time remaining. The key elements are the casualty's condition and ability to endure the environment. Time available is a balance between these conditions and the resources and personnel available.

heading: CONSIDERATIONS
text:
There are many additional considerations for the rescue team during deliberate rescue:
- Typically, team members must distribute and carry all equipment, including hot food and drinks, stoves, sleeping bags, bivouac equipment, warm clothes, ropes, and stretchers.
- Evacuation routes often require extensive preparation and can involve establishing anchor points, belays, fixed ropes, lowers, and raises.
