- Determine raw travel time--8.5 units are then multiplied by 60 minutes, yielding 510 minutes.
- Determine adjusted travel time--this movement involves significant ascent, and the method of travel is walking. Therefore, a modifier of 4 is used. Note. This example assumes the movement is in unrestrictive terrain.
- The raw travel time (510 minutes) is then divided by the modifier (4) to yield an actual projected leg time of 127.5 minutes (or 2 hours and 8 minutes). Record in appropriate box in chart.
- Determine approximate point arrival time--add the actual projected leg time (2 hours and 8 minutes) to the start time for the leg. Record in appropriate box in chart.

heading: FORMULA UNITS MODIFIERS
text:
Calculate travel time from point Y to point Z:
- Determine units--there are 600 meters of elevation loss (6 units) and a travel distance of 4 kilometers (4 units). Therefore, the total units for this leg are 10. Record in appropriate box in chart.
- Determine raw travel time--10 units are then multiplied by 60 minutes, yielding 600 minutes.
- Determine adjusted travel time--this movement involves a significant descent; the method of travel is walking. Therefore, a modifier of 6 is used. Note. This example assumes the movement is in unrestrictive terrain.
- The raw travel time (600 minutes) is then divided by the modifier (6) to yield an actual projected leg time of 100 minutes (or 1 hour and 40 minutes). Record in appropriate box in chart.
- Determine approximate point arrival time--add the actual projected leg time (1 hour and 40 minutes) to the start time for the leg. Record in appropriate box in chart.

heading: NORTHERN WARFARE TRAINING CENTER METHOD
text:
This technique was developed specifically for military mountaineers:
- 4 kilometers per hour flat terrain. 2 to 3 for elevation.
- 1 hour per 300 meters (1,000 feet) elevation gain.
- 1 hour per 400 to 600 meters (1,600 feet) elevation loss.
- + 10 minutes per kilometer for every 20 pounds over 50 pounds.

heading: SECTION I - SAFETY STANDARDS
text: The UIAA Safety Commission develops and maintains safety standards for mountaineering equipment. They are an independent safety commission recognized by 60 manufacturers and certify over 1,800 mountaineering products sold worldwide. Manufacturers must meet the standards set forth by the UIAA to be certified.

heading: NUMBER LISTS
text: There are currently three specialized mountaineering kits available in the Army inventory. They are the HAMK, ACTK, and SIMK. Individual components and quantities in these kits continue to change, as they are developed to fit the needs of the Army.

heading: HIGH-ANGLE MOUNTAINEERING KIT
text: The HAMK is the Army's general-purpose mountaineering kit. It is designed to outfit a platoon with the equipment necessary to negotiate up to 3rd-class terrain with some level 1 trained Soldiers acting as trainers and leaders. This kit can enable a platoon to negotiate 4th-class terrain if used in conjunction with the ACTK and level 2 trained Soldiers establishing rope systems and acting as trainers and leaders. heading: *advanced military mountaineer
text: A Soldier who has graduated from the Basic Military Mountaineer Course and at least one of the Advanced Military Mountaineer courses. An advanced military mountaineer has been trained in advanced mountaineering techniques and is also known as a level 2 mountaineer.

heading: *aid climbing
text: Climbing technique in which standing on or pulling oneself up via devices attached to fixed or placed protection is used to make upward progress.

heading: *assault climber
text: A role assigned to a Soldier or team during tactical operations who is responsible for the location and establishment of technical routes in class 3 or higher terrain; ideally, a level 2 mountaineer.

heading: *basic military mountaineer
text: A Soldier who graduated from the Basic Military Mountaineer Course. Basic military mountaineers have been trained in basic mountaineering techniques, such as fundamental mobility skills necessary to move safely and efficiently in mountainous terrain, and are also known as level 1 military mountaineers.

heading: *belay
text: A system of using a rope as a backup in steep terrain to arrest a Soldier's fall should one occur.

heading: *bolt
text: A type of rock protection or anchoring component comprised of an expansion bolt or glue-in shaft attached to a hanger to which a carabiner can be attached.

heading: *brake strand
text: The strand of a rope system that controls the rate at which a load is lowered or a rappeller descends.

heading: carabiner
text: A D-shaped or oval-shaped metal link, with one spring-hinged side, that is used in mountaineering as a connector between soft materials and to capture a freely running rope.

heading: *cold-weather injury
text: Any preventable injury resulting from exposure to cold environmental conditions.

heading: *coil
text: A secure configuration of rope that allows for easy transport without tangling.

heading: couloir
text: Narrow snow- or ice-filled gully.

heading: dynamic rope
text: Kernmantle rope designed to stretch and absorb force, primarily used to protect climbers from fall injuries.

heading: fall protection
text: Any anchor clipped to a running rope used in belay systems that limits the distance a roped climber falls, should a fall occur.

heading: friction hitch
text: A type of hitch tied with webbing or cordage around a rope that can be moved easily while no force is applied to it but cinches and becomes fixed when tensioned.

heading: guidebook
text: A publication containing detailed climbing routes and approach route information.

heading: gully
text: A channel caused by erosion, especially by water running down a slope; it is generally narrower and steeper than a draw.

heading: hands-free backup
text: A rigging technique, involving friction hitches or mechanical devices that prevent a load from falling should control of a brake strand be lost.

heading: hauling system
text: A technical rope system used to move a load up steep or vertical terrain comprised of rigging that generates increased mechanical advantage and captures progress.

heading: high-strength tie off
text: A single-point anchoring method that retains maximum installation rope strength and releasability, using multiple-round turns around the anchor object to create friction, and securing the end back to itself ensuring no force is applied to any component knots or carabiners.

heading: installation rope
text: The primary load-bearing rope or strand in a rope system.

heading: kernmantle rope
text: A rope constructed with a load-bearing core of twisted synthetic fibers and a protective outer sheath of interwoven synthetic fibers.

heading: knot
text: The fixed portion of a rope that has been manipulated around itself, another object, or both during the process of being tied for some purpose. Sometimes referred to as a "hard knot" since its condition will remain intact until actively untied.

heading: *lead climbing
text: Climbing a route while attached to the end of a rope to place devices in rock, ice, or snow for fall protection with a belayer located below.

heading: *lead climber
text: The first climber to negotiate a route, for whom a top belay is not possible, and who assumes the most risk of injury in a fall.

heading: *load management
text: The act or strategy of planning and packing loads to reduce negative impacts on Soldier physical performance.

heading: *lowering system
text: A technical rope system used to move a load down steep or vertical terrain in a controlled fashion using friction hitches or mechanical devices.

heading: *master military mountaineer
text: A Soldier extensively trained and experienced with mountaineering techniques who the commander appoints to serve as a subject matter expert. Master military mountaineers are graduates of the Basic Military Mountaineer Course and Advanced Military Mountaineer Course. They possess all the skills of the advanced military mountaineer and have extensive practical experience in a variety of mountain environments in both winter and summer conditions.

heading: *mechanical advantage
text: Reduction in the force required to move a load, which comes at the cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage.

heading: multipoint anchor
text: More than one fixed object joined with technical rigging to form an anchor system capable of suspending the weight or arresting the fall of an attached load.

heading: natural anchor
text: A natural fixed object (such as a tree, rock formation, or ice formation) to which a rope system can be secured, and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load.

heading: pitch
text: A section of a climb that comprises the distance between two belay stations, which can be up to a standard rope length (60 meters).

heading: prolonged field care
text: The continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care. (JP 4-02)

heading: redundancy (in rigging)
text: The condition in which a rope system will not fail as the result of any single component of the system failing.

heading: safety knot
text: A backup knot tied to prevent a primary knot from slipping loose.

heading: scrambling
text: The act of moving over difficult or broken terrain, characterized by using mostly walking techniques but requires some use of the hands for balance or other specific climbing techniques.

heading: self-equalizing anchor
text: A multipoint anchor comprised of adjustable strands from each anchor component to a shared attachment point that allows for maximum load sharing even when direction of pull changes during use.

heading: *simul-climbing
text: A belay technique involving two Soldiers climbing simultaneously while attached to the ends of a rope which runs through the fall protection.

heading: snowpack
text: The entire mass of snow covering a given area of terrain.

heading: static rope
text: Kernmantle rope designed for minimal stretch under load, primarily used for hauling, lowering, and anchor systems construction.

heading: *technical route
text: A route through steep or broken mountainous terrain that presents significant risk of fall injury and requires special movement techniques or ropes to ensure adequate safety for Soldiers moving through it.

heading: *vertical danger area
text: Steep terrain that significantly restricts a unit's ability to maneuver, thereby putting the unit at significant tactical disadvantage should enemy contact be made while moving through the VDA. This page intentionally left blank.
